threads.subject: (Non)-accompanying dependents / proof of citizenship-REP-2017-1800
threads.question:
From ### Good morning,
Amongst fellow RCICs we have been discussing how to proceed on a spousal sponsorship when there is a child who may be eligible for Canadian citizenship.
Specifically:
1. Is the child eligible for urgent processing of their Proof of Citizenship application due to the concurrent spousal sponsorship of their parent?
2. Once we've filed their Proof of Citizenship application and included that proof in the Spousal Sponsorship application, how do we indicate on the IMM0008 and otherwise that the child will be accompanying if they AREN'T deemed a citizen? Ie. should they be declared as non-accompanying or accompanying, and when?
3. Since the process ing for Proof of Citizenship is currently much longer than Spousal Sponsorship, does this cause a delay in processing? Ie. will the Spousal Sponsorship be put on hold until the decision on the Proof of Citizenship? How can we ensure that the parent and child can travel together or stay together in Canada?
Thank you for your time and attention.
With kind regards,
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Dear Ms.
Apologies for the delay in responding to your enquiry.
A spousal sponsorship does not result in automatic urgent processing for a Proof of Citizenship application. If you are submitting a spousal sponsorship application for the parent of a child who has applied for a proof of citizenship, you should ensure that the child in question is listed on the applicant's Family Information Form (which all applicants are required to fill out, and on which all children must be listed). The form is found here: Additional Family Information [IMM 5406].
We suggest you also include a short letter of explanation indicating that an application for proof of citizenship has been submitted for a child who will be accompanying the primary applicant parent to Canada, and attach evidence of this proof application to that letter. This will provide the information that the visa officer processing the primary applicant's application needs, to look into the status of the proof application and take any necessary next steps in processing. Where appropriate, this may involve coordination with the office which is processing the proof application.
We trust this responds to your enquiry.
Regards
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Les demandeurs peuvent répondre «non» à la question 9C s'ils ne comptent pas de temps pour des travaux du gouvernement à l'extérieur du Canada, tel que spécifié ci-dessus et n'auront pas à remplir le formulaire CIT0177. threads.subject: Work permit-LMIA EXEMPTION-Date of start to work-REP-2018-0013
threads.question:
Dear Officer, We have applied for LMIA Exemption for a client and have received an approval. The date of start initially was from April 28, 2018, and been submitted accordingly but now the foreign worker has to be in Canada on April 21 for a race.
How can we amend and correct it?
I look forward to hearing from you
Thank you
Sincerely
threads.answer:
Good day,
Question
We have applied for LMIA Exemption for a client and have received an approval. The date of start initially was from April 28, 2018, and been submitted accordingly but now the foreign worker has to be in Canada on April 21 for a race.
How can we amend and correct it?
Answer
While it is important that the information in the offer of employment be accurate, IRCC understands that the foreign national or the employer may not have control over when the foreign national can actually travel to Canada. The start date indicated in the offer of employment can be a best estimate. Therefore, it is not necessary to withdraw the current (yet-unused) offer and submit a new one with the more accurate start date indicated. However, if the foreign national is unable to arrive in Canada until well beyond the expected start date, we recommend that the offer be withdrawn and a new one submitted with more accurate information.
Procedure for requesting a withdrawal of an offer of employment
If the foreign worker has not arrived to Canada yet, AND/OR has not applied for a work permit application yet, the Offer of Employment that you submitted to us is only 'pending' in our system. In other words, it has not been 'matched' to a work permit application yet, therefore, you are able to go into your Employer Portal account and request to 'withdraw' that Offer of Employment and create a new one that indicates the correct work start date. Note that the withdrawal request will trigger a refund of the initial compliance fee paid, back to you credit card.
If you don't see "Withdraw application" next to your offer, it has most likely been matched to the temporary worker's work permit application. The work permit application will be in progress or has already been finalized. In this case, you won't be able to withdraw your offer using the portal.
If you still want to withdraw the offer, email us. Explain that you want to withdraw the offer and include: the offer of employment number the reason you want to withdraw the offer
Withdrawing an offer that has already been matched will result in the refusal of the work permit application.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Questions on Misrpresentation-REP-2017-2226
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam: I am seeking some clarification on the misrepresentation provisions of s.40 IRPA. An applicant, a past PR, innocently forgot to mention a very old Canadian criminal conviction on a TRV application was refused the TRV for " misrepresentation". The refusal letter does not mention anything about a 5 year ban or inadmissibility of 5 years. As such, is every misrepresentation automatically a 5 year ban?
Second, the applicant is now in process of obtaining a Canadian pardon. Once he obtain the pardon, can he re- apply for the TRV even if the 5 years have not yet elapsed?
Thank you.
mmigration, Refugees
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
[mailto: ] ### Good afternoon,
Thank you for consulting with the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
On November 21, 2014, the Governor in Council approved changes to the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and the Immigration Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), bringing into force amendments relating to the consequences for misrepresentation.
Previously, the consequence for misrepresentation was a two-year period of inadmissibility. With the changes described on November 21, 2014, the consequence is now a five-year period of inadmissibility and a ban on applying for permanent residence for the same period of time (five years). The period of inadmissibility (five years) begins on the date of the refusal letter for overseas applicants and begins once the the removal order is enforced for in-Canada applicants. It is important to check in with the Canada Border Services Agency prior to departing Canada to ensure the removal order is enforced and recorded as such.
The ban does not apply to applications for temporary residence; the procedures for inadmissible persons applying for temporary residence remain the same (i.e., if the person is inadmissible, they may be considered for a temporary resident permit (TRP) where warranted).
The Parole Board of Canada has the authority to grant and or issue a record suspension (formerly known as “pardons") who have been convicted in Canada of an offence under an Act of Parliament. The Immigration Refugee Citizenship Canada officers do not counsel applicants about record suspensions. Only once a record suspension is issued to the applicant will the IRCC officer review the totality of the information before them in order to take a fulsome decision on the application for temporary or permanent residency.
We trust that this information will be useful to you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Signatures for Forms-REP-2018-0017
threads.question:
Dear sir or madam,
We are in the process of submitting an Overseas Sponsorship Application as the authorized representatives of a couple. We would like clarification about the following:
1. Can printed copies of signed forms be provided or will only originally signed forms be accepted?
2. Are forms considered stale dated after three (3) weeks or three (3) months of their signature?
3. What is the time threshold for old versions of forms to be accepted for processing after a new version has been released?
Thank you for your time and attention, and Happy New Year.
Kind regards,
threads.answer:
Thank-you for your enquiry.
1. Can printed copies of signed forms be provided or will only originally signed forms be accepted?
Printed copies of signed forms will be accepted, as original signatures are not required when you submit applications. Faxed or scanned signatures are also accepted within the application package sent to the Case Processing Centre in Mississauga. However, (IRCC) reserves the right to request documents with an original signature at any time during the processing of an application.
2. Are forms considered stale dated after three (3) weeks or three (3) months of their signature?
Forms are considered stale dated after three (3) months of their signature and when it is received 91 days after the signature date indicated on the form. For more information please visit the following link: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/service/rep/complete.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/service/rep/complete.asp)
3. What is the time threshold for old versions of forms to be accepted for processing after a new version has been released?
The time threshold for old versions of forms being accepted for processing after a new version has been released varies, depending on the type of application. Generally, for applications made using an old form, staff receiving the application will review for completeness only and IRCC would be flexible where "old" forms were mistakenly submitted (i.e. we would go back and ask the applicant for additional information).
We trust this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

2. Parent or child had a permanent residence application that was either pending on May 3, 2017 or was received on or after May 3, 2017 and before October 24, 2017 (the child must have been previously identified as "additional family" on their parent's application);
3. Child is not a spouse/common-law partner; and, 4. Child is not otherwise inadmissible.

The IRCC web form request must be submitted by January 31, 2018.

threads.subject: Common-law/Marriage-REP-2017-2313
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam:
The client was previously married in Pakistan and processed a divorce from his first wife, there was an error in his divorce
paperwork and his new marriage was finalized prior to his divorce effective date.
The couple have lived together in Pakistan, in a monogamous relationship since June 2015. Despite being married, would they be eligible under the common law stream.
Kind regards
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your question.
In this scenario outlined below, one person is legally married however is now living with a different partner for the past 18 months. The couple currently cohabiting may be considered common-law partners provided the marriage has broken down and they have lived separate and apart from their spouse during which time they must have cohabited in a conjugal relationship with the common-law partner for a period of at least one year. Cohabitation with a common-law partner can only be considered to have started once a physical separation from the spouse has occurred. A common-law relationship cannot be legally established if one or both parties continue to maintain a conjugal relationship with a person to whom they remain legally married.
When the sponsor is legally married to someone else, there must be sufficient evidence that there is a separation and the separated partner is no longer cohabiting with the legal spouse. The subsequent marriage that took place, while the first marriage is still legally binding, is not considered to be a legal marriage by IRCC. A common-law or conjugal partner relationship cannot be established with more than one person at the same time. Applicants must be truthful and self-identify their marital status within an application. If there is any change during the processing of the application, applicants are obliged to inform the Department of these aspects of their life change prior to the finalization of their case, including their marital status.
Applicants should provide the Statutory Declaration of Common-Law Union (IMM 5409), used in a spousal sponsorship application where the applicants are not married. A common-law couple must have lived together for at least one year, and also have intermingled financial or other affairs. In addition to submitting this form with the application, the applicants should include as many pieces of evidence to show that they are in a committed, marriage-like relationship. When information provided in the Sponsorship Evaluation and Relationship Questionnaire (IMM5532) is insufficient, an officer may request additional evidence.
For more information on documentation to prove a common-law relationship please see the following link: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=347&top=14](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=347&top=14)
Thank you,

threads.subject: bridging work permit-REP-2018-0071
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
If an applicant is working based on a bridging work permit issued on the basis of the PR application. If her PR application is refused, can she still work? Please advise.

mmigration, Refugees
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good morning,
Question: If an applicant is working based on a bridging work permit issued on the basis of the PR application. If her PR application is refused, can she still work? Answer: As you are aware, an individual who meets program eligibility requirements in their application for permanent residence under certain economic classes is eligible for a bridging open work permit pursuant to s.205(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. Please see our website for full details: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-) citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign- workers/provincial-nominees-permanent-resident-applicants/bridging-open-work-permits.html.
Once an individual has been issued a bridging open work permit, there is a limited set of circumstances that would cause the work permit to become invalidated. S.209 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations reads as follows: Invalidity 209 A work permit becomes invalid when it expires or when a removal order that is made against the permit holder becomes enforceable.
As such, unless and until the work permit expires or a removal order made against an individual becomes enforceable, the work permit remains valid and, should the individual continue to meet the conditions imposed by the work permit, they would be able to continue working. We trust that the above has been helpful in answering your question.
Sincerely,

FW: IMP-Work Permit for Spouse under C41-REP-2018-0010
Question: We wish to clarify that if the Principal Foreign Worker holds a Working Holiday Work Permit, the spouse of the Principal Foreign Worker can apply for a C41 open spousal work permit
Answer:
The spouse or common-law partner may apply for a work permit under the "Spouses or common-law partner of skilled workers" (i.e., C-41 exemption) if the principle foreign worker holds permit that is valid for a period of at least six months, •is in an occupation at the NOC O, A, B level, and physically resides or plans to physically reside in Canada while working.
If the principle foreign worker holds an open work permit, the onus is on the spouse or common-law applicant to demonstrate that the principle foreign worker is in an occupation at the NOC O, A, B level. The spouse or common-law
partner should provide information about the principle applicant's employment by attaching supporting documents
including:
a letter from the principal foreign worker's current employer confirming employment or a copy of their employment offer or contract; and

threads.subject: Query re document requirements for official and translated documents, specifically citizenship certificate
threads.question:
Dear Sir or Madam,
I have some related questions about the requirements to submit documents from Sri Lanka, given some of the quirks of how they issue documents and the availability of “official" translations. If it differs between types of application, I am specifically interested in citizenship certificate applications for children born overseas to previously-naturalized Canadian citizens, but the issue comes up for other applications as well.
1. In Sri Lanka, birth (death, marriage, etc) registrations are entered into a book. The closest thing to an “original" document which an individual can obtain is a certified extract from the registry, which usually takes the form of a print-out or photocopy bearing original stamps from the local government authority confirming that it is an extract of the registration. The wording of the stamps is similar to that for a certified copy, for example: "Appl. No. XXX, I do hereby certify that the foregoing is a true copy of the Marriage / Birth / Death registration entry filed at this office" followed by the official's credentials.
a. Would this be considered an “original", of which a properly-executed certified copy could be submitted?; or
b. If IRCC would consider this a “certified copy", rather than an original (the original being a large bound book somewhere), would the wording of the certification set out above suffice?
2.The instructions for a translated document require (1) the translation; (2) the affidavit of translation and/or proof that the translator is accredited in Canada; and (3) a certified true copy. Does the certified true copy need to be certified by the same person or, for example, could the certified true copy be sent from abroad and the translation done in Canada by an accredited translator, or could the translation be done from a photocopy as long as this was clearly indicated?
3. As English is an officially-recognized language in Sri Lanka, the government Department of Registrar
General will provide official translations of birth (etc) certificates. Are these acceptable translations or would an additional translation be required? They are stamped to indicate that they were translated by a
L'information divulguée en vertu de la loi sur l’accès àlinformatio government translator and what that person's name it, etc, and again they are issued by the government itself.
I look forward to your response. Thank you for your kind attention to this matter.
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
applications-REP-2018-0021
Good morning,
Thank you for your inquiry.
There are many countries in the world with non-computerized birth records of the type you describe. This means the only true 'original' is housed at a civil registry, and the birth certificate issued to the client is a copy of that document. That copy is generally 'legalized' in some way, possibly the issuing authority or possibly by another government department, who place original stamps, seals and/or signatures and dates directly on the client's copy. For many countries, including Sri Lanka, that department is the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. IRCC is aware of and generally accepts this type of document as a 'primary' document issued by the civil registry and therefore regards it as the applicant's 'original' birth certificate.
With regard to translation, the translator generally needs to be provided with the original birth certificate because of IRCC's requirement that a translation be accompanied by an affidavit in which the translator swears before an official that that the contents of the translation are a true representation of the contents of the original document. Very often, after creating the translation, professional translators will create a certified copy of the original birth certificate and bind it to their translation (and/or possibly add a seal or other mark to it). By creating their own certified copy, translators can ensure that the client does not provide IRCC with a copy of a different foreign language document that the client falsely represents as the birth certificate that was translated.
Certified professional translators within Canada do not need to provide an affidavit, but their attestation will normally indicate whether or not they were reviewing an original, a certified copy, or a photocopy. A certified translator in Canada could potentially translate a certified copy, but in that case the translator would need to add a seal or mark to that certified copy to verify to IRCC that it was the document used to prepare the translation. However, if the same translator was provided with a photocopy only and he verified it in the same way, the paperwork might be rejected by IRCC if the validity of the source document was in doubt.
In many countries, birth certificates are issued in bi-lingual or even multi-lingual formats, and if one of the languages reflected on that document is English or French, no translation is required. Similarly, in many countries, civil registries will issue a birth certificate in the official language of that country, as well as a separate document in English (or in some countries, in French). While some of these registry-issued documents are marked as 'translations', IRCC views them as 'primary' documents and not as translations, and it is expected that the standard 'legalizations' by the appropriate government department will appear on the English version document as well. Therefore, no additional attestations by the
migration, Refugees mmigration, Réfugiés
Inmn government translator are required, and no sworn affidavit needs to accompany the English document.
We hope this information proves helpful.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Question: Today, I'd like to know what the "case type" codes on work permits refer to. Answer: The case type codes listed on work permits, and in fact on all permits issued by IRCC, are used for statistical purposes on IRCC's end. Officers enter the case type depending upon the type of work permit being issued. The case types specify the permit or document according to broad categories, such as Officials, Seasonal workers, those under application for permanent residence, those who also hold a study permit, etc. For example, the "usual" case type is 20, and would also be used for Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) - exempt work permits where an offer of employment was not submitted through the Employer Portal, whereas cases of LMIA-exempt work permits where an offer of employment was submitted through the Employer Portal would be case type 52. threads.subject: question about subsidized housing-is it "social assistance"? - REP-2018-0138
threads.question:
Dear Immigration Representatives,
Can you please advise whether living in subsidized housing amounts to “receipt of social assistance” for the purposes of sponsor eligibility under R133(1)(k)?
Thank you in advance.
I am a full member in good standing with the Law Society of Alberta, member ID #
Yours truly,
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Thank-you for your enquiry.
Does living in subsidized housing amount to "receipt of social assistance" for the purposes of sponsor eligibility under R133(1)(k)?
Please be advised that officers processing family class sponsorship applications do not treat subsidized housing as social assistance. Notwithstanding that "shelter" is included among the list of basic living requirements described in Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations R133(1)(k), subsidized housing is not considered to be social assistance in the context of
sponsorship undertakings and the enforcement of a sponsor's obligations.
There are a number of reasons why subsidized housing is not considered to be social assistance, including, but not limited to: it is not an entitlement program; it does not provide income assistance directly to those who receive it; it is allocated according to an established formula linked to availability of housing units; and, it may be administered municipally, outside
of provincial authority.
Trusting this addresses your concerns.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Hellc
This is in response to your follow up questions regarding the eligibility to work for secondary school international students.
International students at secondary level may not work without a work permit.
International secondary school students who intend to perform work that is an essential part of their Canadian program at the secondary school level may apply for a co-op work permit. This includes vocational training programs offered by a Designated Learning Institution (DLl) in Quebec and programs that require students to work in order to obtain their secondary or high school diploma or certificate of graduation.
To avoid disruptions in student's study plans and co-op placements, IRCC encourages study permit applicants to apply for a co-op work permit at the same time as their initial study permit, if the acceptance letter provided by the DLl clearly establishes their participation in a co-op program. In that case, their co-op work permit will be issued simultaneously with their study permit, thus avoiding the additional processing delays when applying for a co-op work permit separately.
To note, applicant's acceptance letter provided by the DLl should clearly establish that the work is an essential part of the academic, vocational or professional training program that all participants enrolled in the program are required to complete in order to receive their degree, diploma or certificate. If the same program is offered without a work component, the work component cannot be considered as an essential part if the program.
The only type of work that doesn't require a work permit by the international secondary school students is volunteering. The volunteer work that the high school students will undertake fits with the "the activity is not considered to be work" description listed on the following page: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/partners-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/partners-) service-providers/educational-institutions/volunteer-work-conducted-foreign-students-when-work-permit-esdc- confirmation-required.html

Persons who previously sponsored family members who received social assistance during the validity period of an undertaking are deemed to have defaulted. Provincial/territorial authorities will seek to recover the amount of money paid in social assistance from the sponsor, who is ineligible to sponsor any other member of the family class until this debt is repaid in full. In this scenario, the sponsor is sponsoring a spouse who has a dependent child. That dependent child is not accompanying the parent, who is the principal applicant. Whether a dependent child accompanies or does not accompany the parent to Canada, that dependent child must be medically examined. Non-accompanying dependants must undergo a medical exam to make sure they are admissible to Canada. They must be admissible to maintain their eligibility to be sponsored by their family members in the future. Having inadmissible dependants might make the principal applicant inadmissible as an applicant for permanent residence.
On the Generic Application Form for Canada, the IMMo08, for question number 3 the applicant must indicate the total number of family members included in the application, which includes the principal applicant and any family members, regardless of whether those family members intend to accompany the principal applicant to Canada or not. threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your questions.
The Department has made changes to the Interest to Sponsor web form this year to include additional questions to assist potential sponsors to self-assess their eligibility before submitting the web form. Based on the answers provided, contextual information will be displayed in separate windows, informing potential sponsors about sponsorship eligibility requirements. While a decision on eligibility is not being made at this stage, potential sponsors are encouraged to self-assess their eligibility before submitting the Interest to Sponsor web form. If the potential sponsor is successful in submitting their online Interest to Sponsor web from, a computer generated confirmation number will appear on the webpage that the client must retain. Once a confirmation number is issued the submission will be included in the randomized selection process as long as it is not a duplicate submission. Confirmation numbers of persons randomly selected will be posted on the Departmental website and anyone can self-check if they were selected.
Persons requesting a special grant of an exemption from a requirement of the Act can request humanitarian and compassionate consideration (H&C). Potential sponsors who have been randomly selected to submit a complete application to sponsor their parents and grandparents may request humanitarian and compassionate considerations if they selected “proceed with the application for permanent residence" (if found ineligible to sponsor), on the Application to Sponsor, Sponsorship Agreement and Undertaking form (IMM1344).
Please note that as per Ministerial Instructions that came into force on January 1, 2017, there is no authority for acceptance and
processing of requests for humanitarian and compassionate consideration for persons outside of Canada. Specifically, “a
request made under subsection 25(1) of the Act from outside Canada and that accompanies an application that was not accepted for processing under these Ministerial Instructions, will not be processed."This means that requests for humanitarian and compassionate consideration for persons outside of Canada will not be accepted unless the sponsor was selected under the Randomized Selection Intake process and submitted a sponsorship application.
Alternatively, parents and grandparents can reunite with their loved ones in Canada by applying for a Super Visa. The Super Visa is a multiple-entry visa issued for up to ten years that supports family reunification by allowing applicants to remain in Canada for up to two years without the need to renew their status. The Super Visa assists with the long-term sustainability of the PGP program by encouraging temporary residence as an alternative to entering the permanent residence queue.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

The ban does not apply to applications for temporary residence; the procedures for inadmissible persons applying for temporary residence remain the same (i.e., if the person is inadmissible, they may be considered for a temporary resident permit (TRP) where warranted).
Are you saying that an applicant is able to apply for a TRP (to visit Canada) within the 5 year inadmissibility period?
mmigration, Refugees
Thank you.
threads.answer:
Thank you for consulting with the Immigration Representatives Mailbox,
A person is ineligible to apply/re-apply for permanent residence during the same period as the inadmissibility for misrepresentation. As of 2013 Bill C43 changed the period of inadmissibility from 2 to 5 years meaning the applicant is inadmissible for a 5 year period from the date the removal order was enforced. It should be noted that the ban does not apply to applications for temporary residence; the procedures for inadmissible persons applying for temporary residence remain the same (i.e., if the person is inadmissible, they may be considered for a temporary resident permit).
A TRP can be issued to a foreign national who, in the opinion of an officer, is inadmissible or does not meet the requirements of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The TRP is always issued at the discretion of the delegated authority and may be cancelled at any time. The delegated authority will determine whether the need for the foreign national to enter or remain in Canada is compelling; and the need for the foreign national's presence in Canada outweighs any risk to Canadians or Canadian society.
We trust that this information will be useful to you.

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your question on whether there is a specific "cool down period" after a visiting professor completes two academic years in Canada, before they can return to Canada again under Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) exemption
Work permits for visiting professors are authorised for a maximum period of two academic years, however the guidelines are silent on the length of time between visits to Canada under this category. If a foreign national seeks to return to Canada under LMIA exemption C22 at a later time, they must be able to satisfy the processing officer that an exchange still exists and remains temporary in nature. The onus is on the foreign national to demonstrate the temporary nature of their intended stay in Canada.
The limit of two years has been in place for decades and reinforces the temporary nature of these opportunities and mitigates potential impacts on Canadians' access to academic teaching opportunities.

Processing times are the general length of time it takes to process an application during a specific period. Processing times tell you how long it took (IRCC) to process applications in the past after receiving a complete application package. threads.subject: Two employers on one (or more) closed work permit (s) - is it possible? - REP-2018-0179
threads.question:
## Dear ImmReps,
Is it possible for a foreign worker to be employed part-time by two employers using one or more LMIA-exempt closed work permits? In this hypothetical situation, the employers are not related companies. The part-time work would be less than 25 hours per week at each employer for a total of approximately 40 hours per week of work.
Thank you in advance for your assistance.
Best regards/Meilleures salutations,
threads.answer:
Good morning,
Thank you for your question.
No, two unrelated employers must each register in the Employer Portal, and each fill out and submit (and pay $230 fee) their own Offer. The worker would need to apply (and pay processing fees) for 2 separate work permits, which will need to be assessed/authorized based on each separate Offer of Employment.
In the case of a LMIA-exempt, employer-specific work permit, several conditions are imposed automatically on the employer
by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations <[http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2002-227/page-](http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2002-227/page-)
91.html#docCont> (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer. These conditions include that an employer must: · be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; · comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; · provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; · make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR. Under the IMP Employer Compliance Regime, employers may be inspected on these conditions and they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. Each work permit is issued based on the Offer of Employment provided. Once the work permit is issued the employer must meet the conditions in that offer until the end of the work permit. If the employer changes the offer–e.g. the job offer was for three years, and now the employer cannot provide employment for a period of one year during the validity period of the work permit, then this is considered to be not meeting the conditions of the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC. A new offer of employment is only required to be submitted to IRCC if:
- changes affect the conditions on the foreign worker's work permit, such as a change in employer, work location or NOC; OR
- there are changes to the offer that are significantly different from the offer that the work permit was based on, or if the changes can be perceived to have a negative impact on the foreign worker. For changes that do not require a new offer of employment to be submitted, IRCC does not require proactive notification of these changes; however, it is required that the employer keep all documents pertaining to the employment of the foreign national for six years beginning on the first day of employment and provide it as justification when requested to do so as part of an inspection.
We trust this information is of assistance to you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
Dear Madam or Sir,
Through the webform, I have addressed a clear question as to WHY the government decided to cancel an application. We have submitted a new application because the applicant's stipend (benefit) went from 0 to 20,000 (which is clearly above the acceptable 2-3% increase. The said application was cancelled and no reason was given whatsoever. We have inquired via the webform and the response below was given. Again, this does not answer our question. Please at least confirm we can pay the CAD $20,000.00.
Thank you in advance,
migration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Canada-REP-2018-0169
Good afternoon,
Question Please at least confirm we can pay the CAD $20,000.00.
Answer
Providing a salary that is higher salary to the foreign worker than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC after the work permit was issued would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker – i.e. employer, occupation or location. [Note: that may be the reason for the cancelled application]
However, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the IRPR on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
The employer cannot amend benefit information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker.
Proactive notification to IRCC of inconsistencies surrounding working conditions, including salary and benefits, are not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC.
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker).
Typically, any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). An officer may find that a change in an employee contract that increases the salary is justified under R203(1.1) in that it is similar to a change in the provisions of a collective agreement. In
addition, an increase in wages may result in a finding that the employer did not provide “substantially the same" wages if the increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the LMIA-exemption.
Wages under the International Mobility Program must meet the minimum wage requirement in the province of employment as per the condition to meet federal or provincial laws. Wages paid that are higher than those in the offer of employment, it may indicate a change in duties that would mean a different occupation than offered.
In cases where the employer has promoted or otherwise changed the foreign worker's duties, the foreign worker must receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to implementing the change.
If a new work permit for the promotion or change in occupation has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non-compliance by the employer.
Foreign workers are also subject to other federal (such as ESDC who leads the Temporary Foreign Workers Program) and provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should also meet those requirements for compliance purposes.]
We hope this information will assist you.

threads.answer:
immigration Kepresentatives / Représentants immigration (IRCC)
Good afternoon,
Question
Our client is undergoing a merger of two entities. In a few months, the two entities will merge and the new entity will have a new name. We understand that IRCC guidelines note an amended work permit should be sought within 90 days, but can you please confirm if this requires a new Offer of Employment to be submitted for each employee on an employer-specific work permit?
Answer
Please see Guide to Corporate Mergers and Acquisitions – IRCC website help [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/mergers.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/mergers.asp)
In a merger, the surviving entity assumes all of the assets and liabilities of the merged entities. If Company B is the successor of interest and operates the same type of business as Company A, and if the conditions of the work permit have not changed, i.e. if the worker's employment conditions, including wage, tasks, location, etc, remain unchanged, then, the foreign worker is not obligated to obtain a new WP and can continue to work legally in Canada for the duration of the period stated on the WP. Neither does the employer (Company B) need to submit a new offer of employment to IRCC – until Company B wishes to extend the foreign worker's work permit.
If the foreign worker(s) prefers to hold a work permit that indicates the new company name, then the new employer would need to submit a new offer(s) of employment, including the compliance fee payment for each new offer submitted. The new offer will need to indicate the LMIA-exemption for the job position, and the NOC indicated will need to match the duties described in the offer. With a new offer, it is an opportunity to change anything about the employment of the foreign national, for example, benefits, wages, job locations or contact information.
The new employer (Company B) assumes all liabilities associated with the conditions under subparagraph R209.2(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), for the Offer of Employment whereby the foreign worker was issued the work permit. Those conditions include:
- providing a workplace that is free from abuse
- complying with Canadian federal and provincial labour laws
- remaining active during the work permit period, and
- ensuring that working conditions and occupation comply with the original offer of employment (as submitted to IRCC).
Note that, Company A is responsible for these conditions until the date the merger takes effect.
Generally, any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR Both employers should keep all documents related to the title change to ensure they can be provided if inspected.
Company A can facilitate the changeover of employer information maintained by IRCC to use in the event of employer compliance inspections, we suggest they follow the instructions for Voluntary Disclosures in the webpage titled After Hiring a Temporary Worker and send IRCC the new employer contact information.
In the event of a name change as the result of the merger, for the duration of the existing work permit, the employee(s) should be provided with a letter signed by the employer confirming the name change. This is to ensure that, should the foreign national be required to present their work permit at any time – up until the expiry of the existing work permit-they will have the documentation/proof to link the two employer names.
The letter should include the following information: Employee information Name Address IRCC client ID number
Occupation
Location of employment Date of issuance and expiry of the work permit Employer information – prior to change of name Name Address Phone number Revenue Canada Number Employer name change information Name Address Phone number Revenue Canada Number Effective date of change of employer's name Location of employment Employer contact representative and contact information Reason for name change Acquisition
Merger
Consolidation other
Note: It is advisable that the employer who submitted the offer of employment to IRCC, as well as the successor of
interest employer, retain a copy of this letter/information in order to demonstrate compliance with the conditions of employment in the event of a compliance inspection. Information about the Employer Compliance Regime can be found on the IRCC website here.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

threads.subject: Query re application for citizenship as an adopted person-REP-2018-0143
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam:
We are writing with respect to the following general scenario:
- Husband is a Canadian citizen living outside Canada;
- Wife is a foreign national and has a teenage biological daughter (17 years old);
- Husband wishes to adopt wife's teenage daughter and they are finally getting around to it;
- It is anticipated that the adoption will take approx. 1 year to process, as such, when the adoption is completed, the child
will be 18.
Would you please provide guidance on the above scenario and the following questions:
1) in order for an individual to apply for citizenship as an adopted person, does the application for adoption need to be completed/finalized at the time the application for citizenship is submitted?
2) under section 5.1, it reads...Subject to subsections (3) and (4), the Minister shall, on application, grant citizenship to a person who, while a minor child, was adopted by a citizen on or after January 1, 1947, [...] - does this mean that the adoption had to occur while the person was minor, but the citizenship application can be at any time? (including after the person's 18th birthday)?
We look forward to receiving your response to the above question.
Thank you and kind regards,
migration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Good afternoon, Thank you for your inquiry.
The application you are referring to is the Application for Canadian Citizenship for a Person Adopted By a Canadian Citizen’. As you may be aware, this is a two part process. The Part 1 application is a 'Confirmation of Canadian Citizenship of the Adoptive Parent(s)’, and it is submitted to IRCC's Case Processing Centre in Sydney NS. Once it has been confirmed that the adoptive parent is a Canadian citizen, and that his/her adoptive child is eligible to be granted under section 5.1 of the Citizenship Act, a Part 1 approval letter is sent out to the parent with directions on where to send Part 2. Part 2 is the actual application for the adopted person to be granted citizenship.
The Part 1 application is completed by the adoptive parent in those cases where the adopted person is still under 18 years of age, or by the adopted person in those cases where he/she is already 18 years of age or older. The Part 1 can be submitted in advance of the adoption being finalized. In the scenario you describe, the family might want to submit Part 1 now since the adoption is apparently pending (another advantage of applying now is that the fee for a minor is $100, whereas if the family waits until she is 18 the fee will be $630). The Part 2 is not normally submitted until the adoption is finalized because the adoption order is one of the required supporting documents.
If the adoption is completed after the child turns 18, she can still be granted under 5.1. As per subsection 5.1(2), "the Minister shall, on application, grant citizenship to a person who, while at least 18 years of age (i.e. 18 years of age or older) was adopted by a citizen ..", as long as a genuine parent-child relationship existed before the adopted person turned 18 years of age.
In your scenario, you have indicated that the husband is ‘a Canadian citizen living outside Canada’. Please note, in order for a Part 1 application to be approved, and the adopted person to be eligible to be granted under 5.1, the adoptive parent must either have been born in Canada or have been granted Canadian citizenship. If the adoptive parent is a Canadian citizen who was born outside of Canada and acquired citizenship by virtue of his birth to a Canadian citizen (i.e. he is a citizen by descent), any child adopted by him outside of Canada would not be eligible to be granted under 5.1. This is because since April 17, 2009, Canada's Citizenship Act has included a first generation limit on citizenship. The limit means that persons born outside of Canada in the second or subsequent generation do not necessarily acquire citizenship by virtue of birth to a Canadian parent, and children adopted by a Canadian citizen parent who was born outside Canada (and is Canadian by descent through a biological parent) are not necessarily eligible to be granted under section 5.1.
We hope this information proves helpful.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Question regarding acceptable IDs for Certificate of Canadian citizenship application-REP-2018-0225
threads.question:
Sent: February 3, 2018 10:18 PI Dear ImmReps,
When applying for a Certificate of Canadian citizenship, the document checklist/instructions indicate that one should submit copies of "Two pieces of personal identification, such as a passport, a driver's license or a health insurance card, one of which must have your photo on it" and "Social Insurance number (SIN) cards, bank cards and credit cards are not acceptable pieces of identification."
Can you please tell me some other examples of acceptable IDs? Or, if an applicant is submitting a US passport as the first form of ID, what types of information must be on the second form of ID for it to be acceptable? Minors
C e ca
L'information divulguée en vertu de la loi sur l’accès àlinformatio don't always have driver's licenses, and if not in Canada, do not have heath insurance cards either.
Would a US Social Security card (with name and social security number on it) be acceptable? Or perhaps a high school ID card (with picture, name, and school year on it)?
Thank you for any guidance!
Sincerely,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
Thank you for your inquiry.
Applicants for a Canadian citizenship certificate must provide two personal identifications, and at least one of those IDs must display the applicant's photo. As you have pointed out, the document checklist (CIT 0014) only makes three suggestions for acceptable personal IDs: passport, driver's license or health insurance card. Other government-issued IDs can be accepted from persons residing inside or outside of Canada, including: age of majority cards, senior citizen cards, income tax notices of assessment, municipal tax/utility bills, federal or provincial/state voter enumeration cards, student ID cards, provincial/state school or university records, and immigration documents.
Proof of citizenship applicants should provide the most authoritative ID documents in their possession, which normally means government-issued IDs. In those cases where a second ID is hard to obtain will accept non-government IDs such as hospital cards, health records, insurance policies/cards, professional membership cards, etc. For children who are not yet of school-age, one ID is acceptable, but a letter explaining why only one ID has been provided must be included with the application or it may be returned as incomplete.
The restriction on the use of credit cards or other types of bank cards applies to all applicants. The restriction on using the Canadian SIN card as an ID is specific to Canada, which means US applicants can provide their social security cards as ID.
We hope this information proves helpful.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Question; Authority to make H&C decision for medically inadmissible cases-REP-2018-0084
threads.question:
Immigration Representatives
I was advised by an & Citizenship Canada (IRCC) Officer of the following;
A decision regarding an application for Permanent Residence (PR) to Canada under Humanitarian and Compassionate (H&C) can be made by an IRCC Officer for low level “medically inadmissible cases”
Other H&C decisions for higher “medically inadmissible cases" must be reviewed by Case Management at NHQ before she makes a decision
Can you confirm that this is true? If so what section or policy guidelines is this addressed under?
Is it not incumbent on the IRCC Officer to make an H&C decision based on the merits of the PR application
first rather than take into consideration whether the applicant is “medically inadmissible"?
What level of “medically inadmissible cases” can an IRCC Officer make an H&C decision?
What level of “medically inadmissible cases" is the H&C decision made by Case Management at NHQ?
I appreciate your reply to the above. Thank you.
Sincerely,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Hello Mr
We have provided responses to your questions below.
“I was advised by an & Citizenship Canada (IRCC) Officer of the following;
•A decision regarding an application for Permanent Residence (PR) to Canada under Humanitarian and
Compassionate (H&C) can be made by an IRCC Officer for low level “medically inadmissible cases”
Other H&C decisions for higher “medically inadmissible cases” must be reviewed by Case Management at NHQ before she makes a decision
- Can you confirm that this is true? If so what section or policy guidelines is this addressed under?"
The Delegated authorities to examine and either refuse or approve an application for permanent residence based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations where a medical inadmissibility exists are listed under items 50 and 51 in the "Instrument of Designation and Delegation" found at the following url:
[https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/ircc/migration/ircc/english/resources/manuals/il/il3-eng.pdf](https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/ircc/migration/ircc/english/resources/manuals/il/il3-eng.pdf)
The delegation to examine and refuse an application where there is a suspected medical inadmissibility rests with the C&l Case Processing Officers and Senior Immigration Officers in the regions in Canada as well as with the Director, Assistant Director, and Senior Decision Makers in Case Management Branch at NHQ.
In cases where there is a confirmed medical inadmissibility, the delegation to grant an exemption and grant permanent residence rests with Managers (Western & Ontario regions) and the Assistant Director (Western & Eastern regions) as well as with the Director, Assistant Director, and Senior Decision Makers in Case Management Branch at NHQ.
- “Is it not incumbent on the IRCC Officer to make an H&C decision based on the merits of the PR application first rather than take into consideration whether the applicant is “medically inadmissible"?"
An Officer will first review an application to determine if there are sufficient H&C consideration to warrant refusing or approving the application.
In cases where there are insufficient H&C grounds, an Officer will proceed to refuse the application.
However, in cases where there appear to be compelling H&C considerations but the Officer suspects that the case involves a medical inadmissibility, the Officer will further investigate before referring the case to a designated decision maker. The steps to follow in these cases is found in the Program Delivery Instructions (PDI) for dealing with H&C applications where a potential medical inadmissibility exists and has been included at the end of this response for reference.
- “What level of “medically inadmissible cases” can an IRCC Officer make an H&C decision?"
C&I Case Processing Officers and Senior Immigration Officers have been delegated the authority to refuse any H&C applications, including those where there is a suspected medical inadmissibility.
However, C&I Case Processing Officers and Senior Immigration Officers do not have the delegation to grant an exemption and/or grant permanent residence in cases where there is a confirmed medical inadmissibility.
- “What level of “medically inadmissible cases” is the H&C decision made by Case Management at NHQ?"
The "Instrument of Designation and Delegation" was updated in recent years to authorize Managers (Western & Ontario regions) and Assistant Directors (Western & Eastern regions) to review and either grant or refuse cases where the applicant is inadmissible as a result of a confirmed medical inadmissibility. Since that time, these types of cases are no longer forwarded to Case Management Branch at NHQ for decision.
Background
The PDI for dealing with H&C applications where a potential medical inadmissibility exists states the following:
If discovered at Stage 1
A medical inadmissibility must be confirmed through a medical examination before an exemption can be granted to overcome it. If you intend to refuse an application at Stage 1 and a possible medical inadmissibility would not change that decision, the applicant can be refused without a medical examination.
You should request the applicant complete a medical examination at Stage 1 [R30(1)(d)] if either of the following applies:
- the applicant has specifically requested an exemption from inadmissibility requirements related to health (A38) and you believe that the H&C considerations might outweigh the inadmissibility or you suspect that the case involves medical inadmissibility and there appear to be compelling H&C considerations.
If a medical inadmissibility is confirmed by Migration Health Branch and granting an exemption might be warranted, do the following:
- follow the instructions for procedural fairness for immigration officers
- assess any declarations of ability and willingness
Consult with the provincial health authorities, if deemed necessary. The results of any consultation should be included as part of the referral package for the delegated decision maker. Refer to a delegated decision maker. If a medical inadmissibility is confirmed by Migration Health Branch but you determine an exemption is not warranted, refuse the application.
If discovered at Stage 2
You may either:
- refuse the application for permanent residence if you determine that there are insufficient H&C grounds to grant an exemption to overcome section A38 or

threads.subject: Self-Funded Researcher-REP-2018-0165
threads.question:
Dear Madam or Sir,
We are not certain to understand the work permit exemption for self-funded researchers visiting a University for research purposes.
Please advise if, in the context of researchers paid exclusively by their home institution or government, such researchers are eligible to enter Canada as Self-Funded Researchers.
If so, is there a limited duration for their stay in Canada? In other words, can self-funded researchers visit an University for 1 year?
Thank you in advance for your response,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
Question:
We are not certain to understand the work permit exemption for self-funded researchers visiting a University for research purposes.
Please advise if, in the context of researchers paid exclusively by their home institution or government, such researchers are eligible to enter Canada as Self-Funded Researchers.
If so, is there a limited duration for their stay in Canada? In other words, can self-funded researchers visit an University for 1 year?
Answer:
In order for a foreign national to qualify for a work permit exemption as a self-funded researcher, they must meet the definition of a business visitor, as outlined below ([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-) citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/work- without-permit/business.html):
General criteria
●There must be no intent to enter the Canadian labour market (i.e., no gainful employment in Canada). •The activity of the foreign worker must be international in scope (i.e., that is, there is the presumption of an underlying cross-border business activity, e.g., after-sales service). ●There is the presumption of a foreign employer, as o the primary source of the worker's remuneration remains outside Canada; othe principal place of the worker's employer is located outside Canada; othe accrual of profits of the worker's employer is located outside Canada. In terms of those paid exclusively by their home institution/government, it would appear that they meet the criteria: "the primary source of the worker's remuneration remains outside Canada".
As always, officers at IRCC offices and at Canadian ports of entry must be satisfied that the foreign national meets the criteria set out for business visitors. Each case is assessed on its own merits, and the onus is on the applicants and employers to provide the documentation that supports their application.
In terms of duration, there is no limited duration per se, however again, an officer must be satisfied and will determine the length of stay, either at the port of entry, or for extensions, by issuing a visitor record. Generally speaking, the longer the expected duration in Canada, the more difficult it is to prove that the requirements laid out in the definition of a business visitor are met (e.g., principal place of employment is outside Canada, accrual of profits outside Canada, etc).
Finally, I will draw your attention to IRCC's International Mobility Worker Unit (IMWU). The IMWU helps employers
determine if the temporary worker they wish to hire is exempt from the requirement for an Labour Market Impact Assessment, or exempt from a work permit. The IMWU can provide an opinion if the temporary worker is from a visa-exempt country, and is outside Canada. I would suggest that, if you have a specific case or cases, you submit a request to the IMwu for an opinion, as each case will be assessed individually on its own merits. I also note that the opinion provided by the IMwU is an opinion, and as such, does not guarantee entry to Canada.
We trust that the above is of assistance.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Online/Distance Education for Express Entry-REP-2018-0080
threads.question:
From Subject: Online/Distance Education for Express Entry Hello, Would a diploma or degree earned online via distance education qualify for education points in Express Entry? Would a diploma or degree earned online from a Canadian institution qualify for Canadian Education Credential points in Express Entry? Would a diploma or degree earned online from a Canadian institution require an Education Credential Assessment if the program does not require the student to be in Canada? Would a diploma or degree earned through part-time studies qualify for education points in Express Entry? Thank you.
Regards,
mmigration, Refugees
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good morning,
Thank you for your questions to the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
1. Would a diploma or degree earned online via distance education qualify for education points in Express Entry? As per subsection 11(3) of the Ministerial Instructions (MIs) respecting to the Express Entry System, to be awarded points for education under the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS), a candidate must either: have been educated in Canada, or have a valid Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) for completed foreign education The candidate may be eligible for CRS points for education as long as the credential meets the definition of Canadian educational credential, defined under R73(1) of the Regulations. Further, they must be able to provide evidence that they received a credential for the program (ie. certificate of completion, etc). A foreign education credential (diploma/degree) must have a positive assessment from a designated organization in order to be eligible for CRS points.
2. Would a diploma or degree earned online from a Canadian institution qualify for Canadian Education Credential points in Express Entry? Under section 30 of the Mls, the criteria to obtain points for studies in Canada are the following: Points are to be assigned for the eligible credential corresponding to the highest level of education if the foreign national, for the purpose of obtaining the credential:
(a) studied in Canada at a Canadian educational institution;
(b) was enrolled in full-time study or training for at least eight months; and
(c) was physically present in Canada for at least eight months. For the purpose of this section, the following are not eligible credentials:
(a) credentials obtained in a study or training program in which the study of English or French as a second language amounted to more than half of the program;
(b) credentials obtained in a study or training program in which distance learning amounted to more than half of the program; or
(c) credentials obtained in a study or training program while receiving a scholarship or fellowship that stipulated that the recipient return to their home country to apply the knowledge and skills gained In order to be assigned points for a Canadian Education credential, the candidate has to demonstrate by answering questions in the Express Entry system that the above-mentioned criteria are met.
3. Would a diploma or degree earned online from a Canadian institution require an Education Credential Assessment if the program does not require the student to be in Canada? No, diplomas/degrees issued by Canadian Designated Learning Institutions, as defined under R73(1) of the Regulations, do not require Educational Credential assessments (ECA) distance or in person.
4. Would a diploma or degree earned through part-time studies qualify for education points in Express Entry? Provided the diploma or degree earned meets the requirements of section 11 of the MIs respecting to the Express Entry System, a candidate would receive points under Core Human Capital and Skill Transferability regardless if the diploma or degree was earned through part-time or full-time studies. We trust this information will assist you. Sincerely, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Yes. H&C can be used to request an exemption from an inadmissibility on an eAPR. Applicants are free to make submissions on any aspect of their personal circumstances that they believe are relevant to their request for H&C consideration. However, please note that H&C can't be used to overcome insufficient points in the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) to be invited to apply.
In other words, will IRCC grant an exemption from inadmissibility pursuant to A 25 on H&C grounds in the context of an economic PR application (such as Express Entry or Caregivers)?
We cannot comment on individual cases, however, IRCC is able to grant an exemption to the requirements and IRPA or IRPR on H&C grounds. This includes inadmissibility, except for misrepresentation. According to A10.1(4): A foreign national may not submit an expression of interest (Express Entry profile) if they have been determined to be — and continue to be — inadmissible for misrepresentation.
The onus is on the applicant to satisfy the decision maker that the H&C factors of their individual circumstances are sufficient to warrant an exemption.
We hope this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representative Mailbox

threads.subject: Express Entry-Arranged Employment points-REP-2018-0098
threads.question:
Hello ImmReps,
I have a clarification question about the Arranged Employment points in the Comprehensive Ranking System:
The ministerial instructions essentially say:
if you have a valid work permit for a NOC 0. A or B job that is exempt from needing an LMIA, and you:
are currently working for an employer specified on the work permit have one year of full-time work experience (or an equal amount of part-time work) for that employer have a valid job offer from that employer for at least one year after we issue your permanent resident visa
the instructions do not specify that the candidate must have worked in Canada on that LMIA-exempt work permit in the NOC 0, A or B position for one year before they are eligible for the 50-200 points. It merely instructs that candidates must have one year of full-time work experience for that employer.
Two hypothetical situations:
1) Candidate on an open work permit for a Canadian employer in a NOC 0, A or B position and has worked for one year for the employer. Switched over to an LMIA work permit in the same position and same employer. Is the candidate eligible for the 50-200 points immediately upon switching to the closed work permit or must the candidate wait for 1 year of work on that closed work permit before being eligible for the 50 points?
2)Candidate on an LMIA-exempt, employer specific work permit in NOC 0 for one year. Employer signs an offer letter for the candidate offering him/her a position in a NOC 00 level upon receipt of Permanent Residence status. Without having worked in the NOC 00 position for one year for the same employer, is the candidate eligible to receive 200 points for arranged employment? Assuming they meet the qualifications for the NOC 00 job offer and have the relevant experience, can they get 200 points based on a job offer for a NOC 00 position, while currently working in a closed work permit in a NOC 0?
Thank you for your assistance and clarification to these questions.
Kind regards,
1*1 mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
Two hypothetical situations:
1)Candidate on an open work permit for a Canadian employer in a NOC 0, A or B position and has worked for one year for the employer. Switched over to an LMIA work permit in the same position and same employer. Is the candidate eligible for the 50-200 points immediately upon switching to the closed work permit or must the candidate wait for 1 year of work on that closed work permit before being eligible for the 50 points? Provided that the candidate is able to demonstrate that they meet the definition of section 29(2)(a)(i) of the Ministerial Instructions (Mls) respecting to the Express Entry System that the offer is supported by a valid LMIA assessment AND that the requirements set out in subsection 203(1) of the Regulations with respect to the offer have been met, the candidate would be assigned the points for having a qualifying offer of arranged employment. There does not exist a requirement that the applicant must wait for 1 year of work on the closed work permit as long as he meets the 1 year. An applicant with a valid job offer by an employer with a new positive LMIA may receive the 200 additional points for arranged employment in a NOC 00 or 50 points in NOC A or B.
2)Candidate on an LMIA-exempt, employer specific work permit in NOC 0 for one year. Employer signs an offer letter for the candidate offering him/her a position in a NOC 00 level upon receipt of Permanent Residence status. Without having worked in the NOC 00 position for one year for the same employer, is the candidate eligible to receive 200 points for arranged employment? Assuming they meet the qualifications for the NOC 00 job offer and have the relevant experience, can they get 200 points based on a job offer for a NOC 00 position, while currently working in a closed work permit in a NOC 0? The LMIA exemption as noted in the MIs, only states that the applicant must have a job offer for the same employer for which they were previously employed while under the LMIA-exempt work permit. There does not exist a requirement that the applicant must be working in the same occupation for their future job offer. Provided that there was no break in between employment authorization while the foreign national worked with this same employer, an applicant may receive the 200 additional points for arranged employment without having acquired previous work experience in a NOC 00, and also without having to work one year in the new NOC. The officer will assess all supported documentation provided in the application. However, the onus remains on the applicant to satisfy the officer that the job offer is reasonable and they possess the appropriate qualifications to be able to undertake a higher skilled position.
We trust this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
Can a current holder of a Mobilité francophone work permit apply for a new Mobilité francophone work permit-for a new employer-at a port of entry? threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your question on applying for a work permit. Please accept our apologies for the delay in responding. Question: Can a current holder of a Mobilité francophone work permit apply for a new Mobilité francophone work permit-for a new employer-at a port of entry? Response: While it is stated in the PDI on C16, Mobilité francophone that renewals of these work permits may be submitted by mail to the Case Processing Centre in Vegreville or online, the Regulations do not prevent an applicant from applying at a port of entry, provided they meet the requirements of sections R198 and R200. To be eligible to apply for a work permit at a port of entry, an applicant must be exempt from the requirement for a temporary resident visa and their job falls within the International Mobility Program (i.e., they are not required to obtain a Labour Market Impact Assessment [LMIA]), including C16. The onus is on the applicant to demonstrate that they meet the eligibility of being able to apply at a port of entry, as well as that of LMIA-exemption C16. We trust this information will be of assistance.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Good Afternoon,
If a person is currently in Canada as a temporary resident and wants to make an application for PR under Express Entry, does the fact that their spouse is currently banned from Canada for 5 years for misrepresentation have any bearing on their application if the spouse is listed as non-accompanying?
When I read section 42 of IRPA, my interpretation is that a temporary resident would only be inadmissible as a result of their spouse's inadmissibility if the inadmissibility were due to security reasons (s. 34), human or international rights violations (s. 35), or organized criminality (s. 37). You are correct that, according to A42(2)(a), the client would not be inadmissible for temporary resident status for a non-accompanying spouse unless the spouse is inadmissible under A34, A35, or A37.
However, according to R23(b)(i), the client in the scenario would be inadmissible for permanent resident status. This falls under the 'prescribed circumstances' referred to in A42(1)(a).
