threads.answer:
Studies deemed completed-REP-2018-0016
Dear Ms
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's (IRCC) Immigration Representatives mailbox. Apologies for the delayed response.
Question 1: What is the definition of "engaged in full-time study" in Canada for the purpose of express entry?
Response: If the full-time status is not specified in the documents provided by the institution (transcripts), which is usually the case, we would use the FSW provisions for guidance in determining full-time. As per section 83(2) of the regulations, which explains that when awarding adaptability points to an applicant in the Foreign Skilled Worker stream "full-time study means at least 15 hours of instruction per week during the academic year, authorized under a study permit or under section 188, at a secondary or post-secondary institution in Canada that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institutions, including any period of training in the workplace that forms part of the course of instruction.
Question 2: Does the foreign national have to have completed their program for the work to count towards Canadian work experience for the purposes of Express Entry?
Response: yes, because work while a full-time student does not count. Work experience acquired while on a Post Graduate Work Permit (i.e. after graduation) or while on implied status (the student has received a letter from the education institution announcing end of study program and the student has applied for PGWP) can be applied towards meeting the EE requirements. Any work acquired before implied status period is considered unauthorized and will not count toward EE programs.
Question 3: The IRCC website uses the terms "completed their program" and "graduated" interchangeably. At what point does a study permit holder's full-time work following the completion of their program begin to count towards the 12 months of work experience required to qualify under the Canadian Experience Class? Is it sufficient to have a transcript, official letter, certificate, etc, or must the applicant have received their degree, in which case the effective date of full-time experience is the date the degree was conferred?
Response: The student must stop working as per the conditions of their study permit as soon as they have been issued their final marks or the day formal written notification of program completion (e.g., an official letter or transcript) from the educational institution indicating that they have met the requirements for completing their program of study, whichever comes first. The student can restart working if they had authorisation to work off campus during their studies and have now applied for a PGWP. The work may start to be counted toward CEC once the student is in implied status. However, the student must adhere to the conditions in their student visa until a PGWP is issued.
We trust this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
mmigration, Refugees
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
Dear Immigration Representatives Mailbox,
Ihad a question about the undertaking application to Québec:
1. Does IRCC expect a sponsor to make an undertaking application to Québec if he or she intends to live in Québec once the visa is granted to their spouse but does not currently live in Québec?
The specific situation is that the couple currently lives in the United States, and they will be moving together to Quebec only after the visa is granted.

The instructions for the sponsor eligibility assessment state that “Sponsors who reside or intend to reside in Quebec need not complete Questions 8, 9, 10 or 15." That implies that someone who intends to reside in Quebec would also benefit from the exemptions in R137(c). That same language is not used in the operative parts of the
undertaking, however, which states that it is “[f]or those residing in all provinces EXCÉPT Quebec."
Additionally, the instruction guide implies that the separate undertaking requirement only for sponsors living in Quebec, and that is also what the sponsor eligibility decision says: “As a reminder, if you are a resident of the province of Québec, you must submit an undertaking application to the Provincial Government."
Iwanted to make sure that IRCC policy corresponds to my understanding of the law, as it is not 100% clear to me whether someone who intends to reside in Quebec must also submit an undertaking application to Quebec.
Thank you.
Lnformon
threads.answer:
Good day,
A Canadian citizen residing abroad who wants to sponsor a spouse, and intends to live in Quebec, must submit the Undertaking to Quebec as indicated on the IMM1344 'Application to Sponsor, Sponsorship and Undertaking Agreement'.
As per Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations 130 (1) and 130 (2):
130 (1) Subject to subsections (2) and (3), a sponsor, for the purpose of sponsoring a foreign national who makes an application for a permanent resident visa as a member of the family class or an application to remain in Canada as a member of the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class under subsection 13(1) of the Act, must be a Canadian citizen or permanent resident who
(a) is at least 18 years of age;
(b) resides in Canada; and
(c) has filed a sponsorship application in respect of a member of the family class or the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class in accordance with section 10.
Sponsor not residing in Canada
(2) A sponsor who is a Canadian citizen and does not reside in Canada may sponsor a foreign national who makes an application referred to in subsection (1) and is the sponsor's spouse, common-law partner, conjugal partner or dependent child who has no dependent children, if the sponsor will reside in Canada when the foreign national becomes a permanent resident.
Further, Section 10 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations outlines the forms and content necessary for applications under the family class and sponsorship applications.
Note that potential sponsors who are Canadian citizens residing outside of Canada, who wish to apply to sponsor a spouse and together reside in a province other than Quebec, must complete and submit a full application package to this Department. This is the same manner as potential sponsors living outside of Canada who wish to apply to sponsor a spouse and together reside in Quebec.

threads.subject: Citizenship by Descent (Children of Adopted Canadians) - REP-2018-0312
threads.question:
Dear ImmReps
I’m seeking clarification regarding the second generation limit to citizenship for children who were born abroad, but were adopted by Canadian-born parents.
Specifically, when an adopted person is granted citizenship under s.5.1 (pursuant to an application for citizenship as an adopted person), does the date of citizenship go back to the date of adoption, or rather the date the application was granted?
If it is the date the application is granted (rather then the adoption date), it would be based on the fact that that pre-2007's Bill C-14: An Act to Amend the Citizenship Act (Adoption), adopted children weren't entitled to apply for citizenship at all.
However, if it instead goes back to the date the adoption was (for example in 1998), would the foreign born adopted person be able to pass on citizenship to their child if the child is also not born in Canada? In 2009, a limit to citizenship by descent was imposed on adopted children who obtained citizenship via s.5.1. IRCC's website outlines the following:
Adopted people who become citizens through the direct route are limited in their ability to pass citizenship to their own children as a result of the first generation limit to citizenship by descent, unless the other parent is eligible to pass on citizenship.
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/improvements/act-changes-2009-2015/adoption.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/improvements/act-changes-2009-2015/adoption.html)
If the adopted persons were already Canadian citizens prior to the limit's imposition in 2009 (due to citizenship dating back to the adoption date), then their children would not be caught by the second generation limit.
Could you please confirm which of the above interpretations are correct?
I look forward to hearing your response.
Best Regards,
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
mmigration, Refugees
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
immigration κepresentatives / κeprésentants immigration (IRCC)
Good morning,
Thank you for your inquiry.
The legislation you are referring to is the first generation limit (FGL) on claims of citizenship by descent, and it is described under subsection 3(3) of the Citizenship Act. That provision came into force on April 17, 2009. The generational limit means that a person born outside of Canada to a Canadian parent is not eligible for citizenship by descent, and a person adopted outside of Canada by a Canadian parent is not eligible to apply to be granted under section 5.1, if the Canadian parent:
was also born outside of Canada and was a citizen by descent, or was born outside of Canada, adopted by a Canadian, and then was granted citizenship under section 5.1.
The adoptive grant provision under 5.1 was added to the Act on December 23, 2007. Persons adopted by Canadian citizens prior to that date were eligible to apply to be granted Canadian citizenship, but that grant was under the regular grant provisions of the Act, which meant the adopted person (adult or minor) had to be a permanent resident of Canada. This created a problem when a family was not planning to relocate to Canada and the adopted child was therefore not eligible to be sponsored for permanent residence. This problem was sometimes addressed by means of a discretionary grant of citizenship under subsection 5(4).
Section 5.1 allows for a person adopted by a Canadian citizen to be granted citizenship without the requirement of first having to immigrate to Canada as a permanent resident. However, upon the implementation of an FGL on claims of citizenship by descent in 2009, the facilitative 'descent' component of the 5.1 grant was recognized and incorporated into subsection 3(3). The application of the FGL to grants under 5.1 is described in detail in subsection 5.1(4) of the Act.
There are exceptions to the FGL for the children and grandchildren (both natural born and adopted) of serving Crown servants of Canada. Those exceptions are described at subsections 3(5) and 5.1(5).
Please note: the effective date of citizenship for a person granted under section 5.1 is always the date of granting. It is not the date of adoption. Therefore, with regard to your scenario about a foreign born person adopted by a Canadian citizen in 1998, the following applies:
- If that adopted person was granted citizenship under the regular grant provisions-i.e. 5(1) or 5(2) - or (if applicable) under 5(4), that person can ‘pass on' citizenship by descent to a natural born child, AND any child that person might adopt would be eligible to apply to be granted under 5.1. If that adopted person was granted under 5.1 (so grant was on or after December 23, 2007), any child born to that person between the date of the 5.1 grant and April 16, 2009 (inclusive) would be a citizen by descent, AND any child adopted by that person before April 17, 2009 would have been eligible to apply to be granted under 5.1. On and after that date, however, the limit applies to that adopted person's natural born and adopted children. The application of the FGL is based on date of application, not the date of adoption. This means if a person was adopted before April 17, 2009, by a parent who is Canadian by descent or by way of grant under 5.1, that person will need to have applied for a grant under 5.1 prior to April 17, 2009. Otherwise, the FGL will apply.
I hope this information proves helpful.
mmigration, Refugees
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
FW: ITA clarification-REP-2018-0224
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox. We hope that you will find the answer to your question below of assistance.
Question: We are seeking clarification, in a scenario where a candidate has been invited to apply under the Federal Skilled Worker Class and at the time of their ITA they have completed 2 years and 11 months of foreign work experience, however by the time they submit their eAPR they will have completed the full 3 years of foreign work experience that is required to obtain the 50 transferability points assigned for 3 years or more of foreign work experience. Our question is as follows:
May the candidate submit their eAPR despite the fact they had 2 years and 11 months of foreign work experience at the time they receive their ITA and will IRCC count it as 3 years of foreign work experience?
Or must they decline their ITA and wait for a potential new ITA to be issued after they have completed 3 years of foreign work experience?
Answer: When the Comprehensive Ranking System triggers an invitation to apply early, officers will look for evidence that the job is continuing or if the required work experience was obtained before the time of application. In situations where the applicant completed or left the employment and the duration of that employment did not meet the criteria under which the candidate was invited to apply the candidate should decline the ITA and re-enter the pool. A letter of explanation may assist the officer with the assessment of the applicant's work experience.
Please note that our calculation is based on monthly units and we do not take into account days. When inputting work experience “From and To” dates, the system only asks for month and year for each entry. This results in some applicants being invited “early". That said, the date range is inclusive, meaning the month in the To date will count towards the calculation of full time equivalent units for that particular work experience entry. Example: Using the February 1st date, and assuming the candidate worked for a year (full-time and met relevant definition of work experience), the calculation would be as follows depending on whether To Date is set to January or February:
February 2016 - January 2017 = 12 months full-time equivalent duration February 2016 – February 2017 = 13 months full-time equivalent duration
The onus remains on the applicant to demonstrate they meet the criteria under which they were invited to apply.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
migration, Refugees

A foreign national may be able to restore their status as a student within 90 days of losing it, if they meet the Restoration of Status eligibility criteria. Thank you for consulting with the Immigration Representatives Mailbox and Integrity Risk Guidance Branch,
To immigrate to Canada, the applicant and any family members 18 and older must include their police certificates as part of the application for permanent residence. They need one for every country, other than Canada, where they stayed for more than six months in a row.

Police certificates must be a scan of the original certificate(s) in colour. Certified true copies or unauthorized copies will not be accepted and will result in the application being rejected.
Find out how to get a police certificate.

threads.answer:
FW: Live In Caregiver Program Work Permits-REP-2018-0184

Aside from the date on which the Work Permit was issued (pre-program closure or post program closure), are there other indicators on a Work Permit that would clearly distinguish whether the Work Permit was issued under the LCP or a regular LMIA?
Yes, a work permit issued under the Live-in Caregiver Program must the words "Live-in Caregiver" printed on it.

Yes, the Live-in Caregiver Program came to an end when the caregiver pathways were created on November 30,
2014. Work permits under this program would only be accepted if a Labour Market Impact Assessment was received by Service Canada on or before this date. More information can be found on this webpage. We trust this information will assist you.

threads.answer:
Dear Mr.
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
In cases where a candidate is the owner and employee of the business for which they have a qualifying job offer as per paragraph 29 (2) (a) of the Express Entry Ministerial Instructions (Mis), it is possible that the candidate may receive 200 additional Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points for arranged employment in a NOC 00 or 50 points in NOC O, A or B.
However, work in Canada by the owner of the company may be considered "self-employed" work. As per our Program Delivery Instructions which are published on our IRCC website as a courtesy to stakeholders, IRCC officers consider the
following factors in determining whether an applicant is considered an employee or self-employed:
- the degree of the worker's control or autonomy in terms of how and when work is performed, and the method(s) used to do the work; whether the worker owns and/or provides tools and equipment to accomplish the work; the degree to which the worker has to perform the work personally and whether the worker has the option of subcontracting work or hiring others to help and assist with completing the work; the degree of financial risk assumed by the worker, including whether the worker is required to make any investment in order to complete the work or provide the service and whether the worker is free to make business decisions that affect his/her ability to realize a profit or incur a loss (as opposed to the opportunity to earn commissions or other productivity bonuses); and any other relevant factors, such as written contracts. The onus is on the applicant to satisfy the officer that an employee-employer relationship exists as part of the eligibility requirement. In your example, should the candidate be considered self-employed, it would not necessarily preclude him/her from claiming arranged employment in Express Entry, it will however disqualify him/her from the Canadian Experience Class (CEC). Pursuant to paragraph 15(7)(b) of the MIs and paragraph 87.1(3)(b) of the Regulations, periods of self-employment do not count for purposes of CRS points for "Canadian work experience" or meeting the work experience requirement under the CEC. The candidate might, as per paragraph 75(2)(a) of the Regulations, qualify under Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) program if he/she has one year of continuous work as a self-employed person to meet the minimum requirements for FSW. Please visit this link regarding information about arranged employment. We trust this information will assist you. Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Comme tous les médecins résidents au Québec, il sera payé par la RAMQ.
Cela va à l’encontre d’un critère de la lettre d’invitation sous C-45 à cet effet: «que le revenu offert au travailleur étranger ne provient pas de fonds publics canadiens ».
Je me questionne quant à l'intention d'IRCC derrière ce critère.
Si l'intention est de s'assurer que les canditats citoyens canadiens et résidents permanents soient priorisés, dans le cas qui nous concerne, c'’est bel et bien le cas. Si l’intention est également de collaborer et de respecterle mode de fonctionnement du Ministère de la santé et des services sociaux (MSSS) et du Collège des médecins du Québec (CMQ), c'est aussi bel et bien le cas.
En effet, le règlement quant aux « Modalités relatives à la détermination du nombre de postes de résidents en médecine disponibles dans les programmes de formation médicale postdoctorale » prévoit un contingent régulier qui donne priorité aux diplômés québécois, puis canadiens ou américains, mais aussi un contingent particulier, quì précise que « ces postes peuvent aussi être offerts à des candidates et candidats canadiens et
étrangers susceptibles de combler les besoins prioritaires de la société québécoise ou contribuer au
rayonnement des universités hors de nos frontières, à l’émulation des étudiants et à la diffusion des connaissances scientifiques ».
C'est le cas de notre médecin résident étranger. Il a été admis dans une spécialité déterminée prioritaire. Son poste a été autorisé par le MSSS et le CMQ aurait une procédure de comptabilisation spéciale pour ce type de cas.

mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Dear
Foreign nationals wishing to work temporarily in Canada may do so through two programs: The Temporary Foreign Worker Program, which requires a labour market test, and the International Mobility Program, which does not. Under the International Mobility Program, exemptions from the requirement to submit a labour market test are determined, in accordance with the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, on the basis of reciprocity, public policy and competitiveness of Canadian institutions or economy and trade agreements.
The exemption for foreign medical residents (C-45) was created under the International Mobility Program to maintain the competiveness of Canada's institutions. This exemption is aimed at foreign nationals whose medical residency in Canada is funded entirely by their home country or by private Canadian institutions and as such does not take away employment, training opportunities, or funding for medical residency programming from Canadian medical residents. This facilitation allows Canadian institutions to maintain global networks and benefit from knowledge exchange without compromising residency opportunities for Canadian medical graduates.
Alternatively, the LMIA exemption for significant benefit (C10)could be an option if is able to demonstrate that the individual they intend to hire would bring significant social, cultural or economic benefits to Canada by the work they will undertake. Each cases are assessed by officers on their own merits and therefore a complete rationale as to how the individual will bring significant benefits to Canada is required.
We trust this respond to your questions.

threads.subject: temporary resident permit-A36; authorization to re-enter-REP-2018-0403
threads.question:
Good evening,
This is in regard to a client matter. Our client has received a work permit extension and a temporary resident permit. There was no issue of inadmissibility.
On the client's TRP there is a notation of “A36" and the following comment: "departure from Canada will invalidate this
Temporary Resident Permit under Regulation 63(b)."
Could you please clarify what “A36” refers to, as well as the process to obtain authorization for our client to leave and re-enter Canada while holding a temporary resident permit? I have looked on IRCC's website but am not clear as to the office to contact for authorization or the forms to use.
Thank you,
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
Lnformon
threads.answer:
Hello,
Persons who are described under A36 are inadmissible to Canada on grounds of criminality. The Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) subsection 24(1) authorizes the issuances of TRPs to inadmissible foreign nationals when it is "justified in the circumstances". A TRP allows the holder either to enter or to remain in Canada. The foreign national has temporary resident status in Canada during the validity period of the TRP.
In order to obtain authorization for your client to re-enter Canada, he/she will need to apply for rehabilitation. The IRPA provides authority for the Minister to approve the rehabilitation of persons described in A36(1)(b) or (c) and A36(2)
(b) or (c); the granting of rehabilitation removes the grounds of inadmissibility.
This link provides additional information on rehabilitation and how to apply for it: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5312-rehabilitation-persons-inadmissible-canada-past-criminal-activity.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-5312-rehabilitation-persons-inadmissible-canada-past-criminal-activity.html)

threads.subject: Non-Recognized Institution-ECA-REP-2018-0412
threads.question:
Subject: Non-Recognized Institution-ECA Dear ImmRep, Does IRCC maintain a list of recognized and non-recognized institutions? Does a finding by a designated Credential Assessment Organization, such as WES, that a university or school is a Non-Recognized Institution, render the equivalency null for the purposes of points under express entry? WES sometimes finds a Canadian equivalency but finds that the School is a Non-Recognized Institution. What does this means in terms of ability to get points for the education under Express Entry? Thank you,
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
immigration κepresentatives / Représentants immigration (IRCC)
Deal
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question 1: Does IRCC maintain a list of recognized and non-recognized institutions?
Response to 1st question: for the list of designated educational institutions in Canada please navigate the following link: List of Recognized Educational Institutions.
IRCC does not maintain information/lists for unrecognized educational institutions.
Questions 2 & 3: Does a finding by a designated Credential Assessment Organization, such as WES, that a university or school is a Non-Recognized Institution, render the equivalency null for the purposes of points under express entry?
WES sometimes finds a Canadian equivalency but finds that the School is a Non-Recognized Institution. What does this means in terms of ability to get points for the education under Express Entry?
Response for 2nd and 3rd questions: in order to be eligible for CRS points, a foreign education credential must have a positive assessment from a designated organization. The ECA report must indicate the equivalency of the foreign credential to a Canadian credential and must indicate the institution where the candidate obtained the credential is recognized by the authority of the home country.
Each organization may have a different way of reporting their educational credential assessment.
According to WES, post-secondary education is regulated by national legislation in most countries and has defined guidelines that should be in place in order to bestow official degree granting authority on institutions. For all such institutions, WES ECA reports will indicate the status as recognized if the documents assessed are issued by an institution that has power to award academic credentials.
An institution that is not recognized by the appropriate educational authorities in the home country as a degree granting institution is considered not recognized by WES. Study completed at such institutions is assessed by WES and the ECA report will indicate the status of the foreign institution as not recognized.
Institutions that are not licensed or registered as teaching institutions in the home country do not have the right to operate or issue degrees. In such instances, WES does not issue an ECA report due to lack of sufficient and reliable information.
In summation, if WES indicates that the organization is 'not recognized' then IRCC will not assign any points for the credential.
We trust this information will assist you.
Lnformon
Sincerely, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
FW: IMM0008 Schedule 14 - Failed refugee claimants? - REP-2018-0435
QUESTION:
My client made a refugee claim in Canada with his wife and children. My client was accepted but his wife and children were rejected. My client is now applying for permanent residence from inside Canada and has completed all forms including the IMM0008 Schedule 14. Should his wife and children over 18 yrs also complete the IMM0008 Schedule 14? If so, Question 5 on that form is problematic as it does not provide an alternate response other than to imply the person completing the form has been recognized as
a refugee by Canada, which is not the case for my client's spouse and children.
RESPONSE:
A protected person is a person on whom refugee protection is conferred under Section 95(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and whose claim has not subsequently been deemed to be rejected under IRPA Sections 108(3) or A109(3), or whose refugee protection application is deemed to be rejected under IRPA
Sections 114(4) [A95(2)].
In Canada, the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) and IRCC decide who is a Protected Person. If the IRB determined a person in need of protection or a Convention refugee or if a positive decision on a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) from IRCC was received, the client is considered to a Protected Person.
As per the Instruction Guide (IMM 5205) for Application for Permanent Residence in Canada — Protected Persons

threads.subject: Inclusion in an Express Entry Invitation to Apply Round-REP-2018-0045
threads.question:
Dear sir or madam,
We have a client who is in the following situation:
1. Client created an Express Entry profile on 13 December 2017 with a score of 439.
2. On 1 January 2018, client's profile received additional points for 1-year of Canadian work experience by client's common law partner. The profile score is now 444 but this appears to be because the EE profile only allows entry of Month and Year for work experience. Based on real world facts, the common law partner will not have 1-year of Canadian work experience until near the end of February 2018.
My understanding is that, prior to the end of February 2018, if the client receives an ITA with a minimum score of 440 or above, then the client must decline the ITA. Once the 1-year of Canadian work experience by the common law partner can be properly awarded to the client, then it would be fine to go ahead with the ITA.
My question, however, is what happens if there is a minimum score of 439 for an ITA round before the end of February 2018? In that case, the client would like receive an ITA and would otherwise be entitled to proceed with the ITA but for the inability for the client to determine if the profile would have met the requirements of the profile submission date-based tie breaker.
If it is later determined that the proper profile score for the client should be 439 and that the profile was submitted after the final profile with a score of 439 that fits within the ITA round, then would a subsequent eAPR be rejected?
Thank you in advance for your time and assistance in this matter.
Kind regards,
mmigration, Refugees
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Hello Mr.
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox. We hope that you will find the answer to your question below of assistance.
Question: What happens if there is a minimum score of 439 for an ITA round before the end of February 2018? In that case, the client would like receive an ITA and would otherwise be entitled to proceed with the ITA but for the inability for the client to determine if the profile would have met the requirements of the profile submission date-based tie breaker.
If it is later determined that the proper profile score for the client should be 439 and that the profile was submitted after the final profile with a score of 439 that fits within the ITA round, then would a subsequent eAPR be rejected?
Answer: In situations where the candidate does not meet the criteria under which they were invited to apply the candidate should decline the ITA and re-enter the pool. To check whether a candidate should have been included in a round of invitations, compare the profile submission date with the cut-off date and time listed on our website. If the candidate's CRS falls to the CRS cut-off for the round they were invited in without the points for their partner's Canadian work experience, they have to make sure they also meet the tie-breaking rule for that round (l.e. that they submitted their EE profile before the date and time specified on our website).
When the Comprehensive Ranking System triggers an invitation to apply “early", officers will look for evidence that the job is continuing or if the required work experience was obtained before the time of invitation. The onus remains on the applicant to demonstrate they meet the criteria under which they were invited to apply. A letter of explanation may assist the officer with the assessment of the applicant's work experience in this situation. In situations where the applicant did not meet the criteria under which they were invited to apply the candidate should decline the ITA and re-enter the pool.
Please note that our calculation is based on monthly units, and we do not take into account days. When inputting work experience “From and To" dates, the system only asks for month and year for each entry. This results in some applicants being invited “early". That said, the date range is inclusive, meaning the month in the To date will count towards the calculation of full time equivalent units for that particular work experience entry. Example: Using the February 1st date, and assuming the candidate worked for a year (full-time and met relevant definition of work experience), the calculation would
be as follows depending on whether To Date is set to January or February:
February 2016 - January 2017 = 12 months full-time equivalent duration February 2016 – February 2017 = 13 months full-time equivalent duration
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
Chers Représentants de l'immigration au Canada
J'ai deux questions à vous poser:
1) Si mon client a une EIMT et un CAQ valides jusqu'au 31 mars 2019 mais que le permis de travail expire le 4 mai 2018 à case de son passeport qui expire à cette date:
a) Est-ce que mon client peur renouveller son permis de travail, une fois son passeport renouvellé, sans faire de nouvelles
demandes d'EIMT et CAQ?
b) L'EIMT a une date d'expiration de 6 mois pour faire une demande de permis de travail, du 30 septembre 2017, mais une
validité de 24 mois, jusqu'au 31 mars 2019. Puisque la demande du premier permis de travail a été faite avant le 30 septembre 2017, pouvons-nous faire une autre demande avec cette même ElMT pour un permis valide jusqu'au 31 mars 2019?
2) Si mon client est français donc dispensé d'un visa et eligible pour une demande de permis de travail au point d'entrée et que nous sommes entrain de faire les demandes de CAQ, EIMT:
a) Pouvons-nous en attendant faire les demandes de permis d'études des enfants de plus de 6 ans en ligne sans le permis de
travail du père, avec le CAQ études approuvés?
b) Lorsque nous les avons faites, les demandes ne sont pas allées au consulat canadien de France mais à Vegreville puis
refusée car nous n'avions pas soumis la lettre d'admission de l'école et tous les documents d'un enfant mineur voyageant sans les parents. Or, l'enfant voyagera avec ses parents et nos lettres le précisent puis l'enfant est dispensé de lettre d'admissioon puisqu'accompagnant un travailleur étranger.
c) Serait-il mieux de faire les demandes de CAQ puis ensuite, plutôt que des permis d'études en ligne, des demandes de fiches
vsiiteurs au point d'entrée avec autorisation d'étudier (enfant de 6 à 16 ans)?
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Nous sommes désolés pour le retard. Veuillez trouver nos réponses aux questions posées ci-dessous.
J'ai deux questions à vous poser:
1) Si mon client a une ElMT et un CAQ valides jusqu'au 31 mars 2019 mais que le permis de travail expire le 4 mai 2018 à case de son passeport qui expire à cette date: Question :
a) Est-ce que mon client peur renouveler son permis de travail, une fois son passeport renouvelle, sans faire de nouvelles
demandes d'EIMT et CAQ? Réponse
Uniquement pour un cas d’expiration de passeport, pourvu que l'EIMT et la demande de permis de travail initiaux aient été reçues avant la date d’expiration de l’étude d’impact sur le marché du travail, le travailleur étranger temporaire sera autorisé à présenter une demande de renouvellement de son permis de travail existant auprès du CTD-V, et ce, sans avoir à obtenir une nouvelle EIMT. Ainsi, même si la date d’expiration de l'EIMT est passée, le travailleur étranger temporaire a respecté le délai initial de présentation de sa demande et peut alors obtenir un renouvellement de son permis de travail jusqu’à la fin de la durée de l'emploi précisée dans l’EIMT initiale, pourvu que son passeport ait été renouvelé en conséquence.
Question :
b) L'EIMT a une date d'expiration de 6 mois pour faire une demande de permis de travail, du 30 septembre 2017, mais une validité de 24 mois, jusqu'au 31 mars 2019. Puisque la demande du premier permis de travail a été faite avant le 30 septembre 2017, pouvons-nous faire une autre demande avec cette même ElMT pour un permis valide jusqu'au 31 mars 2019?
Réponse :
Dans le cas où le permis de travail n’a pas été émis à pleine validité à cause de la date d’expiration du passeport, un autre permis de travail pour le même poste et les mêmes conditions d’emploi peut être émis avec la même EIMT.
Question :
2) Si mon client est français donc dispensé d'un visa et eligible pour une demande de permis de travail au point d'entrée et que nous sommes entrain de faire les demandes de CAQ, EIMT:
a) Pouvons-nous en attendant faire les demandes de permis d'études des enfants de plus de 6 ans en ligne sans le permis de travail du père, avec le CAQ études approuvés? Réponse : Non, car la validité du permis d’étude doit coïncider avec la validité du permis de travail du père en tant que demandeur principal. Bref, il faudrait attendre qu'une décision soit prise concernant le permis de travail du père avant de faire les demandes de permis d’études pour les enfants.
Question :
b) Lorsque nous les avons faites, les demandes ne sont pas allées au consulat canadien de France mais à Vegreville puis refusée car nous n'avions pas soumis la lettre d'admission de l'école et tous les documents d'un enfant mineur voyageant sans les parents. Or, l'enfant voyagera avec ses parents et nos lettres le précisent puis l'enfant est dispensé de lettre d'admissioon puisqu'accompagnant un travailleur étranger. Question :
c) Serait-il mieux de faire les demandes de CAQ puis ensuite, plutôt que des permis d'études en ligne, des demandes de fiches vsiiteurs au point d'entrée avec autorisation d'étudier (enfant de 6 à 16 ans)?
Réponse à la question 2 a) s'applique.
Nous espérons que le tout est à votre satisfaction.
Cordialement,
La boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration

Question:
Would a foreign national that is not from a temporary resident visa exempt country, such as China, be eligible to apply to enter Canada under the above captioned short-term work permit exemption category under Global Skills Strategy at the port-of-entry (i.e. airport or land border)?
If not, then how can the foreign national request to enter Canada under the above work permit exemption category?

threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
Question:
Would a foreign national that is not from a temporary resident visa exempt country, such as China, be eligible to apply to enter Canada under the above captioned short-term work permit exemption category under Global Skills Strategy at the port-of-entry (i.e. airport or land border)?
If not, then how can the foreign national request to enter Canada under the above work permit exemption category?
Response:
Apologies for not responding to your question sooner.
The same entry rules that apply to TRV-required foreign nationals who enter Canada under R186(a) as business visitors or under any other work permit exemptions under R186 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations applies to those foreign nationals who wish to enter Canada to work under the Public Policy: Short-term work permit exemption.
Foreign nationals that are coming from temporary resident visa required countries must obtain a TRV prior to enter Canada if they wish to enter Canada under R186 provision or the Public Policy on short-term work. Once the foreign national obtains a TRV, they may be eligible to enter Canada as temporary workers without obtaining a work permit. However, they must meet the requirements for short-term work permit exemption (15 or 30 days). The work permit exemption may be for 15 or 30 consecutive days if the foreign national intends to perform work in an occupation that is listed in skill type 0 (management occupations) or skill level A in the matrix of the NOC, as defined in section R2, for up to the following periods:
- 15 consecutive days (and the foreign national has not been granted an exemption under the public policy facilitating entry into Canada for short-term work in the last 6 months)
- 30 consecutive days (and the foreign national has not been granted an exemption under the public policy facilitating entry into Canada for short-term work in the last 12 months)
We trust this information will be useful to you. Sincerely, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Question AEGC-Transfert intragroupe-REP-2018-0299
threads.question:
Chers représentants,
Je me permets de vous soumettre la question suivante :
■ Un employé européen qui a été à l'emploi au moins un (1) an auprès d’une entreprise européenne, mais qui n’est pas présentement à l’emploi de cette dernière, peut-il faire l'objet d’un transfert inter-entreprise au Canada sous l'AEGC?
Une interprétation grammaticale du texte AEGC permettrait de conclure que la personne ne doit pas être présentement à l'emploi de la société européenne, il suffit qu'elle ait été à l'emploi de celle-ci pour 12 mois. Ainsi, En anglais le texte de l'AEGC va dire « who have been employed for at least one year and who are temporarily transferred» En français, le texte indique «qui ont été employées par une entreprise au moins un an et qui sont transférées temporairement»
Toutefois, les directives sur votre site internet peuvent porter à confusion cette interprétation puisque :
Informatn od eAomtinAct Lnmanon " Les dispositions de l’AECG se rapportant aux personnes faisant l’objet d’un transfert temporaire intragroupe, énumérées à la catégorie « Personnel clé », sont semblables à la dispense C12 avec l'ajout des stagiaires diplômés. "
"The intra-corporate (company) transferee provisions of CETA, described under the key personnel category, are similar to the C12 exemption. with the addition of graduate trainees."
Si la dispense de l'AEGC dans le cadre du transfer inter-entreprise est similaire à la catégorie générale C-12, ceci implique l'exigence selon laquelle l'employée qui fait l'objet de la mutation soit actuellement à l'emploi au sein de la société étrangère?
Vous remerciant à l’avance de votre réponse, je vous prie d’agréer, chers représentants, mes sincères salutations.
Cordialement,
threads.answer:
Bonjour-
Nous vous remercions de votre patience.
Pour répondre à la question, en effet, l'employée qui fait l'objet de la mutation doit être actuellement à l'emploi au sein de la société étrangère, en plus, avoir occupé de façon continue un poste semblable au sein de l'entreprise à l’étranger pendant un an (à temps plein).
Nous avons pris note de cette question et nous effectuerons la correction de cette page web afin de l'indiquer plus précisément.
Nous espérons que cette information vous est utile.
Cordialement,
La boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration

Hello Ms.
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox. We hope that you will find the answer to your question below of assistance.
Question: Could you please let me know what other proof would be acceptable for the purposes of proving sufficient settlement funds?
Answer: In extenuating circumstances, a letter of explanation may help officials with their assessment of an applicant's settlement funds. Ultimately, the applicant must satisfy the officer that funds are available and transferable, unencumbered by debts or other obligations, and sufficient to support initial establishment in Canada. Applicants are advised to provide as much detail as possible. Applicants are advised to provide as much detail as possible to satisfy an immigration officer that they have sufficient available and transferable funds, unencumbered by debts or other obligations, at the time of application. This might include detailed bank statements for the previous six months but must include a letter from one or more banks presenting "the average or the balance for each month ending." Dear Sir/Madam,
Ms ecommended that we direct this query to IMMReps.
A30(2) regarding children being allowed to study without a study permit if they are the child of a work permit or study permit holder only applies to minor aged children. The age of majority in Ontario and some other provinces is 18 (whereas it's 19 in BC). The impact of this is that children who turn 18 during grade 12 (which will happen as long as the birthday is between January 1 and late June) technically are supposed to be converting over to a study permit from a visitor record before their
s.16(2)(c) Lnfomn
birthday.
We have a case where this will happen. Our questions are:
1. Does IRCC enforce this requirement to transition over to a study permit or do they exempt children of work permit or study permit holders who are still in grade school? For instance, could the student avail themselves of the study permit exemption under R188(1)(c) because the duration of studies from the birthday until the end of the academic year in June will be less than six months (despite grade 12 being a "program" that is longer than six months)?
2.Can the student still attend grade school while waiting the 30 days that CPC-Vegreville will take to process the online study permit application if the child turns 18 before the study permit is issued? Interestingly, the online guidance under study permit restoration applications states that a student can continue going to school while a restoration application is being processed. In the absence of such a statement, our understanding is that the student would need to refrain from studying while the restoration application is in process. This suggests that leniency is shown for students.
Any guidance would be greatly appreciated!
Thank voul
threads.answer:
Hello
This is in response to you enquiry regarding study permit requirements for minors.
Minor children intending to study in Canada are required to apply for a study permit before entering Canada. As noted in our PDIs and public website, there are some exemptions to this rule, cases including minor children attending kindergarten, minors who are refugees or refugee claimants, minors whose parents are refugees or refugee claimants.
The intent behind section 30(2) of the Immigration and Refugees Protection Act (IRPA) was to facilitate access to education in exceptional cases where foreign national minor children are already in Canada and did not acquire a study permit prior to their arrival and otherwise would be deterred from studies. Therefore, as per A30(2) a foreign national minor whose parents meet the criteria of A30(2) may initiate studying within a study permit and can apply for a study permit from within Canada as per A215(1)(b).
Therefore, IRCC encourages these applicants to apply for a study permit within 90 days before the expiry of their authorization to engage in studies in Canada under subsection 30(2) of the Act.
Please note that the applicants authorized to engage in studies in Canada under subsection 30(2) of the Act may still apply for study permit within 90 days after the expiry of that authorization, however they will not be able to continue studying while awaiting for a decision on their application as their authorization to engage in studies in Canada under subsection 30(2) of the Act is no longer valid.
I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at .
Sincerely,

Conditional letters of acceptance are intended for applicants who must complete a prerequisite program before being admitted into their primary program. Hello
This is in response to your inquiry sent on January 26 regarding completion of studies and study permit expiry.
A student is considered to have completed their program of studies once they receive written confirmation of program completion (e.g. official letter or transcript) from their DLl. Their study permit becomes invalid 90 days after that date, regardless of printed expiry date.
In the case of students who have stopped enrolling in their program for extended periods for other reasons, these are considered leaves of absences rather than program completion, and their study permit remains valid until the printed expiry date. However, because in this case they are no longer compliant with the condition of their study permit that they must actively pursue studies, they must apply to change their temporary resident status (i.e. to visitor or worker) until they resume their studies, at which point they may continue to use their original study permit. They may also leave Canada and return once their studies resume.

threads.answer:
FW: Camp counsellors work permit exemptions-REP-2018-0391
QuEsTioN: If a foreign person comes to Canada to work as a volunteer camp counsellor for non-autonomous elderly for a Canadian charitable organization, can they be work permit exempt as volunteer workers or do they need to obtain a work permit under LMIA exemption code C50 or C20?
In this case, all camp counsellors, whether Canadian or foreign, are always volunteers and unpaid as the organization would not have funds to pay workers.
ANSWER: Please be advised that whilst many types of volunteer work do not require a work permit, given the information you have provided, it is not clear whether or not the person would qualify for a work permit exemption.
Are they work permit exempt?
We invite you to review our webpage indicating ‘what is work' for foreign nationals in Canada to determine if the activity that will be undertaken for the foreign national meets the definition of work. Questions that can be considered during this assessment are:
- will the foreign national be engaged in a “performance of an activity in direct competition with the activities of Canadians and permanent residents in the Canadian labour market.” If the answer is yes, a work permit is required.
- is the job normally one that is a paid position? If the answer is yes, a work permit is required. o For example, if the foreign national is an accountant or computer programmer, they shouldn't
normally volunteer those skills, as typically those are paid positions.
- Is the job that is not paid usually leads to a paid position? If the answer is yes, a work permit is required. oThere are certain jobs that individuals normally accept with the expectation that they lead to paid
positions. Certain internships or other training positions may not be paid, but they may be considered to be “in direct competition” of Canadians in the labour market.
If they are not work permit exempt, are they LMIA-exempt under C20?
If the foreign national will be working as camp counsellor in a residential camp (where the campers and the camp counsellors are staying overnight at the camp), then the camp counsellor will be exempt from the LMIA requirement under exemption code C20.
If they are not work permit exempt, are they LMIA-exempt under C50?
mmigration, Refugees
Generally, there is a difference between a charitable worker, who needs a work permit, and a volunteer worker, who is work-permit exempt. The difference is based on the definition of “work” and entry into the labour market.
- A volunteer worker, whose activity is incidental to their main purpose for entering Canada and does not meet the definition of work, does not require a work permit (e.g., being a Big Brother or Big Sister to a child, being on the telephone line at a rape crisis centre, canvassing for donations). A charitable worker usually takes a position involving an activity that meets the definition of work and requires a work permit because they are participating in a competitive activity or are being paid wages (e.g., group home worker, carpenter for Habitat for Humanity).
Paragraph 205(d) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) applies to foreign nationals whose work in Canada will be of a charitable or religious nature, regardless of whether a wage is received. Simply being employed by a Canadian religious or charitable organization is not sufficient to meet the requirements for this Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) exemption. For example, an administrator or office manager's work in a charitable organization is generally not of a charitable nature. Similarly, the primary work of a cook for a religious camp or of an accountant for a religious organization is not of a religious nature. Based on the information provided, it is not clear the type of work the foreign national will be performing during their stay in Canada.
We trust this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

Good day,
Question
What happens to an Offer of Employment submitted through the Employer Portal when the work permit is refused? Can that Offer be re-used if a new application for a work permit for the same foreign worker is submitted at a later date?
Answer
No, an Offer of Employment cannot be re-used. Once it is submitted it goes into our processing system and is matched to the work permit application via the A#. However, this would only be possible if there was already a work permit application to work for that same employer, and already sitting in our processing system. See the example given in the processing guidance for our officers.

mmigration, Refugees 1*1

threads.answer:

With a valid eTA a foreign national can travel to Canada as often as they want for short stays during the five year validity period, or up to the expiration date of their passport, whichever occurs first. Only a border services officer at the port of entry can determine the length of stay of a temporary resident upon their arrival to Canada. A Visitor Record will only be issued if a border services officer believes that a foreign national should be limited to a stay of less than six months in length. The Visitor Record would indicate the date by which the individual would have to leave Canada.
Normally, temporary residents are authorized to stay for up to six months, but this may be reduced at the port of entry. If a temporary resident needs to stay in Canada longer, they must apply to extend your stay thirty days before the expiration of their temporary resident status and will require proof of sufficient funds and a medical exam for their application.

threads.subject: PID-2018-0049 FW: Interpretation of 36(3)(c) aquittal-REP-2018-0111
threads.question:
Good day,
I am hoping to receive clarification on IRPA 36(3)(c) which states that inadmissibility under subsections (1) and
(2) may not be based on a conviction in respect of which a record suspension has been ordered and has not been revoked or ceased to have effect under the Criminal Records Act, or in respect of which there has been a final determination of an acquittal; My question is whether an Order for a Dismissal has the same affect on inadmissibility as a final determination of an acquittal. If an individual commits a crime and is inadmissible under 36(2)(c) does a dismissal of the charges against the individual, without trial, remedy the inadmissibility? Thank you for clarifying this point for me. I will be sure to share the result with my colleagues.
Regards,
mmigration, Refugees
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
Thank you for reaching out to the Immigration Representatives inbox with your questions and or request for clarification.
As you probably are aware, we don't have “orders of dismissal” in Canada but generally speaking if charges get dropped, the person is not inadmissible for that act.
That said, outside of Canada can be a different story when referring to Foreign Judicial processes. See section 36(1)(c)
“committing an act”.
These provisions cannot be used where the person has been acquitted. Similarly, when a court has made a finding of not guilty, the process and the decision will be respected and negate any reasonable grounds to believe that the person committed the offence.
However, if a foreign investigating authority decides not to lay or proceed with charges in a country whose criminal justice concepts are similar to ours, (Germany or Australia for example) it should be assumed that a crime was not committed or that there was insufficient evidence to obtain a conviction.
The legislation requires the Minister or the Minister's delegate to consider a completed application for criminal rehabilitation. The Minister's delegate will conduct an equivalency analysis of the act committed, the disposition and the outcomes in order to take a final decision. There are some similarities when referring to an acquittal and an order for dismissal in that both are signed by a judge. That said, an acquittal is the result of an onerous process that gives both the defendant and the prosecution a chance to present evidence in which a judge/jury renders a decision whereas an order for dismissal is the result of a lack of evidence or jurisdiction.
The officer will review the complete application in order to render his or her decision on the rehabilitation application. Rehabilitation will be granted when the Minister or the delegated authority is satisfied that the person concerned meets either the deemed rehabilitation criteria or the individual rehabilitation criteria and is highly unlikely to become involved in any further criminal activities.In addition, the officer may require further documentation (beyond what the applicant has submitted) in order to be satisfied that the applicant is not criminally inadmissible.
We trust that the following information will be useful to you and to your colleagues.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

they are exempt from the requirement for a temporary resident visa and their job falls within the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (i.e., they are required to obtain an LMIA) and a positive or neutral LMIA has been issued by the time they arrive ●they are a national or permanent resident of the U.S., Greenland or Saint-Pierre and Miquelon regardless of whether their job falls with the Temporary Foreign Worker Program or the International Mobility Program they will not be working as a live-in caregiver or as a seasonal agricultural worker The following individuals may apply from within Canada ([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/persons-who-may-apply-within-canada.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/persons-who-may-apply-within-canada.html)): holders of work or study permits and their family members; persons currently working in Canada under the authority of R186, not requiring a work permit, and who are applying for secondary employment in Canada as long as they are not business visitors; ●holders of temporary resident permits valid for a minimum of six months and their family members; refugee claimants and persons subject to an unenforceable removal order; ●in-Canada permanent resident applicants and their family members who are members of the following classes, determined eligible for permanent resident status: live-in caregiver, spouse or common-law partner, protected persons, persons filing an application on humanitarian and compassionate grounds; •persons whose work permits were authorized by a mission abroad, where the permit was not issued at a port of entry; Mexican citizens who have been admitted to Canada as temporary residents may apply for a work permit under any North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) category. U.S. citizens admitted as temporary residents may apply in Canada under the professional or intra-company transferee NAFTA categories only. These provisions are in accordance with reciprocal arrangements; foreign nationals who have the written permission of the Department of Foreign Affairs, Trade and Development to work at a foreign mission (embassy, consulate or high commission) in Canada. Finally, I will draw your attention to the page on the 120-day exemption: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-)
1* citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-
workers/researcher-exemption.html. You will note the following under the section entitled "Implied status":
Section R201 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations allows a foreign national to apply for a renewal of their work permit only if the application is made before their work permit expires. Paragraph R186(u) allows a foreign national to continue working under the same conditions in the event that they submitted an application under section R201 and a decision on the renewal of their application has not yet been made.
Foreign workers entering Canada under the 120-day work permit exemption for researchers or the short-term (15- or 30-day) work permit exemption do not have a work permit, so regulations governing work permit renewals [R201 and R186(u)] do not apply. If they were admitted for 6 months at the port of entry, they can stay as visitors until the end of the period authorized for their stay, but they cannot work past the period allowed by the exemption unless otherwise authorized. Those foreign nationals must submit their initial work permit applications online or via a visa application centre overseas.
In regards to your second question, I will draw your attention to the section on “Renewals" found at the same location as the link above:
Applicants may be granted this 120-day work permit exemption only once within a 12-month period.
Example of a 12-month period
Foreign nationals may be able to use the 120-day exemption offered for research activities as well as the 15- or 30-day exemption. However, foreign nationals must ensure the required amount of time has elapsed since they last used a short-term work permit exemption.
Foreign nationals who have already used the 120-day research exemption must wait 12 months before using this exemption again.
The following cases provide guidance for when foreign nationals may be granted the 120-day exemption, or short-term work permit exemptions if they have previously benefited from the 120-day exemption.
If a foreign national has benefited from the 120-day exemption, they may be granted one of the following:
a subsequent 120-day exemption if they have not been granted a short-term work permit exemption in the last 12 months a 15-day exemption once 6 months have elapsed since the 120-day exemption was granted a 30-day exemption once 12 months have elapsed since the 120-day exemption was granted As such, you will note that these specific exemptions can only be used once within the prescribed timeframes.
As it relates to separate exemptions as per R186, however, the individual would have to apply for a visitor record extension and provide all supporting documentation and rationale to support their eligibility for a different work permit exemption. Specifically regarding the exemption for self-funded researchers under R186(a), please note that the officer must be satisfied that the foreign worker is a genuine business visitor. Please see the following for additional information regarding self-funded researchers: Foreign nationals engaged in self-funded research or observational internships (job shadowing) may fall under the
business visitor category, which could include “research and design” activities for those conducting independent
research or research for a foreign entity. There should be no displacement of Canadian or permanent resident workers, nor should there be any employer-employee relationship. In addition, the individual or the Canadian institution must not receive remuneration for the research. There is the presumption of a foreign employer, as
o the primary source of the worker's remuneration remains outside Canada;
o the principal place of the worker's employer is located outside Canada;
o the accrual of profits of the worker's employer is located outside Canada.
I trust that the above information is of assistance.

threads.subject: Response: Questions of Residency Obligation calculations after appeal being allowed at IAD-REP-2017-2088
threads.question:
Dear Sir or Madam,
Questions of Residency Obligation calculations after appeal being allowed at lAD.
1) Please assume that PR of Canada is found NOT to have met the residency obligation upon application for PRTD. The PR appeals to lAD and wins the case at lAD after 3 years by teleconference (assume he won on either by Error of fact or Error of Law or Humanitarian issues) since the appellant did not receive a PRTD to return to Canada. After Appeal is allowed a PRTD is issued and the person returns to Canada and is issued a 5 year PR card. Questions How does IRCC consider the 2 years outside of Canada awaiting IAD decision? For Residency Obligation calculations at a future date, is the person, considered to have been in Canada or outside Canada during the time awaiting lAD decision outside Canada? Does the answer above depend on the reason that the appeal was allowed (for example, what if it was an error in law or fact)? If the time considered during the appeal process is time outside Canada (and is more that three years), then must this person stay in Canada (upon entering Canada after winning the appeal and issuance of PRTD) exclusively for the next 730 days? Because if he leaves for even a day, he may be found not to have complied with his residency obligations?
We look forward to hearing from you.
Thank you and best regards,
threads.answer:
Good day,
Assuming the person was outside Canada and filed the appeal within the prescribed 60-day timeline, the person remains a PR while the lAD reviews the case and renders its final decision, regardless of the reason for which the appeal was allowed.
Time spent outside Canada awaiting the lAD decision is considered as time outside Canada.
To meet the residency obligation, a PR must comply with the requirements of A28 with respect to every five-year period immediately before the examination. So to answer your question above, it means that, on each of 730 days in that five-year period, the PR must meet the requirements listed under A28(2)(a). There are provisions under that paragraph that allow a PR to be outside Canada and still meet the residency requirement.
I trust the above answers your questions.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Current policy guidelines for the issuance of LMIA-exempt work permits [exemption code A75] for foreign nationals who currently resides in Quebec provide that the applicant must hold a valid Certificat de sélection du Québec (CSQ) at the time of the application for work permit.

majority of duties in the NOC description, a change of conditions would be warranted.
However, in this case, our concern is that the permit has a specific job title listed and the Offer of Employment was also submitted with a specific job title. For this reason, we are unsure if a change in job title would warrant the need for a new work permit. threads.answer:
Good day,
Question
Is a new Offer of Employment and Work Permit required? Our concern is that the permit has a specific job title listed and the Offer of Employment was also submitted with a specific job title. For this reason, we are unsure if a change in job title would warrant the need for a new work permit. The working conditions and information supplied in the Offer of Employment remain substantially the same.
Answer
While the job title is printed on the work permit, it is the National Occupational Code (NOC) that we assess against when issuing the work permit and conducting compliance inspections. There are usually many different titles associated to a single NOC code. As long as the duties, education requirements, salary, etc. of the occupation continue to match the NOC code then there should be no requirement for changing the work permit, and therefore, no requirement to submit a new offer of employment through the Employer Portal.
As per the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act Regulations (IRPR), a foreign worker is only required to obtain a new work permit when the employer, work location or occupation changes.
The employer is required [R209.2(1)(b)] to retain all documents related to the employment of the foreign worker for up to six years after the date of issuance of the work permit, including details about the title change, to ensure information can be provided to an IRCC officer in the event of an inspection.
For more information, see the section "Occupation, Wages and Working Conditions" in the Employer Compliance Inspections page on the IRCC website.
We trust this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
FW: Can a student use valid study permit for more than one program-REP-2018-0422
This is in response to your enquiry regarding the validity of a study permit after a student's graduation.
As per IRPR 222(1)(a), a study permit becomes invalid upon the first to occur of the following days:
(a) the day that is 90 days after the day on which the permit holder completes their studies,
(b) the day on which a removal order made against the permit holder becomes enforceable, or
(c) the day on which the permit expires.
If the student continues on with their studies within the 90 days of completing their studies, their study permit does not become invalid, thus they may start their new program under their current study permit. In case if the student plans to start a new program more than 90 days after completing their studies, their original study permit will be invalid, they will need to apply for a new study permit.

From Dear Sir or Madam,
Thank you for your response. However, this response appears to contradict the wording of IRPR 188 and IRCC's policy interpreting R188. See highlighted sections below. Please advise regarding which authority is correct-your email or IRCC's website.
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/who-needs-study-permit.html#courses
"Short-term courses [R188(1)(c)]
Foreign nationals may enter Canada or remain in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study of 6 months' duration or less [R188(1)(c)]. This exemption helps to facilitate access to short-term courses, regardless of their subject matter. The course or program of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry (i.e., up to 6 months).
While a study permit is not required for short-term courses, an officer must accept and process an application for a study permit, even when the duration of the course or program of study is 6 months or less [R188(2)].
Holding a study permit for short-term courses may allow students to apply later, from within Canada [R215(1)(a)], to renew or change the conditions of their study permit for further studies. Study permit holders may also be eligible to participate in work programs that are available to international students [R186(f) and R205].
The duration of the course or program of study is often a more important consideration than the number of months the foreign national intends to study. With the exception of exchange programs, even if foreign nationals plan to study for 6 months or less, if the course or program is longer than 6 months, they need a study permit.
While a foreign national may attend a short-term course or program without a study permit at a non-DLI, they may not be issued a study permit to attend courses at a non-DLI [R216(e)].
Subsequent course or program of study
Generally, foreign nationals in Canada without a study permit wishing to enrol in a subsequent course or program of study must apply outside Canada and obtain a study permit in the normal manner (e.g., at a Canadian visa office abroad).
Foreign nationals without a study permit will not be granted an extension of their authorized stay as a visitor simply for the purpose of completing a short-term course or program of less than 6 months that would last beyond their original authorized period of stay. Paragraph R188(1)(c) was not put in place to allow foreign nationals to take short-term courses, one after the other, simply by extending their temporary resident status—in effect, making it possible for them to complete a whole certificate, diploma or degree without ever having a study permit. (IRCC) recognizes that long-term visitors and foreign workers may engage in occasional studies or programs of study lasting 6 months or less at any time during their stay in Canada.
It is therefore recommended that foreign nationals be encouraged to apply for a study permit for a short-term course or program of study if they intend to apply for another program afterwards or work on the campus of the university or college at which they are a full-time student. Section R215 provides an exemption to allow certain foreign nationals to apply for a study permit after entry to Canada."
Best regards/Meilleures salutations,
Lnmanon

## Good day,
Question: Can the holder of an open work permit (issued in the context of an in-Canada spousal sponsorship) study in Canada without a study permit pursuant to IRPR 188(1)(c) despite the following condition on the open work permit : "Unless authorized, prohibited from attending any educational institution, or taking any academic, professional or vocational training course."

A foreign national is authorized to study in Canada without a study permit under section 188(1)(c).

Answer: The employer compliance fee is refunded when:
1. the work permit is refused; or
2. the employer withdraws the offer of employment and requests a refund before the work permit is issued.
If the work permit application is refused, the processing office should initiate a refund of the employer compliance fee to the employer in accordance with standard guidelines.
If the work permit is refused at the POE, the employer's offer of employment is not matched to a work permit and therefore its status remains “pending". This ensures that the employer can trigger the refund by withdrawing the offer of employment in the Employer Portal once their worker has informed them of being refused.

threads.subject: Parental Sponsorship -URGENT-REP-2018-0434
threads.question:
Dear team, I hope you are well. I have some urgent questions for one of our VIP clients, I hope you can help:
1. How many rounds of sponsor selection happens in a year?
2. Is the sponsor section random?
3. If the sponsor selection is random, what happens if a sponsor is not selected 2-3-4 years in a row?
4. If the sponsor is not selected, is there an option to apply for PR for the parents, based on H&C grounds? If not, what are the available options? Thank you very much for your responses. Kind regards,
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your questions.
Please note that all the responses to your questions can be found on our website under Sponsor your parents and grandparents. Please ensure you check the website before sending questions to the mailbox.
1. How many rounds of sponsor selection happens in a year? If additional rounds of selection are required in 2018, it will be announced on Twitter, Facebook and on the Department's website. If an additional round of selection is announced, persons who have successfully completed and submitted the Interest to Sponsor form between January 2ⁿd — February 1st, 2018, are encouraged to check the email account they used when they submitted their Interest to Sponsor form as well as their junk mail folder.
2. Is the sponsor section random? I will assume the question is whether sponsor selection is random. Yes, sponsor selection is random. The Interest to Sponsor web form opens for 30 days on the first working day of each calendar year. This year, the Interest to Sponsor form closed at noon on February 1, 2018. Once the web form closed, submissions were reviewed and duplicates removed. The remaining submissions were randomized and persons were randomly selected. Potential sponsors that are selected are sent a letter of invitation by email to submit a complete application within 60 days.
3. If the sponsor selection is random, what happens if a sponsor is not selected 2-3-4 years in a row? Persons who are not selected to sponsor their parents and grandparents under the randomized selection intake process each year can reunite with their loved ones in Canada by applying for a Super Visa as an alternative. The Super Visa is a multiple entry visa issued for up to ten years that supports family reunification by allowing applicants to remain in Canada for up to two years without the need to renew their status. The Super Visa assists with the long-term sustainability of the PGP program by encouraging temporary residence as an alternative to entering the permanent residence queue.
4. If the sponsor is not selected, is there an option to apply for PR for the parents, based on H&C grounds? If not, what are the available options? As per Ministerial Instructions that came into force on January 1, 2017, there is no authority for acceptance and processing of applications for humanitarian and compassionate consideration for persons outside of Canada. Specifically, “a request made under subsection 25(1) of the Act from outside Canada and that accompanies an application that was not accepted for processing under these Ministerial Instructions, will not be processed." This means that requests for humanitarian and compassionate consideration for persons outside of Canada will not be accepted unless the sponsor was selected under the Randomized Selection Intake process and submitted a sponsorship application.
We trust this information addresses your questions.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
