threads.question:
#### Dear Immigration Representatives:
We were hoping for your guidance and advise on an intersection of Aboriginal law and Immigration law that neither the Aboriginal Affairs Canada nor the US Embassy were able to speak to.
The general questions are:
1. Are individuals with valid Indian Status granted by Aboriginal Affairs Canada (formerly Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada), considered Canadian citizens automatically?
2. Or, are individuals with valid Indian Status granted by Aboriginal Affairs Canada (formerly Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada), but without Canadian citizenship/passport, given the same permission from an immigration perspective with respect to working in Canada?
3. Or, are individuals with valid Indian Status generally exempt from the requirement for a work permit in Canada just as they are generally exempt from the requirement for a study permit (pursuant to s 188(1)(d) of the Immigration and Refugees Protection Regulations)?
4. If none of the above, please confirm if all foreign nationals, regardless of Indian Status, are required to obtain a work permit in Canada to work, if they are neither Canadian permanent residents nor citizens. The specific question is:
Would a US citizen with a Laminated Certificate of Indian Status (which does not have an expiry date and is still considered valid by Aboriginal Affairs Canada) issued by Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada require a work permit in Canada to work?
Thank you very much for your consideration of these questions. We look forward to your response.
Regards,
Lnfomn
threads.answer:
Good day,
Question:
The general questions are:
1. Are individuals with valid Indian Status granted by Aboriginal Affairs Canada (formerly Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada), considered Canadian citizens automatically?
2. Or, are individuals with valid Indian Status granted by Aboriginal Affairs Canada (formerly Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada), but without Canadian citizenship/passport, given the same permission from an immigration perspective with respect to working in Canada?
3. Or, are individuals with valid Indian Status generally exempt from the requirement for a work permit in Canada just as they are generally exempt from the requirement for a study permit (pursuant to s 188(1)(d) of the Immigration and Refugees Protection Regulations)?
4. If none of the above, please confirm if all foreign nationals, regardless of Indian Status, are required to obtain a work permit in Canada to work, if they are neither Canadian permanent residents nor citizens.
The specific question is:
Would a US citizen with a Laminated Certificate of Indian Status (which does not have an expiry date and is still considered valid by Aboriginal Affairs Canada) issued by Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada require a work permit in Canada to work?
Response:
Status Indians born outside of Canada have the same right to acquire citizenship by descent as any other person, but there are no special provisions that take into consideration Indian status or cross-border Indian lands when determining automatic acquisition of citizenship. Under the Citizenship Act, in order to automatically acquire Canadian citizenship by birth outside of Canada, a person would need to have been born to a parent who was either (1) born in Canada, or (2) naturalized in Canada before that person was born. Please note: since April 17, 2009, claims of citizenship by descent have been limited to the first generation born outside of Canada (with exceptions made for the children and grandchildren of persons who were serving Crown servants of Canada).
For more information about applying for a certificate of citizenship, see [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/proof-citizenship/apply.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/proof-citizenship/apply.html).
If a status Indian is not a citizen of Canada by descent, that person can apply to be granted citizenship, using the date of registration as a status Indian (or the date of entry to Canada, if the registration took place prior to entry), as the equivalent of the date of permanent residence (permanent residence being a requirement to be granted under section 5 of the Act). For more information about applying for a grant of citizenship, see: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-)
mmigration, Refugees
citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/apply.html#toc0.
As per Section A18 ([http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/l-2.5/FullText.html](http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/l-2.5/FullText.html)) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, every person must appear for an examination to determine if they have a right to enter Canada. Under Section A19(1)
([http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/l-2.5/FullText.html](http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/l-2.5/FullText.html)), every person registered has the right to enter and remain in
Canada. Section A19(1) stipulates that an officer shall allow the person to enter Canada if satisfied following an examination that the person is a Registered Indian. Officers must be satisfied that all admissibility requirements have been met before admitting a foreign national. A Certificate of Indian Status ([http://www.aadnc-](http://www.aadnc-)
aandc.gc.ca/eng/1100100032424/1100100032428) issued by Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada (INAC) is considered proof of Indian status.
If the Border Services Officer is satisfied that the applicant is a registered member of a Canadian Indian Band, yes, they may legally work in Canada. However, to work in Canada they would require a Social Insurance Number ([http://www.esdc.gc.ca/en/sin/before_applying.page](http://www.esdc.gc.ca/en/sin/before_applying.page)) and to obtain one as a registered Indian, they must provide their Birth Certificate and Certificate of Indian Status.
In the absence of proof of Registered Indian status, a person seeking entry to Canada would be deemed to be a Temporary
Resident, and depending on the type of work, would require a work permit ([http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/work/apply-](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/work/apply-)
how.asp) until they applied for and received a Certificate of Indian Status.
We trust this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
From ## Dear Immigration Representatives:
Are spouses of R205(a) Canadian Interest (significant benefit) workers eligible for open work permits? The C41 exemption, R199(e), and R205(c)(ii) are the provisions I am looking at.
These would include intra company transferees, cultural/artistic workers and entrepreneurs.

mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
REP-2018-0370
Good day,
Please accept our apologies for the delay in responding.
Question: Are spouses of R205(a) Canadian Interest (significant benefit) workers eligible for open work permits? The C41 exemption, R199(e), and R205(c)(ii) are the provisions I am looking at.
These would include intra company transferees, cultural/artistic workers and entrepreneurs.
I assume so, as spouses of our R205(a) clients have received many such permits in the past, but we have recently been told by CBSA at a port of entry that they are not eligible.
Is there any situation where the spouse of a R205(a) Canadian Interests worker would not be eligible for an open work permit, assuming s/he meets all the other requirements?
Response:
If the principal worker is employed in an occupation in skill type 0 or level A or B of the National Occupational Code, their spouse or common-law partner may themselves be authorized to work without first having an offer of employment. A dependent spouse or common-law partner is eligible to apply for an open work permit if the principal foreign worker
holds a work permit that is valid for a period of at least six months, or, if working under the authority of section R186 without a work permit, presents evidence that they will be working for a minimum of six months; is employed in an occupation that falls within National Occupational Classification (NOC) skill levels 0, A or B (which
generally include management and professional occupations and technical or skilled trades [see the NOC websitel);
physically resides or plans to physically reside in Canada while working.
Please refer to International Mobility Program: Public policy, competitiveness and economy for more information.
If intra company transferees, cultural/artistic workers and entrepreneurs are employed in an occupation that falls within NOC 0, A or B, then their dependent spouses or common-law partners would be eligible to apply for an open work permit provided they meet all other requirements.
For example, spouses or common-law partners of foreign nationals, who are eligible to apply for a work permit under the Start-up Visa, may be eligible to apply for an open work permit as the spouse or common-law partner of high skilled worker. The same rule applies to spouses or common-law partners of foreign workers who are eligible to apply for a work permit under LMIA-exemption code C11 as entrepreneurs.
I trust that the above information is of assistance.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Implied status and authorization to work-REP-2018-0385
threads.question:
To whom it may concern,
If an applicant is in Canada with an open work permit (post-graduate) and they have applied for an open work permit as they have a pending application for permanent residence in the spouse in Canada class before the expiry of their current permit, does the Applicant have the right to continue working after the expiry of
the post-graduate work permit until a decision in the new work permit application?
Many thanks,
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Thank you for your question regarding implied status and authorization to work pending a decision on an open work permit application.
Question:
If an applicant is in Canada with an open work permit (post-graduate) and they have applied for an open work permit as they have a pending application for permanent residence in the spouse in Canada class before the expiry of their current permit, does the Applicant have the right to continue working after the expiry of the post-graduate work permit until a decision in the new work permit application?
Response:
Section R201 allows foreign nationals to apply for a renewal of their work permit only if the application is made before their present work permit expires. Paragraph R186(u) authorizes foreign nationals to work without a permit in the event that they submitted an application under section R201 and a decision on the renewal application has not yet been made.
Note: It is not “implied status" under subsections R183(5) and (6) that allows a foreign national to keep working
while their application for extension is in process. The foreign national must meet the requirements of paragraph R186(u). Paragraph R186(u) applies only until a decision is made on the original work permit renewal application.
It should be noted that “status" and “authorization" are separate in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). A foreign national who submits the “Application to change conditions or extend my stay in Canada – Worker" application form [IMM 5710] is in effect submitting two applications in one. The foreign national is applying under section R181 for an “extension of status" and under section R201 of to “renew the work permit”. If submitted before the expiry of their present work permit, this combined application has 3 effects:
1. Should a decision not be made on the “application" under section R181 before the expiration of their present status, the foreign national will be allowed to remain by operation of law (implied status) under subsection R183(5).
2. The application for renewal under section R201 triggers the ability for the foreign national to “work without a permit" under paragraph R186(u), unless they leave Canada.
3. Any conditions imposed on the initial work permit carry over into the implied status period under subsection R183(6). For example, if a person held an open work permit, they may continue working for any employer until a positive decision made on the new work application (open work permit in this case) or the application is refused.
I trust that the above information is of assistance.
Lnformon
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Question:

Foreign nationals are allowed to exit and re-enter Canada within the prescribed time frame (15 or 30 consecutive days) of work under the exemption. However, the authorized work period begins on the date the exemption is granted and is counted consecutively, regardless of whether the person is actually working in Canada. Any travel outside Canada after the date the exemption was granted will not extend the length of the exemption period. Example of travelling during the exemption period: The foreign national was granted a 15-day exemption on August 1,
2017. If they travel outside Canada for 2 days within that 15-day period (August 6 to August 7, 2017), they may resume work activities on August 8 under this exemption until August 15, 2017, only. Officers at the port of entry should be satisfied that the 15 or 30 consecutive days under the short-term work permit exemption have not elapsed and that the foreign national is admissible to Canada. Please refer to Public Policy: Short-term work permit exemption for more information. I trust that the above information is of assistance.
Sincerely,

threads.subject: Question regarding Arranged Employment-REP-2018-0457
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam:
I have a question in respect to Arranged Employment under Express Entry. I understand that if an applicant holds a closed work permit and works in a qualifying NOC O, A or B position for at least one year, he/she qualifies for either 50 or 200 points. However, if the applicant was on an open work permit (ie: post-graduate work permit) for half of their qualifying work experience, and the other half on an employer-specific work permit, would they still qualify for the 50 or 200 points, or must they work on the closed work permit for the full year, despite having worked in that position previously under the closed work permit?
Thank you,
migration, Refugees
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
threads.answer:
Hello Ms.
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox. We hope you will find the answer to your question below of assistance.
Question: If the applicant was on an open work permit (ie: post-graduate work permit) for half of their qualifying work experience, and the other half on an employer-specific work permit, would they still qualify for the 50 or 200 points, or must they work on the closed work permit for the full year, despite having worked in that position previously under the closed work permit?
Answer: Yes. Work acquired under an open work permit followed by an employer specific's work permit for the same employer performing the same job counts for the purpose of satisfying the requirements s.29(2)(a)(ii) or s.29(2)(a)(iii), of a qualifying offer of arranged employment.
The only distinction is:
- Those who got their employer specific's work permit based on an LMIA s.29(2)(a)(ii) don't need to have "one year over a continuous period of time" for the job offer to be valid.
Those who got their employer specific's work permit by being exempted from an LMlA s.29(2)(a)(iii), need to meet the "one year over a continuous period of time" requirement for the same employer in the same position for the job offer to be valid.

Question: we have a client who is a He has been in Ontario on a visitor record issued pursuant to 186(I) for over two years. He would like to apply for permanent residence. He has a continuing offer of employment from his employer Is he eligible for the 50 points for persons who have worked for their Canadian employer in Canada for a year and have a job offer for at least a year following obtaining permanent residency? The amendments to the Regulations seem to specify that the worker must be on a "work permit" however, the policy behind issuing visitor records rather than work permits to clergy was to facilitate their entry and to eliminate the fee required for a work permit. It would seem strange that a facilitative policy under one category would then negatively affect a worker's prospects under another category. Can you clarify?
Answer: An offer of employment to a person working under R186(I) would not generally earn points for arranged employment in the Comprehensive Ranking System.
In order for a job offer to qualify for comprehensive ranking system points (excluding applicants invited to apply under FST), it must meet the criteria below:
(a) an arranged employment as defined in subsection 82(1) of the Regulations, if

threads.subject: eTAs and the duty to report a change in circumstances
threads.question:
Dear Sir or Madam,
I have a general question regarding eTAs. Does the eTA system create a duty to apply for a new eTA in the event that a foreign national subsequently becomes inadmissible to Canada?
Perhaps this example will allow you to better understand what I am getting at: UK citizen applies for an eTA to visit Canada. 6 months after being issued the eTA, he commits, is arrested and then convicted for an incident which creates an inadmissibility to Canada. He then approaches me to assist him with obtaining a Canadian Work Permit. My thinking here is that the eTA he was previously issued would permit him to board the plane but does not permit him entry to Canada. Is it permissible for him to travel on his still valid eTA and when he arrives at a Canadian POE, he applies for his Temporary Resident Permit and Work Permit? Or should he first apply for a TRP at a consulate and then have a new eTA issued to him?
In addition, does a foreign national also have to apply for a new eTA if certain circumstances change, like marital status, employer, etc.?
I'm wondering what situation creates a need to apply for a new eTA as the online materials are silent on this subject.
Thank you in advance for your reply.
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
### FW: eTAs and the duty to report a change in circumstances-REP-2018-0554
Foreign nationals may reapply if a mistake was made on their initial eTA application or if their information changes. Please refer to our website for more information.
If a client has an approved eTA application, and subsequently applies for another immigration document with derogatory information (ex. Criminality), an officer will proceed to make an admissibility determination on their file. If the determination is negative, the previously approved eTA will be cancelled, but the officer may consider issuing a TRP.
eTA's are not issued alongside a TRP. A client can apply for a TRP only after a finding of inadmissibility has been made. The client should check the visa office responsible for their country or region to find out about its specific application procedures. Visa-exempt foreign nationals who have been issued a TRP by an overseas office to permit travel to Canada will be able to board a plane to Canada, so long as their TRP document remains valid and they have the appropriate travel document (e.g. a passport) in their possession.
In the situation you've outlined below, we would recommend that the client apply to the appropriate overseas office for his work permit so that he obtain the necessary documents prior to travel to Canada.
Kind regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

For all Express Entry programs an applicant's CRS score is automatically recorded in GCMS at the time when •their ITA is issued; and
their e-APR is submitted (for the last time).
An officer will compare the CRS score and information in the applicant's profile at the time of the round of invitations to the information in their e-APR to ensure that the applicant meets the requirements of section A11.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
Any change in circumstance declared in an e-APR will result in the CRS score being adjusted accordingly. If an applicant's offer of arranged employment became invalid prior to submitting their e-APR, the points previously assigned for arranged employment would be subtracted from the applicant's CRS score.
However, after an e-APR is submitted, an application cannot be refused due to a change in circumstance unless:
the officer determines that the change occurred before the applicant submitted their e-APR and that the
change would have caused the applicant to be refused under section A11.2: therefore, the application
should be refused under section A11.2; or
•the change in circumstance means the applicant no longer meets the minimum requirements of the
program to which they are applying; therefore, the application may still meet the requirements of section
A11.2 but can be refused for failing to meet program requirements.
Therefore if an applicant's offer of arranged employment became invalid after having submitted their e-APR, and this change in circumstance would not result in the applicant no longer meeting the minimum requirements of the program they were invited under, this would not result in the application being refused.

threads.answer:
FW: Interpretation of Partner for ICT CETA-REP-2018-0170
You have asked whether the term "partner" in the definition of intra-corporate transferee (ICT) in the CETA's Temporary Entry Chapter "includes a shareholder (i.e. part owner of a EU corporation) and holds an executive position with the EU organization (i.e. not an employee)." In our view, whether or not a person qualifies as a "partner in an enterprise" for the purpose of the ICT category may be generally understood as an individual, under contract or understanding, that shares in the profits and losses of a lawful commerce or business. The simplest example would be a partner in a firm, with a partnership agreement. A shareholder holding an executive position would appear to better fall under the category of "investors" for the purposes of the CETA's TE Chapter's definition of "key personnel".

threads.answer:
Good day, Question: I would kind ask you to provide clarification on the allowed activities for a valid B-1 Visitor-Business visa in the event the foreign national, B-1 visa holder, would be required to travel to Canada to complete a short after-sales services assignment. It is my understanding that work without a work permit, after-sales services provision is typically associated with WX-1 visa as I have seen marked in passport in a few cases. Is this correct? Does this mean that a regular B-1 Visitor-Business visa does not allow any after-sales services activities and a new visa (WX-1) would need to be applied for to request entry to Canada under after-sales services provision?
Response: As per s.186(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, activities carried out by "business visitors" are defined in s.187, as follows: Business visitors 187 (1) For the purposes of paragraph 186(a), a business visitor to Canada is a foreign national who is described in subsection (2) or who seeks to engage in international business activities in Canada without directly entering the Canadian labour market. Specific cases
(2) The following foreign nationals are business visitors:
(a) foreign nationals purchasing Canadian goods or services for a foreign business or government, or receiving training or familiarization in respect of such goods or services;
(b) foreign nationals receiving or giving training within a Canadian parent or subsidiary of the corporation that employs them outside Canada, if any production of goods or services that results from the training is incidental; and
(c) foreign nationals representing a foreign business or government for the purpose of selling goods for that business or government, if the foreign national is not engaged in making sales to the general public in Canada.
Factors
(3) For the purpose of subsection (1), a foreign national seeks to engage in international business activities in Canada without directly entering the Canadian labour market only if
(a) the primary source of remuneration for the business activities is outside Canada; and
(b) the principal place of business and actual place of accrual of profits remain predominately outside Canada.
mmigration, Refugees
According to guidance on the IRCC website, after sales and lease services may be part of the activities of a business visitor, under s.187(c):
After-sales and lease services
After-sales and lease services include those provided by persons repairing and servicing, supervising installers, and setting up and testing commercial or industrial equipment (including computer software). Setting up does not include hands-on installation generally performed by construction or building trades (electricians, pipe fitters, etc.). Section R187 also applies to persons seeking entry to repair or service specialized equipment purchased or leased outside Canada, provided the service is being performed as part of the original or extended sales agreement, lease/rental agreement, warranty or service contract. After-sales and lease services also include situations where the sales or lease agreement or purchase order is for a software upgrade to operate previously sold or leased equipment. A service person coming to Canada to install, configure or give training on the upgraded software should receive consideration as a business visitor, as long as the after-sales or lease services activity is clearly articulated in the new sales or lease agreement or purchase order. A sales or lease agreement or purchase order for upgraded software is a new contract for a new product. As with NAFTA, hands-on building and construction work is not covered by this provision. As such, if the visa was issued by an officer who assessed the intent of the applicant to carry out activities as defined above, the applicant would effectively be a business visitor.
We trust this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

We have two non-client specific questions:
Are Canadian visa offices abroad required to enforce removal orders by issuing a Certificate of Departure when specifically requested to do so by way of an application in compliance with ENF10, s28 and ENF10,28.5?

Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
HKONGIMMIGRATION@international.gc.ca
REP-2018-0191
Thank you for sending us your questions and trust that the following information will be useful to you.
Foreign nationals subject to a removal order don't always know or understand that they have to verify their departure before leaving Canada, or simply do not want to. In order to address the oversight of a foreign national inadvertently failing to confirm their departure at the POE, the Immigration Refugee Protection Regulations provides for a very specific and narrow set of circumstances in which an officer at a mission abroad may verify departure and enforce an unforced removal order.
Specifically, 240(2) of the IRPR states:
If a foreign national against whom a removal order has not been enforced is applying outside Canada for a visa, an ARC or an electronic travel authorization, an officer shall enforce the order if, following an examination, the foreign national establishes that:
a) they are the person described in the order; (It is up to the officer to reach a determination on whether the requirement under R240(2)(a) has been met)
b) demonstrating that they were lawfully admitted to the country in which they are physically present at the time that the application is made; and
c) proving that they are not a threat to security, have not violated human or international rights and have not been involved in serious or organized criminality.
To maintain the integrity of the immigration system, section 240(2) of the IRPR holds that in order for an unenforceable removal order to be enforced outside of Canada, the subject of the removal order must be making an application to an officer for a permanent resident visa (PRV), a temporary resident visa (TRV), an electronic travel authorization (eTA) or an
ARC by an officer.
Effectively, this means that under the current immigration system, an unenforced removal order can only be enforced in one of two ways: if the individual subject to the removal order presents themselves at a POE or if they apply for a visa/eTA or ARC from outside of Canada and can satisfy the officer that they have been lawfully admitted to the country in which they are applying from and are not inadmissible to Canada on serious grounds.
We trust that this information will be useful to you.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Les demandes de parrainage dans la catégorie du regroupement familial doivent répondre aux exigences de la Loi sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés et son règlement. threads.subject: spousal sponsorship-child born ex wedlock-former USSR-REP-2018-0555
threads.question:
To Immigration Representatives Portal:
My questions may require some background information.
In the Soviet Union from 1968 onwards, the birth certificate of a child born out of wedlock was often accompanied with a second certificate, issued to single mothers for social security purposes (called here “single mother certificate”) explaining that the information in the birth registration records about the child's father was entered according to the mother's instructions, pursuant to a certain section of the Family Code. This naming practice was, and still is done in a number of former Soviet republics to protect the child from the stigma of having no father on her birth certificate. Mothers give the child her family name and then, a first name and patronymic as she wishes. Some choose to give a patronymic based on their own father's first name, while others can make up a name. In any case, there is a legal presumption that the name of the child's father is fictitious. I had this question arise several years ago in an Ontario adoption from Ukraine and, to dispense with the requirement for the father's consent to the adoption, and so that the adopting father could be named on the new birth certificate, the Ontario court was provided with (a) the legal opinion of a Ukrainian lawyer explaining the existence and implications of this “legal fiction" and (b) a statutory declaration from the Immigration Program Manager at the Canadian Embassy in Ukraine whose immigration section was familiar with this practice. However, these 2 documents were submitted for court purposes in an adoption, and not for a sponsorship.
While in Ukraine the unwed mother's application form to name the newborn according to her wishes, refers to the an article of the Family Code that specifically deals with the mother's instructions in such cases, the single mother certificate in Kyrgyzstan for some reason refers to an article of the national Marriage and Family Code (article 70) that says nothing about the mother's instructions in such cases.
Questions:
(1) In the case of a spousal sponsorship from a Kyrgyzstan, where a child of the female applicant was born out of wedlock and is still under 18 years of age, will this single mother's certificate obviate the need for Declaration of Non-Accompanying Parent IMM-5406, i.e., the additional certificate stating that the information about the father in the child's birth record was entered according to the mother's instructions, citing a section of the national Marriage and Family Code, or would it be advisable to include the legal opinion of a local lawyer, etc., as was done for the court in the above-mentioned adoption?
(2) Is the certificate for Kyrgyzstan accepted for obviating the need for the father's consent, even though the article referred to in the Marriage and Family Code says nothing about the mother's instructions?
(3) If the child is 18 years of age or over, is this secondary certificate even necessary?
(4) When completing the child's Schedule “A”, page 1, Personal Details, section 3, “Details about your parents”, should the child's father be marked as "Unknown", or should the name and family name match the birth certificate? If the latter applies, then, since the name given is not really the father, what should be entered for the father's city, country and date of birth, and date of death, or should they just be left blank?
(5) Similarly, when completing “Additional Family Info” IMM-5406, should (a) the father's name, marital status, date and country of birth, and address -all be left blank (b) only the name completed, i.e., as on the birth certificate, and the rest left blank, or (c) some other variation?
Thank you for your invaluable and much appreciated assistance!
Sincerely,
mmigration, Refugees

Thank you for your query.
Please see our responses to each of your questions below:
In the case of a spousal sponsorship from a Kyrgyzstan, where a child of the female applicant was born out of wedlock and is still under 18 years of age, will this single mother's certificate obviate the need for Declaration of Non-Accompanying Parent IMM-5406, i.e., the additional certificate stating that the information about the father in the child's birth record was entered according to the mother's instructions, citing a section of the national Marriage and Family Code, or would it be advisable to include the legal opinion of a local lawyer, etc., as was done for the court in the above-mentioned adoption? Application Guide IMM 5525 -Basic guide: Sponsor your spouse, partner or child instructs applicants to include a letter of explanation in their application to explain why it is impossible for them to provide a form IMM 5604 signed by the other, non-accompanying parent. The example cited in the guide is the scenario where the whereabouts of the other parent are unknown. In the scenario you describe we suggest the applicant provides explanations for both a) the reason why her child's father cannot complete this form as well as b) information about the Marriage and Family Code and the limitations of a single mother certificate issued in Kyrgyzstan.
Is the certificate for Kyrgyzstan accepted for obviating the need for the father's consent, even though the article referred to in the Marriage and Family Code says nothing about the mother's instructions? The absence of a father's name on Kyrgyzstan birth record documents does not automatically obviate the need for the father's consent. Again, we recommend including a letter of explanation in the application. There could be cases, for example, where an applicant knows the identity and whereabouts of the father, notwithstanding that he is not officially on the child's birth record, and should seek his consent in completing the IMM 5604-it's not clear whether a known father would have a claim to the custody of a child at some point, or what his recourse might be through family court to request a DNA test to establish parenthood and then challenge the applicant's right to leave Kyrgyzstan with the child.
If the child is 18 years of age or over, is this secondary certificate even necessary? If Kyrgyzstan recognizes a person who is 18 years old as an adult (age of majority) who is no longer legally bound to meet custody requirements, given that Canada recognizes someone who is 18 as an adult, then the IMM 5604 would not be required, provided the applicant explains and provides evidence of the applicable family law.
When completing the child's Schedule "A", page 1, Personal Details, section 3, "Details about your parents", should the child's father be marked as "Unknown", or should the name and family name match the birth certificate? If the latter applies, then, since the name given is not really the father, what should be entered for the father's city, country and date of birth, and date of death, or should they just be left blank? If the applicant knows the name of the father, they should provide that information, but provide an explanation as to why there is a different name on the child's birth certificate. The applicant should not enter a fictitious or "chosen" name for the father on this or any other form. Where an applicant is asked to provide the father's name, it is recommended they enter, "Please see attached letter", ensuring that the letter they have included in the application explains the situation.

Dear IRCC at ImmReps,

(1) Am I correct that a Canadian citizen who resides outside Canada, may sponsor her dependent child for Canadian permanent residence, as long as she (the sponsor) complies with Reg. 130(2) and will be residing in Canada before or at the time that the sponsored child becomes a Canadian permanent resident? Please assume that the child is not already a Canadian citizen and does not have any children.
(2) Can a Canadian citizen who resides outside of Canada and is the spouse of the sponsor in the scenario described in item (1) above, be a co-signer on an application to sponsor the dependent child for Canadian permanent residence status?
(3) Is there a provision that is similar to Reg. 130(2) that applies to co-signers? Thank you very much in advance for your soonest reply to these questions.
nmigration, Refugees ormation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
nation divulguée en vertu de la loi sur l'accès à l’info
Yours truly, Per:
nmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Dear Sir,
Thank you for you enquiry.
Pursuant to section 130(2) of the Regulations, a sponsor who is a Canadian citizen and does not reside in Canada may sponsor a foreign national who makes an application referred to in subsection (1) and is the sponsor's... dependent child who has no dependent children, if the sponsor will reside in Canada when the foreign national becomes a permanent resident. In these circumstances, an officer must be satisfied of the sponsor's intent to reside in Canada.
As per section 132(5) of the Regulations, to co-sign an undertaking, the spouse or common-law partner of the sponsor must be both 18 years of age and reside in Canada. There are no provisions similar to R130(2) in effect for the co-signer.
Please note, that as per R133(4)(c), there is no minimum necessary income requirement for a dependent child of the sponsor who has no dependent children, thus a co-signer is not required.

threads.subject: Self employed-definition of one year of experience-REP-2017-2176
threads.question:
I am trying to determine how to define one year of employment within the context of an application for permanent
residence under the Self Employed category by an artist, such as a musician or dancer.
An applicant for permanent residence under the Self Employed category requires two years of experience in self-employment in cultural activities within the past 5 years.
I am unclear what constitutes a year of experience. I understand that a year of employment under the Federal Skilled Worker and Canadian Experience Class means 1560 hours of employment activity.
Musicians in an orchestra are often paid a fee for performing a program over a period of several months. The actual time spent performing is two hours per show. If only the time spent performing is counted, a musician would never be able to
accumulate 3120 hours (1560 hours x 2) within 5 years.
The same situation occurs for dancers. A feature ballet dancer will be paid performance fees throughout the year. The dancer is paid to perform for a few hours at a time.
Does the preparation time that an artist spends honing their skills count towards the required period of self-employment?
I would appreciate your guidance.
Regards,
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your question to the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
To qualify as a self-employed person under the Self-Employed Persons Class, the applicant must have acquired relevant experience and have the intent and ability to be self-employed in Canada and to make significant contribution to specified economic activities in Canada.
To qualify as relevant experience, the self-employed person must have accumulated at least two years of relevant experience during the period beginning five years before the date of application for permanent residence and ending on the day a determination is made in respect of the application. You may wish to review the definition of relevant experience in section 88(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. As you will note, "full-time" is not included in the definition, nor is the one year period defined in terms of hours worked. The onus is on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to support their experience in either cultural activities or athletics. To note, officers accessing Self-Employed applications will consider the time an applicant spent preparing and honing their skills as experience in addition to the time spent performing.
We trust this information will assist you.

From ## Dear Sir/Madame,
If a student is enrolled in a program that has no scheduled breaks (i.e. runs continuously with no semesters off) but the school has provided students with the option of taking a semester off as a break; if a study permit holder decides to take the option and takes a semester off, is their study permit invalid after 90 days? Will they therefore be without status and be required to obtain a new study permit before starting the next semester?
Thank you,
migration, Refugees
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Hello
This is in response to your enquiry regarding breaks during programs with no scheduled breaks.
As of March 12th 2018, the off-campus program delivery instructions have been updated to clarify paragraph R186(v) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.
The update states that students must hold full-time student status during the academic session before and after their regularly scheduled break to work off-campus without a work permit. To be considered a regularly scheduled break, the break must be part of the DLI's academic calendar. Since the school provides students with the option of taking a semester off as a break, this break will be considered as a scheduled break by the DLl and the students would be eligible to work off-campus full-time during that time, keeping in mind that the students still meet all other eligibility criteria.
It is important to note, that students who create their own break in a program (where the break is not recognized by the DLl) are not eligible to work on or off campus.
We hope this is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at .
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Urgent-question en lien avec le pont-renouvellement de PE sans le CAQ-REP-2018-0336
threads.question:
Bonjour.
Nous avons une question concernant une étudiante qui est en attente actuellement de faire son dépôt final.
Elle n’est plus inscrite et son permis d’études vient à échéance le 11 mars 2018. Son CAQ est valide jusqu’au 31 mars 2018.
Elle souhaite maintenir son statut d’étudiante valide jusqu’à ce qu’elle puisse terminer officiellement son programme en avril.
Est-ce qu’elle peut demander un renouvellement de permis d’études avec son ancien CAQ et une lettre explicative pour obtenir le statut implicite?
Par la suite, peut-elle demanderle PTPD avec une preuve de demande de renouvellement de permis d’études seulement?
Merci pour les précisions à venir.
Cordialement,
Lmon
threads.answer:
Bonjour
Ceci est en réponse à votre demande envoyée le 8 mars concernant la prolongation des études et la validité du permis d'études.
Lorsqu'un titulaire de permis d'études souhaitant renouveler son permis d'études pour étudier au Québec, il doit soumettre une demande de CAQ ou une lettre d'approbation de MIDI avec sa demande d'extension de permis d'études. Si leur CAQ n'est pas valide pour la période pour laquelle ils souhaitent prolonger leur permis d'études, ils doivent d'abord demander et recevoir un nouveau CAQ à soumettre avecla demande.
Si l’étudiante avait soumise sa demande de prolongation de permis d’études avec le CAQ qui expirait le 31 mars 2018, le permis d’études aurait été émis seulement jusqu’au 31 mars 2018 car la date d'expiration du permis d’études ne peut être plus longue que celle du CAQ.
J'espère que cette information vous sera utile. Si vous avez d'autres questions, vous pouvez nous contacter à .
Cordialement,
La boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration

J’aimerais valider les scénarios suivants au sujet de la validité d’un permis d’études, lorsque l’étudiant interrompt temporairement ses études. Considérant que selon le R222(1), 222 (1) Le permis d’études devient invalide au premier en date des événements suivants :

threads.subject: FWFW: Inquiry regarding admissibility/rehabilitation. - REP-2018-0466
threads.answer:
## Good day,
Thank you for submitting your request.
We understand your question as being: Is an applicant eligible for individual rehabilitation if they have received a positive individual rehabilitation application in the past?
Section 17 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations provides that after a period of five (5) years from the completion of any sentence imposed or from the commission of an offence, a person will no longer be inadmissible if the person is able to satisfy the Minister that he or she has been rehabilitated provided that the person has not been convicted of a subsequent offence other than a contravention under the Contraventions Act or an offence under the Young Offenders Act.
For ease of reference, we break down section 36(2)b requirements of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act:
at least 5 years have elapsed since completion of their sentence they have not been convicted in Canada of an indictable offence they have not been convicted in Canada of a federal offence in the last 5 years (other than a contravention under the Contraventions Act or an offence under the Youth Criminal Justice Act) they have not in the 5 years before that been convicted in Canada of more than one summary conviction offences (other than a contravention under the Contraventions Act or an offence under the Youth Criminal Justice Act) they have not in the last 5 years been convicted outside Canada of an offence that, if committed in Canada, would constitute a federal offence (other than a contravention under the Contraventions Act or an offence under the Youth Criminal Justice Act) they have been convicted outside Canada of an offence referred to in s. 36(2)(b) that, if committed in Canada, would constitute an indictable offence they have not committed an act described in section 36(2)(c)
That said, if less than five years has passed, the applicant can fill out the individual rehabilitation application form and check "For information only". An officer will review and provide a recommendation to the applicant. Without knowing all the specific details in this case, an officer is able to look at the entirety of the applicants criminal record, even the convictions for which he/she was granted an individual rehabilitation, in a case such as this one, it would speak to the issue of recidivism.
We trust that this information will be useful to you.
Sincerely,
mmigration, Refugees

threads.subject: Co-Op Work Permit & Articling (Lawyer)
threads.question:
Could an International Student on a Study Permit obtain a Co-op work permit for their articles in Canada followed by a Post-Graduation work permit following the completion of their articles and Call to the Bar?
In order to become a Lawyer in Canada, law students must first complete a year of articles as per the requirements of their provincial law society. Like residency for doctors, following law school Articles are required in order to be Called to the Bar and become a lawyer.
As law school is typically 3 years and articling is 1 year, could a student obtain a co-op work permit to complete their articles? Could then then use their Call to the Bar as the “completion of their studies" in order to obtain a Post Graduation Work Permit?
Eligibility for exemption code C32 (post-secondary co-op)
Exemption code C32 (co-op for post-secondary international students) is intended for foreign nationals who intend to perform work that is an essential part of a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program offered by a designated learning institution (DLI) in Canada. The work cannot form more than 50% of the total program of study.
The acceptance letter provided by the DLl should clearly establish that the work is an essential part of the academic, vocational or professional training program that all participants enrolled in the program are required to complete in order to receive their degree, diploma or certificate. The most common example is undergraduate co-op programs at universities and colleges.
An open work permit should be issued with the academic institution listed as the employer. In cases where several work periods are necessary throughout the academic course (e.g., five work terms and eight study terms for a degree), the work permit should be valid for the same period as the study permit.
Note: This provision applies only to work that is required for a program offered by a Canadian institution. If the employment is a
requirement of an academic, vocational or professional training program offered by a foreign institution, exemption code C32 does not apply.
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/labour-market-impact-assessments/work-related-research-educational-training-program-r205-1-2-codes-c31-c32-c33.html
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
#### FW: Co-Op Work Permit & Articling (Lawyer) - REP-2018-0485
This is in response to your inquiry sent on March 13 regarding co-op work permits for articling lawyers.
Co-op work permits are issued for work which comprises an essential part of a program offered at a DLl, which all students must complete in order to graduate. The DLl must indicate in the letter of acceptance that this is the case. If the work does not meet these criteria, a co-op work permit cannot be issued. In addition, co-op work permits may only be issued to coincide with the length of the program for which the work is required.
Therefore, if articling is optional or happens following graduation from a law program, it would be ineligible for this type of work permit. If it is required of all students of a program to graduate from a DLl, then it may be eligible if it meets the other criteria set out in the PDI.
I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at .
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
From # Hello,
I need clarification on the following, I have presented the question using different scenarios, just to be clear on holding two permits together, eligibility to apply and an effect of applying the second permit based on the first one.
5. Can a Foreign National hold two permits together-Study Permit as well as an Open work permit?
6. Is a foreign national eligible to apply for an open work permit based on his spouse study permit in case both of them are studying in Canada and can he hold both the status-study and work?
7. In case a foreign national who is on a Study Permit in Canada apply for an Open Work Permit based on the Study Permit of his spouse who is also studying in Canada, will it affect his/ her ability to continue to study while working full time using his open work permit (in case he is granted an open work permit).
8. Will the application for applying for an Open work permit (through the change of status form) consider a change of Status from Study to Work or it will be considered an application for an open work permit based on study permit of the spouse?
Thank you for your assistance in this matter.
mmigration, Refugees
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good day,
QUESTIONS :
1. Can a Foreign National hold two permits together-Study Permit as well as an Open work permit?
2. Is a foreign national eligible to apply for an open work permit based on his spouse study permit in case both of them are studying in Canada and can he hold both the status-study and work?
3. In case a foreign national who is on a Study Permit in Canada apply for an Open Work Permit based on the Study Permit of his spouse who is also studying in Canada, will it affect his/ her ability to continue to study while working full time using his open work permit (in case he is granted an open work permit).
4. Will the application for applying for an Open work permit (through the change of status form) consider a change of Status from Study to Work or it will be considered an application for an open work permit based on study permit of the spouse?
ANSWERS:
1. Yes, a study permit and open work permit can be held at the same time.
2. A foreign national may be eligible for an open work permit based on their spouse's study permit under C42 LMIA exemption. However, this exemption is intended for spouses who are not, themselves, full-time students. Thus, if they are already a full-time student, they would be not eligible for an open work permit under C42 LMIA exemption.
3. A foreign national on a study permit, who receives an open work permit, based on the fact their spouse has a study permit, will still be permitted to study as the study permit would remain valid for the initial duration it was issued for.
4. I am a little unsure what you mean by your question, so will attempt to answer it to the best of my ability. An application for an open work permit, based on a partners study permit, would be considered separate from the applicant's existing study permit, although will only be issued up to the duration of the partners study permit.
We trust this information nwill assist you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Provided all conditions are met, it may qualify for the Foreign Skilled Worker (FSW) program. threads.answer:
#### immigration κepresentatives / Représentants immigration (IRCC)

It is preferable to avoid the possibility of having multiple applications in process at the same time, so it is recommended that clients wait approximately six weeks after submitting their withdrawal request to ensure receipt and necessary action by the responsible IRCC office. threads.subject: Overseas Humanitarian and Compassionate Application-REP-2018-0625
threads.question:
## Dear Sir or Madam,
We would like to inquire about how to fill in the IMM8 Generic Application Form for Canada and IMM5283 Supplementary Information Humanitarian and Compassionate Considerations for overseas humanitarian and compassionate application. For question 2 under the “Application Details" on the IMM8, if we choose “Other" for question 1, it only left 2 choices for us, which are “In-Canada – Humanitarian & Compassionate Considerations” and “Permit Holder Class”. Please advise what we should choose for overseas humanitarian and compassionate application.
Second, the questions on page 3 of IMM5283 are for candidate who lives in Canada. Please advise if this form is mandatory
for overseas H & C application. Looking forward to your reply.
Thanks & Best Regards,
nmigration, Refugees

threads.answer:
mmigration Representatives / Représentants immigration
(IRCC)
Good day
Please find the response to your query below.
We would like to inquire about how to fill in the IMM8 Generic Application Form for Canada and IMM5283 Supplementary Information Humanitarian and Compassionate Considerations for overseas humanitarian and compassionate application. For question 2 under the “Application Details" on the IMM8, if we choose “Other" for question 1, it only left 2 choices for us, which are “In-Canada – Humanitarian & Compassionate Considerations" and “Permit Holder Class”. Please advise what we should choose for overseas humanitarian and compassionate application.
Second, the questions on page 3 of IMM5283 are for candidate who lives in Canada. Please advise if this form is mandatory for overseas H & C application.
Applicants, both in Canada and overseas, can file an application requesting humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) consideration under subsection 25(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). However, the process varies somewhat depending on whether the applicant resides in Canada or overseas and is explained in more depth in the Program Delivery Instructions (PDI) at the following link:
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/permanent-residence/humanitarian-compassionate-consideration/intake-who-may-apply.html
In the case of an overseas humanitarian and compassionate application, applicants must apply under one of the three immigration classes (family, economic or refugee) using the corresponding departmental application forms for the class under which they are applying. Applicants must then also provide additional written information in support of their request for consideration under subsection A25(1).
With regard to the IMM8 Generic Application Form, in response to question 1, the applicant should indicate under which class they are applying (family, economic or refugee). In response to question 2, the applicant should then indicate under which program they are applying (for example, in the case of someone applying under the refugee class, they would indicate "Outside Canada-Refugee"). The applicant should not indicate "Other" under question 1 as this pertains to In-Canada applications.
IMM5283 Supplementary Information Humanitarian and Compassionate applies to H&C applications filed in Canada only. It is not a required form for overseas H&C applications and there is no need to submit it.
Trusting this addresses you concerns.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Question: We have a client (holder of a CSQ-PEQ) who incorporated a company in order to work as a freelancer graphic designer.

threads.subject: How to add duties to an issued IMP work permit-REP-2018-0587 -
threads.question:
Hi there,
Would submitting a new Offer of Employment IMM5802/Employer Compliance submission with the additional duties for the same employer and same NOC be sufficient to allow a foreign worker to take up the additional duties? The salary/remuneration may or may not increase due to the increase in duties and hours to be worked. Would the foreign worker need to apply for a new work permit? If so, how can this be done as previously work permit applications for the same employer, same NOC for the same duration of an already issued work permit have been refused.
Any guidance you ca provide on this would be greatly appreciated. Cheers,
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Hello,
Please find below the response to your inquiry. We hope this information is helpful.
Question:
Would submitting a new Offer of Employment IMM5802/Employer Compliance submission with the additional duties for the same employer and same NOC be sufficient to allow a foreign worker to take up the additional duties? The salary/remuneration may or may not increase due to the increase in duties and hours to be worked. Would the foreign worker need to apply for a new work permit?
Response:
Providing additional duties, thereby increasing weekly hours, and a salary that is higher salary to the foreign worker than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC after the work permit was issued would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker-i.e. employer, occupation or location. Or, if the change in working conditions negatively impacts the worker, such as reduction in hours or salary, then a new Offer of Employment and a new work permit would be required before the change takes effect, otherwise the employer risks being found non-compliant with the original job offer submitted to IRCC.
The employer cannot amend duties, hours or salary information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker.
Proactive notification to IRCC of inconsistencies surrounding working conditions are not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC.
Additional points to note:
· An increase in wages may result in a finding that the employer did not provide "substantially the same" wages if the increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the LMIA-exemption.. Wages under the International Mobility Program must meet the minimum wage requirement in the province of employment as per the condition to meet federal or provincial laws. Wages paid that are higher than those in the offer of employment, may indicate a change in duties that would mean a different occupation than offered. In that case, a new Offer of employment and new work permit may be required. · In cases where the employer has promoted or otherwise changed the foreign worker's duties outside of the original NOC, the foreign worker must receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to implementing the change. If a new work permit for the promotion or change in occupation has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign
Lnfomn
worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non-compliance by the employer.. Foreign workers are also subject to other federal (such as ESDC who leads the Temporary Foreign Workers Program) and provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should also meet those requirements for compliance purposes.]
Sincerely
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

“on the date on which their application for a permanent resident visa is made and on the date on which the visa is issued, the skilled worker holds a valid work permit or is authorized to work in Canada under section 186 and
(i) the circumstances referred to in subparagraph (a)(ii) or (iii) do not apply, (ii) the circumstances referred to in paragraph (b) do not apply, and (iii) the circumstances referred to in subparagraphs (c)(i) and (ii) apply."
Subparagraphs (c)(i) and (ii) state:

requirements set out in subsection 203(1) with respect to the offer have been met".
I am uncertain how to interpret s. 82(2)(d) as the underlined portions appear to be contradictory.

mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act

FW: Exemption from the FSWP settlement funds requirement-REP-2018-0591

threads.subject: QUESTIONS: Applying for Canadian PR, parent born in Canada
threads.question:
Good afternoon,
A client and his accompanying dependents (spouse and children) were all born in the UK and are UK citizens. The client's mother was born in Canada and so he may have a claim to Canadian citizenship. The client has not applied for a Canadian citizenship certificate and therefore there is no record that he is a Canadian citizen.
QUESTIONS:
1. Can the client apply for permanent residence through Express Entry and include his dependents?
2. Or is he barred from doing so because of his potential claim to Canadian
citizenship?
3. Is he also unable to obtain an eTA even though he has not exercised his claim to Canadian citizenship?
This would be much easier than him applying for proof of Canadian citizenship to find out if he is a Canadian citizen and then sponsoring his family members. À legislative/policy reference would be appreciated.
mmigration, Refugees
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Immigration Representatives / Représentants immigration (IRCC) QUESTIONS: Applying for Canadian PR, parent born in Canada -
REP-2018-0616
Hello
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox. We hope that you will find the answers to your questions below of assistance.
Questions
A client and his accompanying dependents (spouse and children) were all born in the UK and are UK citizens. The client's mother was born in Canada and so he may have a claim to Canadian citizenship. The client has not applied for a Canadian citizenship certificate and therefore there is no record that he is a Canadian citizen.
1. Can the client apply for permanent residence through Express Entry and include his dependents?
2. Or is he barred from doing so because of his potential claim to Canadian citizenship?
Answer
A person in this situation may be considered a Canadian Citizen by descent and if so, would not be eligible for Express Entry. In order to determine if he is a citizen by operation of law, the individual should submit a proof of citizenship application. The application and guide can be found here: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/proof-citizenship/apply.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/proof-citizenship/apply.html)
According to the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations officers may issue permanent resident visas to foreign nationals who qualify under economic programs. Individuals who do not meet the definition of a foreign national according to the Immigration and Refugee Protection act cannot be issued a permanent resident visa through Express Entry. Please find the relevant regulation and definition below.
IRPR 70 (1) An officer shall issue a permanent resident visa to a foreign national if, following an examination, it is established that
a. (a) the foreign national has applied in accordance with these Regulations for a permanent resident visa as a member of a class referred to in subsection (2);
b. (b) the foreign national is coming to Canada to establish permanent residence;
c. (c) the foreign national is a member of that class;
d. (d) the foreign national meets the selection criteria and other requirements applicable to that class; and
e. (e) the foreign national and their family members, whether accompanying or not, are not inadmissible.
mmigration, Refugees
IRPA 2 (1) foreign national means a person who is not a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident, and includes a stateless person. (étranger)
Question 3
3. Is he also unable to obtain an eTA even though he has not exercised his claim to Canadian citizenship?
Answer
A person born outside Canada to a Canadian citizen who was never issued a citizenship certificate and was born in the first generation (means that the Canadian parent was either born or naturalized in Canada) are considered Canadian citizens by descent. [Note that there are exceptions to the first generation limit which includes, if the parent, at the time of the person's birth, was employed outside Canada in or with the Canadian Armed Forces, the federal public administration or the public service of a province.] As a Canadian citizen, they cannot apply for an eTA because they have a right to enter and remain in Canada. For Canadian citizens, including dual Canadian citizens, when travelling, they must present an acceptable travel document that shows that they are a Canadian. This means they need, for example, a valid Canadian passport (or a Canadian temporary passport, or a Canadian emergency travel document) to allow airline check-in staff and border officials to confirm that they are Canadian. The applicant should be advised to apply for a Canadian passport.
In this particular scenario, the client must obtain proof of citizenship. To obtain a proof of citizenship needed to make an application for a Canadian passport, the person can apply for a citizenship certificate and, if they meet the urgent criteria for persons who have imminent travel needs and are impacted by eTA, they can contact their closest Embassy, Consulate or High Commission for assistance with this process.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

; OMC-GOCImmigration@cic.gc.ca C

QUESTION: When comparing a foreign offence to a Canadian offence to determine whether the foreign offence is a crime in Canada, do we look at the version of the Canadian criminal code as it existed at the time the offence

For example, possession of marijuana is set to become legal in Canada in July 2018. For those with foreign marijuana possession convictions from before this date, are they currently inadmissible but admissible as of July 2018?
Additionally, I would appreciate it if you could include a policy/legislative reference with your reply.

threads.answer:
determining admissibility? - REP-2018-0540 -
Dear,
The principles to be followed when determining equivalency were developed in the context of foreign convictions and are set out in several leading decisions of the Federal Court of Appeal. Robertson v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1979] F.C. 197 (C.A.).
The facts at the time of the offence must be assessed based on the Canadian law as it reads at the time of an application that would render a final decision, such as during the admissibility hearing or appeal. Thus a person may no longer be inadmissible as a result of changes to the Criminal Code occurring after their criminal conviction.
The Federal Court of Appeal stated that unless Parliament has clearly indicated otherwise, the correctness of the decision must be measured by the law in force at the time of the decision. Bubla v. Canada (Solicitor General), [1995]2 F.C. 680

threads.subject: question C-41 - (REP-2018-0498) - REP-2018-0666 -
threads.question:
1*1 Lnfomn
Thank you.
What happens if the holder of a C-41 open work permit gets divorced is separated from their spouse? Can they still work in Canada on their C-41 work permit, after the divorce or separation?
Thank vou.
threads.answer:
Hello
Question: What happens if the holder of a C-41 open work permit gets divorced is separated from their spouse? Can they still work in Canada on their C-41 work permit, after the divorce or separation?
Answer: A foreign national that was issued a C41 open work permit can continue to work so long as the work permit remains valid. Once the work permit is issued, it may only be revoked, as per the Ministerial Instructions described in A30(1.41). The justifications for revoking a work permit are:
Revocation of a work permit where the associated LMIA has been revoked Revocation of an LMIA-exempt work permit where the employment of the foreign national is having a significantly greater negative effect than benefit with respect to the development of a strong Canadian economy
Revocation of a work permit where the employer has provided false, misleading or inaccurate information
Revocation of a work permit where the employer's name has been added to the ineligible employer list under subsection 209.91(3) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR)
Revocation of an LMIA-exempt work permit issued to any foreign national on the basis of their relationship with another foreign national and the principal foreign worker's work permit is now revoked (e.g., exemption C41)
In the case of a foreign national under C41, their work permit may only be revoked if the principle work permit holder's work permit is now revoked (as per the ministerial instructions).
Once again, once the work permit has expired, the spouse or common law-partner of the TFW will not be able to renew their open work permit under exemption code C41 since the conditions on which the work permit was issued to the spouse/common-law partner are no longer valid.
Sincerely
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: conviction "Spent" - REP-2018-0614 -
threads.question:
I have a question about admissibility for people who have “spent convictions" in the UK. How does your office treat convictions that are considered spent in the UK under the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act?
I understand that there has been some inconsistencies on how “spent convictions" are interpreted. I believe that prior to the changes to the Canadian pardon regime, IRCC was taking the view that spent convictions were not “convictions" per the meaning of s. 36 and therefore did not render someone inadmissible. However, with the changes to the Canadian pardon regime (now record suspension regime), the interpretation has been that the Canadian and UK systems are no longer sufficiently similar for the principle in Burgon to apply.
Can you provide any guidance for me in terms of whether we should treat “spent convictions” as sufficiently similar to the Canadian record suspension and thus a spent conviction would not render a person inadmissible to Canada?
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
mmigration, Refugees
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Dear
Thank you for consulting with the Integrity Risk Guidance Branch.
In order for the officer to complete a fulsome review, the applicant's information on the charge, the arrest, the conviction and the disposition will also need to be provided for the analysis.
As stated in Saini v. Canada (M.C.I.), [2002] 1 F.C. 200 (C.A.), the convicted person must establish that three elements are met before a foreign discharge or pardon may be recognized:
1) The foreign legal system as a whole must be similar to that of Canada;
2) The aim, content and effect of the specific foreign law must be similar to Canadian law, and;
3) There must be no valid reason not to recognize the effect of the foreign law.
We do recommend that applicants obtain criminal records from their corresponding country when making an application. Even when the foreign spent conviction is similar to a Canadian pardon in aim and effect it is the content of the Foreign statutes that differs in that the relief scheme is automatic rather than like Canada's where one needs to apply.
The intent is similar as it intends to restore a person's respect/law abiding position in society where there past mistakes/record would no longer be considered due to their reformed life style. It is our understanding that since the record is completely erased it would not necessarily be disclosed unless probed or prompted since spent records would be sufficiently similar to the Canadian statutes and the deemed rehabilitated process.
Our guidance to officers do refer to accepting foreign court decisions whose legal system is based on similar foundations and values as ours which reflects goals and objectives analogous to those encompassed within our own system. Basically, that the foreign law should be accorded respect for the purpose of Canadian immigration law objectives unless the officer have a solid rational for departing therefrom from this opinion.
I have attached here for reference other jurisprudence that you may find of interest:
(Minister of Manpower and Immigration v. Brooks,[1974])
(Barnett v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) (1996))
Additional, legal opinions can be found in The Canadian Legal Information Institute [https://www.canlii.org/en/ca/scc/index.html](https://www.canlii.org/en/ca/scc/index.html) on the spent convictions methods in the UK, New Zealand and Australia, that were found to be equivalent to a Canadian “pardon” record suspension notwithstanding the lack of discretion during the application process.
Since officer discretion is very deliberate and unless there is no good reason or a solid rational for refusing the disposition and taking into account the officers knowledge and discretion during the application then the officer may find the decision
to be equivalent to the needs of the Canadian immigration law objective.
As with any case, the officer may require further documentation (beyond what the applicant has submitted) in order to be satisfied that the applicant is not criminally inadmissible.
We trust that this information will be useful to you.
Sincerely.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Imm Reps, your new guidelines [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-)
citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study- permits/campus-work.html are vey helpful, but I have a scenario that doesn't seem to be addressed.

The guidelines state:
Full-time or part-time course load during a regularly scheduled break
Students who are enrolled full time during the academic sessions before and after a regularly scheduled break and who decide to undertake a full-time or part-time course load during that regularly scheduled break are eligible to work off campus on a full-time basis.

threads.answer:
## Hi
Regarding your question, the student might not be allowed to work full time, only up to 20 hours per week.
As per the instructions, the student would have to be enrolled full-time before and also after the scheduled break, which does not seem to be the case. (Note that the educational institutions define what is full-time enrolment for their institution.)
The instructions do mention that if the student has maintained full-time status for the duration of their program of study, and only require a part-time course load in their final academic session in order to complete their program of study, the student may work off campus up to 20 hours per week during their final academic session – which seems to be the case here.
Once they receive written confirmation of program completion they no longer meet this requirement and are therefore no longer eligible to work using their study permit. However, once they have submitted an application for a PGWP, they become eligible to work under R186(w) until a decision is made regarding their application.
Study permit holders are therefore not eligible to work after receiving written confirmation of program completion before submitting a work permit application.
