threads.subject: Can I have both an Open Work Permit & a Study Permit? - REP-2018-0525 -
threads.question:
From ##
Dear Sir or Madam:
At this time our firm would like to request clarification with regard to an individual who is currently in Canada with a valid Open Work Permit (based on marriage to a worker with an employer-specific Work Permit), but would like to apply and obtain a Study Permit in order to go to school.
Please provide us with guidance on whether an individual can continue to keep an Open Work Permit along with a Study Permit i.e. have two valid permits at the same time? Or will the individual's Open Work Permit be no longer valid once he is issued the Study Permit?
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Dear
Please accept our apologies for not replying sooner. Question: Please provide us with guidance on whether an individual can continue to keep an Open Work Permit along with a Study Permit i.e. have two valid permits at the same time? Or will the individual's Open Work Permit be no longer valid once he is issued the Study Permit? Response: An individual can continue to keep an Open Work Permit along with a Study Permit i.e., have two valid permits at the same time. R215 (1)(c) states that a foreign national may apply for a study permit after entering Canada if they hold a work permit. R209 states that a work permit becomes invalid when it expires or when a removal order that is made against the permit holder becomes enforceable. As such, unless and until the work permit expires or a removal order made against an individual becomes enforceable, the work permit remains valid and, should the individual continue to meet the conditions imposed by the work permit, they would be able to continue working while they hold their study permit. Hoping this information is of assistance.
Sincerely
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Question:
Je vous contacte aujourd’hui pour connaître la procédure à suivre dans un cas particulier-Ayant eu des réponses et conseils différent en contactant IRCC au téléphone, et suite au déplacement du TET à un poste frontalier, je préfère vous contacter afin de connaître les démarches exactes.
Nous avons une cliente qui a obtenu un permis de travail sous « Expérience Internationale Canada », catégorie des Jeunes Professionnels. La candidate est citoyenne française et occupe un poste au sein d’un groupe multinational.
Le permis de travail a été obtenu pour un emploi situé à Montréal. Par contre, après quelques semaines à l’emploi, le groupe a décidé de placer le TET à son bureau de Toronto (pour des raisons de stratégie d’affaires).
Comment pouvons-nous faire changer le lieu d’emploi indiqué sur le permis de travail?
Response:
Tel que décrit dans les instructions Prolongation de la durée de validité des permis de travail au titre du programme Expérience internationale Canada scénario 5,
Si l’étranger reçoit une nouvelle offre d’emploi du même employeur, mais pour travailler à une autre adresse (bureau) ou dans une autre ville, une autre province ou un autre territoire :
- Ce changement est considéré comme étant une modification aux conditions de participation à EIC. Le fait de travailler pour le même employeur et d’accomplir les mêmes tâches, mais à un endroit différent, sera considéré comme une nouvelle participation, car le permis de travail du participant a été délivré pour un employeur et un emplacement précis (à moins que l’employeur a indiqué dans son offre d’emploi que le travailleur va travailler dans différents emplacements au Canada)
- Il est possible que le client puisse créer un nouveau profil ElC en vue d’une deuxième participation : o si son pays de citoyenneté permet plusieurs participations; o s’il répond toujours aux critères d’admissibilité à EIC.
- Il est également possible que le client soit en mesure de présenter une demande de permis de travail en dehors du programme EIC. S’il présente effectivement une demande pour un nouveau permis de travail au titre d’un autre programme (obligation d’obtenir une ElMT obligatoire ou dispense de cette obligation), il doit le faire au moins 30 jours avant la date d’expiration de son permis de travail au titre d’EIC pour pouvoir présenter sa demande depuis le Canada.
Lorsque l’employeur a plusieurs franchises, par exemple, il faut que le permis de travail reflète l’emplacement physique de l’emploi indiqué dans l’offre et que cet emploi se limite spécifiquement à cet endroit. Par contre, si l’offre
mmigration, Refugees
Inmn d’emploi indique différents lieux de travail, le travailleur sera autorisé à travailler dans différents emplacements au Canada.
Question:
Si la procédure suppose une demande en ligne, avec les délais impliqués, est-ce que la TET bénéficie d’un statut implicite pendant le traitement de la demande?
Response:
Si le demandeur peut soumettre une demande de permis de travail en ligne : Conformément à l’article R201, un étranger peut présenter une demande de renouvellement de permis de travail seulement si celle-ci est présentée avant la date d’expiration de son permis. Aux termes de l’alinéa R186u), l’étranger peut travailler sans permis de travail dans la mesure où il a présenté une demande aux termes de l’article R201 et que la décision concernant sa demande de renouvellement n’a pas encore été rendue.
Cordialement,
La boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration

threads.question:
Dear Sir, Madam,
We hope this message finds you well. We are writing for clarification on eligibility for criminal rehabilitation in the event an applicant receives a suspended sentence with a period of good behaviour (not probation). We understand that, to be eligible for criminal rehabilitation, 5 years must have passed since the completion of the imposed sentence for a criminal offence.
nmigration, Refugees
According to ENF 14 /OP 19, Section 16, the calculation of the 5 years for a suspended sentence starts on the day of the conviction. However, if an applicant receives a suspended sentence and is placed on good behaviour for 3 years, would the 5 year calculation start on the date of conviction or only after the 3 year period of good behaviour has ended?
Furthermore, ENF 14 /OP 19, Section 16 states that, if an applicant receives suspended imprisonment, the 5 year calculation date starts on the day the imprisonment would have ended. However, if an applicant receives a suspended imprisonment sentence and placed on good behaviour for 3 years, would the 5 year calculation start on the day the imprisonment would have originally ended or when the period of good behaviour ends?
Thank you in advance for your assistance.
Respectfully yours,
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
REP-2018-0630
Good day,
Thank you for consulting with the Immigration Representatives inbox.
We understand your questions as being: Can you identify the day the rehabilitation period begins for an act and for various types of imposed sentences?
Suspended Sentence: The date following sentencing or the day after the end of the probation period.
Where the court sentences the accused to a suspended sentence, the accused is placed on probation for a period of up to three years. During this time the accused must comply with these conditions. A suspended sentence is not considered a final sentence, since an accused who is convicted of breaching the conditions of the probation order may in addition to being sentenced for the offence of breach of probation, may also have the suspended sentence revoked. Once a suspended sentence is revoked, the court which originally sentenced the accused may re-sentence the accused.
Suspended imprisonment: The date following the end of the term of imprisonment that was suspended,
Meaning the date the sentence would have ended had the sentence started immediately after the sentencing date. For example, if a judge imposes a sentence of one month, but suspends the execution of the order for two years, the
rehabilitation period would begin one month and a day after the execution order was completed.
We trust that this information will be useful to you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: -W: Question regarding eligibility for Deemed Rehabilitation -
threads.question:
I hope that this email finds you well.
If a foreign national has two previous convictions outside of Canada, one of which is equivalent to a pure summary offence in Canada, and the other of which is equivalent to a hybrid offence in Canada which carries a maximum penalty on indictment of less than 10 years, would s/he be eligible for to apply for deemed rehabilitation provided that all other deemed rehabilitation eligibility criteria are met? I understand that the single summary offence alone would not render a foreign national inadmissible to Canada, but would it become relevant in the context of deemed rehabilitation eligibility when there is also a subsequent conviction for the equivalent of a hybrid offence?
I have reviewed Deemed Rehabilitation applicability examples in OP 19 but cannot find a clear answer on whether someone in this situation is eligible for Deemed Rehabilitation.
Many thanks in advance for your guidance.
Kind regards,
migration, Refugees 1*1 mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
REP-2018-0645 -
Dear
Thank you for consulting with the Immigration Representatives Inbox. Criminal rehabilitation can be assessed in two ways: Deemed rehabilitation: can occur when an applicant has a criminal inadmissibility but they meet certain requirements that allow an officer to declare that they are “deemed rehabilitated” and therefore no longer criminally inadmissible to Canada. Application for rehabilitation: may be submitted by a person convicted of an offence or who has committed an act or omission and who does not meet the eligibility criteria for deemed rehabilitation. Persons inadmissible under A36(2)(b) and (c) are deemed rehabilitated if they satisfy the requirements for deemed
rehabilitation set out in R18(2) of Immigration Refugee Protection Regulations. R18(2)(b)] deals with [A36(2)(b)], persons
who have been convicted outside Canada of offences equivalent to two or more summary conviction offences in Canada under an Act of Parliament. In order for the applicant to meet deemed rehabilitation eligibility criteria you would need to respond yes to all of the following criteria. Is the offence considered for deemed rehabilitation punishable in Canada by a maximum term of imprisonment of less than 10 years. Has at least 10 years elapsed since the day after the completion of the imposed sentence for the offence considered for deemed rehabilitation. There has been no conviction in Canada for an indictable offence under an Act of Parliament at any time. Within the last 10 years, there has been no convictions in Canada of any summary conviction offence and No more than one summary conviction in Canada prior to 10 years.
- Prior to the last 10 years, no more than one conviction outside Canada, that if committed in Canada, would be equivalent to a summary offence under an Act of Parliament.
These previous questions should help you confirm if he/she is eligible for deemed rehabilitation.
We trust that this information will be useful to you. The Immigration Representatives Inbox.

Hello,
Thank you for your question.
All potential sponsors are informed to self-assess their eligibility to sponsor before they submit an Interest to Sponsor web form. The Interest to Sponsor web form is not an application, however, potential sponsors are expected to be truthful in their responses.
As per Regulation 133(1)(B)(i), a sponsorship application to sponsor parents and grandparents shall only be approved by an officer if, on the day on which the application was filed and from that day until the day a decision is made with respect to the application, there is evidence that the sponsor has a total income that is at least equal to the minimum necessary income, plus 30%, for each of the three consecutive taxation years immediately preceding the date of filing of the sponsorship application. The sponsor must be able to provide evidence in the form of CRA issued documentation such as a Notice of Assessment to prove they have the financial stability and the ability to meet the needs of their family member for the full
length of the undertaking.
Sponsors must indicate on the IMM 1344 whether they wish to proceed with the sponsorship if they do not meet the requirements to sponsor. If the sponsor indicates they wish to continue with the application, humanitarian and compassionate considerations can be requested by the applicant.

manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/campus-work.html are vey helpful, but I have a scenario that doesn't seem to be addressed.
If a student has only one course left to graduate, and will take that course during the summer academic break, can this student work full-time during the summer?
The guidelines state:
Full-time or part-time course load during a regularly scheduled break
Students who are enrolled full time during the academic sessions before and after a regularly scheduled break and who decide to undertake a full-time or part-time course load during that regularly scheduled break are eligible to work off campus on a full-time basis.

# time during the summer? -REP-2018-0711-

As per the instructions, the student would have to be enrolled full-time before and also after the scheduled break, which does not seem to be the case. (Note that the educational institutions define what is full-time enrolment for their institution.)
The instructions do mention that if the student has maintained full-time status for the duration of their program of study, and only require a part-time course load in their final academic session in order to complete their program of study, the student may work off campus up to 20 hours per week during their final academic session – which seems to be the case here.

threads.question:
From mmigration, Refugees
exempt)
Hello ImmReps,
I have a client that submitted a Study Permit Application for 2 children from a visa-exempt country and received a request from IRCC for the completion of the Custodian Declaration form IMM 5646. We submitted a written declaration from the parents explaining that the parents (also visa-exempt) planned to accompany the children in Canada as Visitors, and would apply for Visitor Records at the POE. The parents own a home in Canada and have plenty of funds for their stay. The children planned to attend elementary school for one school year. The study permit applications were refused on the basis that the children failed to provide the Custodian Declaration or proof of parent's legal status in Canada. The parents could not sign the Custodian Declaration as they are not Canadian citizens or PR. In that case the parent was waiting for a PNP work permit support letter, which he received shortly thereafter, so they re-applied once the work permit was issued.
However, I now have another client in the same predicament -the family is from a visa-exempt country, the children will be applying for study permits, and the parents will accompany them as visitors. Can you please advise what documents the parents can provide to demonstrate their anticipated legal status as visitors in Canada? Should they submit the Custodian Declaration IMM 5646, and leave blank the box where it asks for status in Canada?
Alternatively, should the parents be submitting applications for visitor visas to accompany the children, even though they are visa-exempt?
Is there some other way to submit this type of application, or something else that the family could submit in order for this
type of application to be approved?
Thank you very much for your assistance with this question. I look forward to receiving your response. Warm regards,
threads.answer:
Good Day,
If a child is travelling with both parents, the parents would need to satisfy the officer via the travel documents they hold that they are indeed visa-exempt (for instance, holding a passport from a visa-exempt country).
In cases where one parent is travelling with a child without the other parent (because the other parent is not accompanying), the following documents must be presented:
- A copy of the child's birth certificate
- A letter of authorization signed by the parent who is not travelling, containing their address and telephone number, in English or French if possible, and
- A photocopy of the non-accompanying parent's signed passport or national identity card
The accompanying parents should also be prepared to explain their plan for the child should they (the parents) be refused visitor status at the border (for example, they might decide that the child will return with them).
However, the child could also be left with a guardian in Canada. If the parents are refused at the border and they decide to let the child enter Canada, they must provide a custodianship document. They can also provide a custodianship document with a custodian in Canada just in case they (the parents) are refused entry at the border.
Note that visa-exempt foreign nationals might also need an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA) if travelling to Canada by air. The eTA will be linked to the passport used to apply. The foreign national would then need to present this passport when checking in to their flight to Canada.
Visa-exempt foreign nationals do not need to apply for Temporary Resident Visas. However, as mentioned above, the officer would need to be satisfied that the foreign national is indeed visa exempt.
Sincerely.

QUESTION: Compte tenu du contexte exposé pensez-vous que leur relation avec le producteur canadien puisse créer une "relation d'emploi" au sens de l'article R186g)?
Réponse :
En général, bien que non défini dans le règlement, une personne/société peut être considérée comme un employeur et comme ayant une relation d’emploi lorsqu'elle engage, renvoie, paye, supervise ou autrement contrôle et donne des directives concrètes aux employés sur comment et où le travail doit se dérouler. Si le producteur dont il est question accomplit toutes ces tâches, une relation d’emploi serait donc créée. Lorsqu’une relation d’emploi est présente, les travailleurs étrangers ne sont pas éligibles à la dispense de permis de travail sous R186(g) et doivent obtenir une ElMT ainsi qu’un permis de travail.

threads.subject: Losing job after eAPR (CEC and PNP)
threads.question:
Good morning,
I am trying to reconcile s.29(3) of the current Ministerial Instructions, with IRCC's policy guidelines on when to refuse an application for a change post-eAPR.
Question:
1. A CEC applicant submits their eAPR with a valid and qualifying Offer of Employment. They require the 50/200 points for selection. If they lose their job after submission of the eAPR, do they retain the 50/200 points, or are the points retracted and therefore the application refused for falling below the cut-off? The applicant does not need the Offer to meet program requirements as they are a CEC candidate.
2. A CEC/PNP applicant submits their eAPR with a valid EE-stream provincial nomination. They required the 600 points for selection. If they lose their job after submission of the eAPR, do they retain the 600 points, or are the points retracted and therefore the application refused for falling below the cut-off? Alternatively, and assuming the nomination is revoked, are they refused for failing to meet PNP program requirements (even though they also qualify under CEC)?
3. Does s.29(3) of the current Ministerial Instructions apply up to the time of PR issuance? If so, how does that intersect with the guidelines below that say the application cannot be refused for changes that occur after eAPR unless it affects program eligibility?
Thank you!
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
FW: FOR YOUR APPRVAL: Losing job after eAPR (CEC and PNP) - REP-2018-0438
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Sincere apologies for the late reply.
1. The reference is based on the “Change of circumstances declared after an eAPR has been submitted”. The period of time for 11.2 is defined as starting when an ITA is issued and ending when the candidate submits their eAPR. If it is determined that the job was lost before the eAPR was submitted then the points will be removed, and the application will be refused if the new score is lower than the lowest score of the round. If the job was lost after the eAPR submission, points will not be adjusted. In this situation the candidate should decline the ITA, go back to the pool, adjust the profile to reflect the change in circumstances (no longer with a job offer) and have the system recalculate CRS and wait for another invitation. As you point out, the CEC program does not necessitate the applicant have a job offer.
2.The supporting employer and/or nominee applicant are required to notify the Province/Territory (PT) and IRCC (via the webform) if the terms of employment change from those on the job offer, including promotion, new employment, layoff, or termination of employment. In the case of termination of employment, the PT will review the case and may withdraw the nomination if the applicant no longer meets the minimum requirements of the program. If the nomination is withdrawn, the PT will communicate the decision to withdraw to the nominee and to the supporting employer, and notify IRCC of the decision. Therefore, if the nomination is withdrawn, IRCC will refuse the nominee's application for permanent residency, as the applicant is not named in a nomination issued by the government of a PT, as required by R87(2)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.
3. Yes, it does apply until PR issuance in the sense that any change reported by the applicant that occurred before the eAPR, will be applied to the CRS score (so, changing a spouse from non-accompanying to accompanying will change the CRS points, but adding a new spouse from a marriage after eAPR will not change points). For a change that occurred and was reported after the eAPR, the change will only impact the assessment of the eligibility. If the applicant no longer meets the minimum entry criteria (MEC) requirements for the program under which they are applying during the processing of their file, the application may be refused and no PR visa will be issued. Meeting the MEC requirements is mandatory for Express Entry applications.

Thank you for your email correspondence to Immigration, Refugee 's Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
It is not possible to submit an application for permanent residence under any of the immigration programs now managed through Express Entry without being invited to do so as a candidate in the Express Entry pool.
Therefore, only those candidates who meet the eligibility criteria for entry into the Express Entry pool and who receive an Invitation to Apply from IRCC are able to apply through the electronic application for permanent residence (eAPR).
Substituted evaluation for the Federal Skilled Trades Class cannot be used to overcome a prospective candidate's failure to meet minimum entry criteria in the creation of an Express Entry profile. An Express Entry profile is not an application. As per subsection 5(2) of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system, there is no provision for substituted evaluation governing the submission of an expression of interest (i.e. Express Entry profile) to immigrate to Canada.
This means that substitution of evaluation under IPRP 87.2(4) may only be considered in limited circumstances by an officer for applications made under Express Entry (i.e. a change in circumstance after an applicant has been deemed to meet the minimum requirements of the program to which they have been invited to apply and the requirements of section 11.2 of
IRPA).

[I know the maximum is 180 days during each calendar year and, of course he must stop working if extension of study permit is refused]. In July, 2018 he receives (assumed) a new study permit which is valid for whole duration of his new program of study which will starts January 1st.,2019. Since the break/gap between 2 program of studies exceeds 150 calendar days (the initial program of study was completed in March 31st., 2018 and new new
program will start in January 1st.,2019, he must stop working from August 31st. 2018.

Please note that the application for visitor status will not be in replacement of the study permit extension that presumably they will get an approval for, it will be in adjacent to it, merely to provide status for the applicant before the beginning of their new program. Question:
Our question is about minor children extending their temporary status, when already in Canada, to enable them to study in high school. The children are accompanying their mother in Canada. All of them are USA citizens who entered Canada as visitors, but no visitor records were issued to them. The mother continues to holds a valid visitor status, authorizing her to visit with her Canadian husband, while their overseas spousal application goes through the processing queue. However, she is not authorized to study or work without a permit. The children are also included in the sponsorship application. On extension of their temporary status would these minor children require a study permit to attend high school in Canada or can

In addition, if they should apply for a study permit, can they apply inland and what application forms should be used in this case?
Answer:
As per the information on our website ([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/prepare/minor-children/need-permit.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/prepare/minor-children/need-permit.html)), the minor children described in the scenario above require a study permit to study in Canada.
According to A30(2), only minors in the following situations are authorized to study without a study permit (at the pre-school, primary or secondary level):
- they are either accompanying parents claiming refugee status or are claimants themselves;
- one of their parents (biological or adoptive) is a Canadian citizen or permanent resident;
- one of their parents (biological or adoptive) is authorized to work or study in Canada; this includes temporary residents who are o work permit holders, o study permit holders, o visitor status holders (e.g., visitor record holders) who are either authorized to work without a permit, as per section 186 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), or authorized to study without a permit, as per section R188; or
- neither parent is physically in Canada.
As the children in question are minors already in Canada, and will attend secondary school, they are eligible to apply from within Canada. see the information at the following link: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/application-change-conditions-extend-your-stay-canada-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/application-change-conditions-extend-your-stay-canada-) student.html

threads.subject: Owner Operator Work Permit & Express Entry Points-REP-2018-0658 -
threads.question:
### Dear Sir / Madam,
Does employment in Canada under an owner/operator permit in Canada award an express
entry candidate additional CRS points under the experience in Canada transferability factor
or under the arranged employment (50 or 200) points? Thank you.
mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox. We hope that you will find the answer to your question below of assistance.
Question Does employment in Canada under an owner/operator permit in Canada award an express entry candidate additional CRS points under the experience in Canada transferability factor or under the arranged employment (50 or 200) points?
Answer: In cases where a candidate is the owner and employee of the business for which they have a qualifying job offer as per paragraph 29 (2) (a) of the Express Entry Ministerial Instructions (MIs), it is possible that the candidate may receive 200 additional Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points for arranged employment in a NOC 00 or 50 points in NOC O, A or
B. However, work in Canada by the owner of the company may be considered "self-employed" work. As per our Program Delivery Instructions which are published on our IRCC website as a courtesy to stakeholders, IRCC officers consider the following factors in determining whether an applicant is considered an employee or self-employed:
- the degree of the worker's control or autonomy in terms of how and when work is performed, and the method(s) used to do the work;
- whether the worker owns and/or provides tools and equipment to accomplish the work;
- the degree to which the worker has to perform the work personally and whether the worker has the option of subcontracting work or hiring others to help and assist with completing the work;
- the degree of financial risk assumed by the worker, including whether the worker is required to make any investment in order to complete the work or provide the service and whether the worker is free to make business decisions that affect his/her ability to realize a profit or incur a loss (as opposed to the opportunity to earn commissions or other productivity bonuses); and
- any other relevant factors, such as written contracts. The onus is on the applicant to satisfy the officer that an employee-employer relationship exists as part of the eligibility requirement. Should the candidate be considered self-employed, it would not necessarily preclude him/her from claiming arranged employment in Express Entry, this would experience would not allow them to meet the minimum requirements for the Canadian Experience Class (CEC). Pursuant to paragraph 15(7)(b) of the MIs and paragraph 87.1(3)(b) of the Regulations, periods of self-employment do not count for purposes of CRS points for "Canadian work experience" or meeting the work experience requirement under the CEC. The candidate might, as per paragraph 75(2)(a) of the Regulations, qualify under Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) program if he/she has one year of continuous work as a self-employed person to meet the minimum requirements for FSw.
Please visit this link regarding information about arranged employment.
The applicant must submit the necessary documentation specified in the document checklist to substantiate that they have a valid offer of employment. This must include a letter of offer from the employer in Canada with the following details: •expected start date,
•commitment that the applicant will be employed on a continuous, paid, full-time work,
•for work that is for at least one year after issuance of a permanent resident visa, job title, •duties and responsibilities, •current job status (if current job), •number of work hours per week, and
- annual salary plus benefits. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation in support of their application. Any documentation that is available should be submitted, if applicable. Please be advised that the assessment of an individual's employment status is undertaken on a case-by-case basis, considering their particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Response:
Note that there is no experience requirement for C20, this LMIA exemption was not created with the intention to facilitate foreign nationals who do not meet the eligibility criteria of the Intra-Company transferees program (LMIA exemption code C12). threads.answer:

Question:
Can you provide guidance on the availability of a work permit extension in the following circumstances?
ABC Canada Co has operations in Canada and is the parent company of two subsidiary companies with operations in the US and India: ABC US Co and ABC India Co. ABC India Co was sold in 2018 and is no longer a part of the family of companies. ABC US Co continues to be owned by the same parent company.

1)Can she be issued an extension of her work permit, or does the sale of the transferring employer in India affect her eligibility for an extension? You can assume she continues to meet all of the other requirements.

In any event, it's not clear if the continuing existence of another foreign entity can be relied on for an extension in this situation.
Response:
Under the intra-company category and corresponding LMIA exemption [R205(a)] (exemption code C12), renewals of the work duration can be provided under certain circumstances. As indicated in program information, there must be a qualifying relationship between the Canadian and foreign entity and the continual operation of the foreign company. Also, the existence of the US subsidiary does not provide the basis for an extension given the current scenario. However, if the foreign national can obtain employment with the US subsidiary as well as meet all program requirements, including at least one year of experience, a transfer back to the Canadian company may be possible.

The IRCC webpage describing the GSS 15/30 day work permit exemptions states:
The work permit exemption may be for 15 or 30 consecutive days if the foreign national intends to perform work in an occupation that is listed in skill type 0 (management occupations)or skill level A in the matrix of the NOC,

Good Day,
Question:
Because 00 (double zero) skill types are not listed, does this mean that 00 NOCs (i.e. 0013, 0015, 0016) are not included in the exemption? e Response: Yes, NOC codes which start with double zero are included in the short-term work permit exemption. The first digit of the NOC code designates the Skill Type. For example, Management Occupations, which are found across all Skill Types, start with the digit 0. Occupations in health occupations start with the digit 3. Management occupations classified as Skill Type 0, span all other Skill Types from 1 through 9 of the classification structure, and are found in all areas of the labour market. All NoC codes that begin with a zero represent
management occupations. When the second digit is also zero, this represents "senior" management occupations. To
identify all other management occupations, the second digit (1 through 9) corresponds to management within each
Skill Type. To illustrate this concept, let us look at the following:

- Now consider a NOC code that has a zero as its first and second digit. Similar to the example above, we know that this occupation is a management occupation because it begins with zero. We also know that the second digit for management occupations reflects the Skill Type. However, because there is no Skill Type 0, we can conclude that this is a senior management occupation.
Management occupations are at the top of all organizational hierarchies. These occupations are characterized by high levels of responsibility and are also included in Skill Level A. Hope this answers your question.

(a) studied in Canada at a Canadian educational institution;
(b) was enrolled in full-time study or training for at least eight months; and

(a) a degree, diploma, certificate or trade or apprenticeship credential from a Canadian public post-secondary institution or from a Canadian private post-secondary institution that operated under the same rules and regulations as a Canadian public post-secondary institution;
(b) a diplôme d'études professionnelles (DEP) or an attestation de spécialisation professionnelle (ASP) earned through a program of study of at least 900 hours from a private secondary or post-secondary institution in Quebec; or
(c) a Bachelor's, Master's or doctoral degree from a Canadian private post-secondary institution, if a provincial statute authorizes that institution to confer that credential. Exceptions
(5) For the purpose of this section, the following are not eligible credentials:

As per our Program Delivery Instructions which are published on our IRCC website as a courtesy to stakeholders, IRCC officers consider the following factors in determining whether an applicant is considered an employee or self-employed: the degree of the worker's control or autonomy in terms of how and when work is performed, and the method(s) used to do the work; whether the worker owns and/or provides tools and equipment to accomplish the work; the degree to which the worker has to perform the work personally and whether the worker has the option of subcontracting work or hiring others to help and assist with completing the work; the degree of financial risk assumed by the worker, including whether the worker is required to make any investment in order to complete the work or provide the service and whether the worker is free to make business decisions that affect his/her ability to realize a profit or incur a loss (as opposed to the opportunity to earn commissions or other productivity bonuses); and any other relevant factors, such as written contracts. The onus is on the applicant to satisfy the officer that an employee-employer relationship exists as part of the eligibility requirement. Should the candidate be considered self-employed, it would not necessarily preclude him/her from claiming arranged employment in Express Entry, but this experience would not allow them to meet the minimum requirements for the Canadian Experience Class (CEC). Pursuant to paragraph 15(7)(b) of the MIs and paragraph 87.1(3)(b) of the Regulations, periods of self-employment do not count for purposes of CRS points for "Canadian work experience" or meeting the work experience requirement under the CEC. The candidate might, as per paragraph 75(2)(a) of the Regulations, qualify under Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) program if he/she has one year of continuous work as a self-employed person to meet the minimum requirements for FSW. Please visit this link regarding information about arranged employment. The applicant must submit the necessary documentation specified in the document checklist to substantiate that they have a valid offer of employment. This must include a letter of offer from the employer in Canada with the following details: expected start date,
commitment that the applicant will be employed on a continuous, paid, full-time work, for work that is for at least one year after issuance of a permanent resident visa, job title, duties and responsibilities, current job status (if current job), number of work hours per week, and annual salary plus benefits.
The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation in support of their application. Any documentation that is available should be submitted, if applicable.
Please be advised that the assessment of an individual's employment status is undertaken on a case-by-case basis, considering their particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer.

migration, Refugees

threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your question.
One of the conditions imposed upon employers under R209.2 states that "the employer must provide the foreign worker with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as, but not less favourable than, those in the same offer [R209.2(1)(a)(iii)]."
"Substantially the same-but not less favourable -wages" means that:
* Wages paid cannot be less than those outlined in the Offer of Employment provided as per R209.11
* Any unusual deductions (such as recovery of employer compliance fee, transportation costs, etc.) should be stated in the Offer of Employment Therefore, wages paid cannot be less than those outlined in the offer of employment, nor can they be substantially higher, as the employer may have been able to hire a Canadian or permanent resident if higher wages had been advertised in the first place. For both the Temporary Foreign Worker Program and International Mobility Program, "substantially higher" generally means higher than the rate of inflation or 2% per year, whichever is higher. A: Visa-exempt nationals coming to Canada who only need an eTA for their travel are not required to give biometrics. If they need a study or work permit, they will need to give biometrics.

Good morning,

Generally, a person charged with or convicted of a summary offence is not prevented from being granted Canadian citizenship, except in the following situations: Charges or convictions for summary offences under subsection 21.1(1) or 29.2(1) or (2) of the Citizenship Act do prohibit a person under paragraph 22(1)(b) and subsection 22(2). threads.question:
From # Hello ImmReps,
I am looking for clarification on declaring a legally separated spouse on the eAPR application post ITA.
An applicant is legally separated from their spouse (the one and only marriage for the applicant). No children. There is a court proceeding that is ongoing at the time the EE profile is created and an ITA is issued. The EE application included only 1 applicant.The marriage was dissolved as the IRCC was reviewing the eAPR. A copy has been provided to the IRCC office.
In "Marital Status" question, the applicant answered Legally Separated. The Applicant provided court documents showing the divorce proceedings. In "Has the Applicant been previously married or in common-law" the applicant answered No (there was no other marriage other than the one that is currently being dissolved)
How should the Applicant answer in the section "How many family members does the Applicant have? (This includes the Applicant, a spouse or partner, dependent children and their dependent children)? The Applicant is legally separated and the marriage is being dissolved as the application is processed.
Given the above fact scenario, could you advise when and how the legally separated foreign spouse while the couple is in the divorce proceeding could be disclosed. Please advice whether indicating in the cover letter that the divorce proceedings are ongoing and the spouse is not included in the forms is sufficient to satisfy the IRCC requirements.
Thank you in advance!
mmigration, Refugees
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox. We hope that you will find the answer to your question below of assistance.
Question 1: How should the Applicant answer in the section "How many family members does the Applicant have? (This includes the Applicant, a spouse or partner, dependent children and their dependent children)? The Applicant is legally separated and the marriage is being dissolved as the application is processed.
Answer 1: Applicants should include all accompanying and non-accompanying dependants in the number of their family members. All dependants must be declared and examined. As such, associated documents (Medical Exam, custody documents if applicable) will be required to submit the APR. Estranged partners from whom an applicant is legally separated would not usually be considered part of their family.
Question 2: Given the above fact scenario, could you advise when and how the legally separated foreign spouse while the couple is in the divorce proceeding could be disclosed. Please advice whether indicating in the cover letter that the divorce proceedings are ongoing and the spouse is not included in the forms is sufficient to satisfy the IRCC requirements.
Answer 2: For immigration purposes, the definition of legally separated means that the client is married, but no longer living with his/her spouse. In this case, a client should select legally separated for their marital status in the Express Entry system. The onus is always on the client to provide sufficient documentation in support of their application. The client will therefore need to submit a letter of explanation and any documentation when submitting the complete electronic application for permanent residence to support their marital status, such as but not limited to:
- a signed formal declaration that the marriage has ended and that the person has entered into a common-law relationship
- a separation agreement
- a court order about custody of children substantiating the marriage breakdown
- documents removing the legally married spouse(s) from insurance policies or wills as beneficiaries (a "change of beneficiary" form) This will ensure that the system does not request the client's ex-spouse's information, that the client's ex-spouse will not be examined and, therefore, is not a member of the family class. For changes in applicant's circumstances such as a change in address, births, deaths, marriages, divorces, adoptions, changes in employment or urgent requests, please inform IRCC by using the Case Specific Enquiry Web Form: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp) Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Inbox

threads.subject: Requesting consideration of a work permit application under C10 where also requesting another exemption code or where an LMIA is in process - (REP-2018-1060) - REP-2018-1180 - due 17-Aug-18
threads.question:
From Dear Officer,
I thank you for your detailed and thoughtful reply.
I hope that you will permit me a follow-up question. I fail to see the statutory underpinning for the position taken by the Minister. The TFW and IMP are separate programs just as, arguably, the family (or economic) permanent residence and humanitarian and compassionate permanent residence programs are. Yet, it is well-established that once a request is made for consideration under A25(1), an officer is in most situations obliged to consider those submissions.
In the context of work permits, a general C10 exemption request based on economic or cultural benefit can function in a way similar to a request under A25(1). For example, there not infrequently arises situations where an employer may be awaiting an LMIA, a provincial nomination or a CSQ and their employee's work permit is coming to its expiration date. In those situations, IRCC has generally allowed applicants to submit the missing LMIA, PN certificate or CSQ after the initial WP application. In fact, the online application expressly accounts for this possibility. Given the uncertainties as to processing time or even the outcome of the LMIA, PNP or CSQ application, an employer may wish to ensure that the officer considers a C10 exemption for key employees, where appropriate. The C10 guidelines expressly provide for approvals in appropriate cases to allow a TF W to get an LMIA, for example.
While I can understand that an IMP application requires payment of the compliance fee and submission of an offer of employment that are not required for a TFW application, an application offering alternate exemptions for consideration requires only the possibility to indicate these on the application form and the employer's offer of employment. The only difficulty in doing this is that IRCC's forms and employer portal do not provide the option. This is a choice made by IRCC that I do not believe to be supported by legislative authority. Even in the case of the IMP alternative to a TFW application, all that would be required would be the possibility to pay
As the examples provided above show, absent a functioning crystal ball, it is often impossible for an employer and a temporary foreign worker to know at the time of application which LMIA exemption is best suited to their case. That is exactly why the possibility to submit alternative exemptions is so important.
I emphasize that many LMIA exemption codes exist under the authority of a single section of the IRPR-for example C10 and A75 exemptions both are supported by R205. Why then should it be impossible to refer to multiple exemption codes that are both created under the same section of the IRPR?
I look forward to your reply.
Sincerely,
On Thu, Jul 19, 2018 at 3:53 PM,
migration, Refugees
ormation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
wrote: Greetings,
Please find our response to your questions below.
Question 1 - whether it is IRCC's position that a TFW may request consideration of an application to extend his or her work permit either under multiple LMIA exemption codes or under both an LMiA-exempt basis and supported by an LMIA? Answer-Negative ? Question 2 - whether to do so would require a separate job offer for each exemption code to be submitted by the employer with payment of a compliance fee for each offer? Answer-Affirmative Question 3 - whether each exemption code or the LMIA and the LMIA-exempt basis for the application would have to be submitted as a separate application to extend the work permit? Answer-Affirmative Question 4 - if your responses to question 1 is negative and to question 2 and/or 3 is affirmative, the statutory basis for these replies. Answer – The International Mobility Program (IMP) and the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) are two separate programs – the IMP manages the job positions in Canada that do not require a LMIA, while the TFWP oversees the LMlA-required streams. So, it would not be possible for one work permit application to involve the two programs at the same time, nor – under the IMP-to have more than one LMIA exemption for one job in Canada. That is why the Employer Portal does not support multiple LMIA exemption codes for the Offer of Employment.
The International Mobility Program does not allow applications under multiple LMIA exemption codes for the same offer of employment. You must consult IRCC online program guidance (Hire a temporary worker through the International Mobility Program, Find out if you need an LMIA) and select the exemption code that best applies to your situation, then submit the offer of employment through our Employer Portal and pay the employer compliance fee ($230).
Refer to the Employer Portal User Guide for assistance:
Explanation of how the job meets the requirements of the exemption being requested
Explain how the job being offered meets the LMIA exemption you chose. Your explanation must include what agreement (e.g. NAFTA) or requirement (e.g. NOC or significant benefit to Canada) exempts the job from an LMIA.
Make sure the information you provide is truthful and complete. We will use it to decide if the exemption requirements are met.
Note: If you wish to hire a foreign national from a visa-exempt country, and you need assistance in determining which
LMIA exemption code that is most relevant to the position you need to fill, you can contact the International Mobility Worker Unit (IMWU) for an opinion.
For the TFWP, you can find more information about LMIAs, application forms and employers' responsibilities on Employment and Social Development Canada's Temporary Foreign Worker Program web page.
We trust this information will be of assistance to you.
Thank you kindly The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your input regarding the current structure of the Temporary Foreign Worker and International Mobility Programs, specifically regarding the current functionality whereby the work permit application form and the Employer Portal allows for consideration of one category of LMIA-exempt/LMIA-required category for one employment position per application.
We will certainly consider this input during future policy and program reviews; however, (IRCC) does have some latitude to set the processes and procedures its officials deem appropriate for the proper, orderly, and efficient functioning of its operations.
In applying for a work permit, the onus is on the applicant to describe the position and duties that the job entails and, if applicable, to demonstrate that they are eligible for an LMIA exemption. By availing themselves of publically available immigration program delivery instructions, it is reasonable to expect that applicants are able to draw a line from a specific job position and its duties, to the particular LMIA-exemption that IRPR provides under the International Mobility Program..
IRCC processes approximately 100,000 LMIA-exempt work permit applications each year for the International Mobility Program. In the interest of keeping processing times as short as possible, so that applicants can receive their work authorizations in a timely manner, a degree of self-assessment is required on the part of the employer and applicant to determine whether an LMIA is required or, if not, which LMIA-exemption applies. It would not be feasible or operationally efficient to have officers assess each job position in each work permit application for its eligibility pursuant to each of the range of options provided for under the International Mobility Program. This would require review of multiple sets of documents and information, ultimately resulting in separate assessments, which would be extremely time-consuming. In addition, applicants might be compelled to provide fees, for example, for both an Open Work Permit Privilege Fee and the Employer Compliance Fee, just in case they qualify for multiple LMIA exemption streams. The officer would then need to refund either one of the fees depending on the chosen LMIA exemption – again, adding another layer to the processing time and level of complexity involved in the assessments.
The potential to further complicate matters and contribute to inefficient operations also exists. For instance, if an applicant applies for and meets the requirements for more than one exemption, which LMIA exemption stream should be chosen by the officer? IRCC could receive complaints from applicants if the applicants are of the opinion that we have picked the “wrong” LMIA exemption stream. For example, certain streams could benefit the clients more than others (such as facilitating clients to meet permanent resident eligibility requirements).
Thank you kindly
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
! ## Parent and subs-REP-2018-1153 - due 14-Aug-18
Hello,
If the foreign worker remains an employee of the parent company – that is, the employer/employee relationship, the pay, benefits, etc. which are linked to the position – then multiple work locations can be indicated on the offer of employment. When submitting an offer of employment in the Employer Portal, ensure that the physical job location entered is that of the parent company.
If there are two locations, answer “yes" to "Will the worker perform duties at more than one job location?" and complete the second job location section. If there are more than two locations, only complete the first job location section. List all other locations in the "Main duties of the job" field.
Ensure the foreign worker requests a work permit with no restrictions to employment location.
Please note that the work location is part of the employer conditions set forth under the compliance regime. Employers are responsible for ensuring that they meet these conditions, especially in a situation where an employer may have multiple work locations. Each location is subject to inspections by IRCC.
In the case of an LMlA-exempt work permit, there are two different sets of conditions involved – those imposed on the employer based on the offer of employment, and those imposed on the worker as per the work permit.
Employer conditions: location' is normally considered as part of the condition that the employer must provide the 'same working conditions.' The change in work location can't be less favourable to the employee. In addition, the location can't be changed if the location was part of the LMIA- exemption requirement/justification (e.g. provincial nominees). IRCC does not require proactive notification of changes, but it is required that the employer maintain any documentation regarding the changes and provide it as justification at time of inspection. Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the Voluntary Disclosure process.
Worker conditions: the foreign national may have specific conditions imposed on them with the work permit. These conditions may include 'not authorized to work at any other location'. If this condition is imposed and a specific location is specified then the worker would need a new work permit in order to change locations.
We hope this information is helpful.
Thank you kindly
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Clarification-Express Entry & CEC work experience-REP-2018-1164
threads.question:
To Whom It May Concern:
I would like to clarify the regulations regarding work experience that can be counted for Canadian Experience Class and Express Entry.
The occupation of "Apprentice Automotive Technician" is classified as NOC B (7321). The apprentice automotive technician performs the lead duties and majority of the main duties specified in the NOC.
When completing the Express Entry profile, the following statements appear: Date ------ first became qualified to practice in this occupation
If the "primary occupation" is:
- a qualified trade (four-digit code begins with 632, 633, 72, 73, 82, 92), this is the date they became qualified to practice on their own in Canada. (For example, when they moved from apprentice to being a licensed tradesperson.)
We will assess ----'s current and previous jobs for eligibility for Express Entry, and use them to calculate -----'s score. You can tell us about each job by filling in the fields below. Do not enter any work related to or performed during an apprenticeship process.
But IRPR s. 87.1(2) and (3) only requires that to be a member of the Canadian Experience class, the job experience must be obtained in Canada, duration of at least one year full-time or equivalent in part-time, in NOC A, B or 0, performed duties in lead statement and majority of main duties, it was not gained during full-time studies, as self-employed or as an unauthorized worker.
My questions are:
1. What date should be declared as the date person first became qualified to practice in the occupation of Apprentice Automotive Technician, if the next paragraph says that for job code 73, it is the date they are qualified to practice on their own and not as an apprentice?
2. What does the statement "Do not enter any work related to or performed during an apprenticeship process" mean? What if the work as an Apprentice Automotive technician was done after graduation and meets all the requirements of IRPR s. 87.1(2) and (3) for CEC?
3. Is 1-year full-time experience as an Apprentice Automotive Technician (NOC7321) eligible for Canadian Experience class?
Thank you in advance for your assistance.
Sincerely.
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
1. What date should be declared as the date person first became qualified to practice in the occupation of Apprentice Automotive Technician, if the next paragraph says that for job code 73, it is the date they are qualified to practice on their own and not as an apprentice?
The date on which the applicant became qualified to practice the trade on their own depends on the province. Certain provinces require trade certification in order to be able to practice the trade on your own. Other provinces do not require trade certification. In that case, the date on which the applicant became qualified to practice the trade would be after the completion of secondary school. Please refer to the "Employment Requirements" section on the NOC webpage for NOC 7321 in order to determine provincial requirements: [http://noc.esdc.gc.ca/English/noc/QuickSearch.aspx?ver=16&val65=7321](http://noc.esdc.gc.ca/English/noc/QuickSearch.aspx?ver=16&val65=7321)
2. What does the statement "Do not enter any work related to or performed during an apprenticeship process" mean? What if the work as an Apprentice Automotive technician was done after graduation and meets all the requirements of IRPR s. 87.1(2) and (3) for CEC?
Work experience gained on the basis of the candidate's status as a full-time student does not count under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC). The question asking the candidate to identify if they were a full-time student during a given period of work experience is therefore asked to screen candidates against the minimum entry criteria for this program. Any periods of work that are authorized on the basis of the candidate's status as a full-time student are not eligible under the CEC, regardless of whether the candidate was actively studying and in class during the period of work itself (i.e. work experience obtained on a co- op, apprenticeship or off-campus or on-campus work permit). Only skilled work experience gained post-graduation will be counted against the work experience requirement under the CEC.
3. Is 1-year full-time experience as an Apprentice Automotive Technician (NOC7321) eligible for Canadian Experience class?
It may be eligible for the Canadian Experience Class (CEC). If the applicant does not meet the employment requirements of NOC 7321 mentioned in the link provided above, then the officer may not be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the applicant meets the requirements of R87.1 of the CEC. The onus is on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation as proof that he/she acquired in Canada under NOC 7321,
within the three years before the date on which their application for permanent residence is made, at least one year of full-time work experience, or the equivalent in part-time work experience; during that period of employment they performed the actions described in the lead statement for the occupation as set out in the occupational descriptions of the National Occupational Classification; and, during that period of employment they performed a substantial number of the main duties of the occupation as set out in the occupational descriptions of the National Occupational Classification, including all of the essential duties.
I note that the NOC website does indicate "automotive service technician apprentice" as a title that can be held by someone who engages in the duties of NOC 7321. This title appears to be very similar to the title held by the applicant in question. In this case, as it is stated in the above, the onus would be on the applicant to demonstrate that he/she meets the minimum requirements for CEC even through he/she was an apprentice at the time.
We hope this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

In circumstances where a work permit is issued with a remark such as “authorized to work at locations across Canada as required by employer", is the employer required to notify IRCC of the mistake on the OOE?
What steps should employers be taking in these circumstances to maintain their obligations under the employer compliance head of the IMP?
Kind regards,
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your question about work location on the offer of employment.
First, please note that an officer cannot change the information in an offer of employment, even if it is deemed incorrect. The only way to correct an error in an offer of employment is for the employer to withdraw the offer and submit a new one with correct information.
With the implementation of the employer compliance regime, for all employer-specific work permits, there are 2 different sets of conditions involved:
1. those imposed on the employer based on the offer of employment
2. those imposed on the worker as per the work permit
When issuing work permits and imposing conditions, officers should try to ensure that the conditions imposed on the worker under section R185 match the conditions that will be imposed automatically on the employer under section R209.2.
Worker conditions: The foreign national may have specific conditions imposed on them with the work permit. These conditions may include "not authorized to work at any other location". If this condition is imposed and a location is specified, the worker will need a new work permit (including a new offer of employment in case of an LMIA-exempt work permit) in order to change locations. Employer conditions: "Location" is normally considered as part of the condition that the employer must provide the "same working conditions". The change in work location can't be less favourable to the employee. In addition, the location can't be changed if the location was part of the LMIA exemption requirement or justification (for instance, provincial nominees).
(IRCC) does not require proactive notification of changes, but the employer is required to maintain any documentation regarding the changes and provide it as justification at the time of inspection.
Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the voluntary disclosure process.
Thank you kindly

threads.answer:
immigration κepresentatives / Représentants immigration (IRCC)
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
Can a person on an LMIA owner/operator work permit, who puts himself on the payroll in the Canadian company
for one year or more, apply for CEC and be successful.
Answer:
Work in Canada pursuant to an LMIA Owner/Operator based work permit, is considered "self-employed work" and, as such, could disqualify them from the Canadian Experience Class due to the requirements indicated in R87.1(3) Of IRPR.
IRCC officers consider the following factors in determining whether an applicant is considered an employee or self-employed. You may wish to provide any type of document in support of the below listed items in order to strengthen your clients' cases as self-employed:
- the degree of the worker's control or autonomy in terms of how and when work is performed, and the method(s) used to do the work;
- whether the worker owns and/or provides tools and equipment to accomplish the work; the degree to which the worker has to perform the work personally and whether the worker has the option of subcontracting work or hiring others to help and assist with completing the work;
- the degree of financial risk assumed by the worker, including whether the worker is required to make any investment in order to complete the work or provide the service and whether the worker is free to make business decisions that affect his/her ability to realize a profit or incur a loss (as opposed to the opportunity to earn commissions or other productivity bonuses); and
- any other relevant factors, such as written contracts. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation in support of their application. Any documentation that is available should be submitted, including bank statements, third party references, invoices, etc., if applicable. Please be advised that the assessment of an individual's employment status is undertaken on a case-by-case basis, considering their particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. R87.1(3)of IRPR:

(a) any period of employment during which the foreign national was engaged in full-time study shall not be included in calculating a period of work experience;
(b) any period of self-employment or unauthorized work shall not be included in calculating a period of work experience; and

threads.subject: work permit case type 22 - REP-2018-1262 - due 5-Sep-18
threads.question:
From # Good morning.
I have a couple of minor children whose parent is stationed in Canada under the Visiting Forces Act. They were issued open work permits at the port of entry with case type 22. Could you please advise as to which regulations encompass case type 22 work permits, as it is unusual to find a minor child with a work permit?
Thank you in advance.
Kind regards,
threads.answer:
Hello,
Question:
Could you please advise as to which regulations encompass case type 22 work permits, as it is unusual to find a minor child with a work permit? Response: Under the terms of reciprocal agreements between Canada and 7 countries, family members— as defined in subsection R1(3) —of foreign military personnel stationed in Canada who themselves are exempt from work permits pursuant to R186(d), are work permit required but LMIA-exempt under R205(b) - C20. The work permit is fee-exempt.
Reciprocal agreements covering family members of military personnel are in place with Denmark, France, Germany,
Great Britain, the Netherlands, Norway and the United States. Family members of military personnel covered by reciprocal arrangements must seek approval from the Department of National Defence. The family member should be in possession of a 'letter of approval of employment' from the applicable DND official, acceptable proof of identity and relationship to the head of family and proof of the duration of
the official assignment in Canada.
If such approval is given, the family member may approach IRCC directly and request a work permit (R199). If the principal applicant is under the Visiting Force Act, the work permit is fee-exempt. The Case type code is 22, “official status”. I will draw your attention to the program delivery instructions related to Military personnel and family members. The instructions provide that an open work permit to family members of certain military personnel may be issued for a duration coinciding with the expiry of the military principal applicant's tour of duty. Prior to the issuance of an open or unrestricted work permit, an applicant must meet immigration medical requirements. Conditions as well as a definite period of stay may be imposed on work permits issued to family members, but when needed, an extension of status should not be withheld unnecessarily.
It should be noted that employment in most occupations is covered under provincial/territorial legislation that deals with labour and employment standards. Employers must comply with all the requirements in order to hire foreign workers and must also be aware of their responsibilities and obligations.
Minimum age for working in Canada differs between provinces/territories. For example, the minimum age for working in Ontario is 14 years for most types of work. However, 14-, 15-, 16- and 17-year-olds are not to be employed during school hours unless they have been excused from school attendance under provisions of Ontario's Education Act.
Thank you kindly
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
Our client is applying for PR and has received an ITA. The applicant holds an LMIA based under the owner/operator category. Can you please advise, if the applicant has arranged employment, given that they hold a valid work permit, is in Canada working and plans to continue for over 1 year. Or will they need to show settlement funds?
Essentially, do they need to show they meet LICO? And do they have arranged employment?
Answer:
Generally, you are not required to demonstrate settlement funds if you are applying under the Canadian Experience Class, or if you are authorized to work in Canada and you have a job offer. Specifically, in order to be exempt from the funds requirements of R76(1)(b)(i), the applicant must be awarded FSW points for arranged employment as per R82(a), (b) or (d) of IRPR. If the applicant meets the requirements of R82(a), (b) or (d), then the he/she is not required to demonstrate settlement funds.
Question:
If they do need to show settlement funds, can an irrevocable gift from a blood relative be used as an authentic source of this purpose?
Answer:
Yes, the gift may be used to meet the settlement fund requirements of R76(b)(i). The onus is on the applicant to satisfy the officer on balance that these funds are not borrowed and that they are available to the applicant.

threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam:
My name is a Calgary-based RCIC representing clients for applications before IRCC. I am seeking
nmigration, Refugees
clarification on IRCC's policy and the Regulations concerning eligibility for a spousal open work permit of a skilled worker.
The section 205(c)(ii) of the “Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (the Regulation)” pertains spousal open work permit eligibility requirements for spouses of skilled workers in Canada. IRCC's operational instructions and guidelines at [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/exemption-codes/public-policy-competitiveness-economy.html#skilled-workers, refers to specific situations where spouses of a bridging open work permit holder may apply for an open work permit.
The aforementioned section of "the Regulation" stipulates that the bridging open work permit holders must be performing work as a skilled occupation at NOC skill levels 0, A or B for their spouses to be eligible for an open work permit. No sections of the "Immigration and Refugee Protection Act", "the Regulation", or the IRCC's operational instructions and guidelines mentions about having a pending permanence residence applicatíon under economic stream as a requirement for spousal open work permit.
Background A client had an active permanent residence file under caregiver program that met R10 requirement. Subsequently, a bridging open work permit was applied for and issued to the client. The permanent residence application received refusal íater on, few months after issuance of the bridging open work permit.
With the bridging open work permit, the client started his job as a skilled worker in Canada. (the new job is not a care-giver position). With more than six months remaining on the bridging open work permit, the client and the spouse want to know if a spousal open work permit may be issued, so that the coupīe can earn living in Canada.
Question: Is the spouse eligible for an open work permit given that the client (BOwP holder) works in a full-time skilled position and has more than six months left on the BÓwP? (i.e. Will absence of an active, pending permanent residence application render ineligibility to spousal open work permit application despite the fact that the BOwP holder is working in a skilled job position?)
I would greatly appreciate if you could clarify IRCC's policy on this matter.
Sincerely,
threads.answer:
Good morning
Question:
Is the spouse eligible for an open work permit given that the client (BO WP holder) works in a full-time skilled position and has more than six months left on the BO WP? yes
(i.e. Will absence of an active, pending permanent residence application render ineligibility to spousal open work permit application despite the fact that the BO WP holder is working in a skilled job position?) no
Answer:
As per R205(c)(ii), the spouse or common-law partner of a skilled worker is eligible to apply for an open work permit (Labour Market Impact Assessment exemption code C41) provided the principal applicant meets the following criteria:
- The principal foreign worker must be doing work which falls within NOC Skill Levels 0, A or B;
- The principal foreign worker must hold a work permit that is valid for a period of at least six months; and
- The principal foreign worker and spouse must physically reside, or plan to physically reside, in Canada while working.
The spousal applicant should submit all the supporting documents, including
- a letter from the principal foreign worker's current employer confirming employment or a copy of their employment offer or contract; and
- a copy of the principal foreign worker's last three pay slips.
More information can be found on our website regarding eligibility for spouses of bridging open work permit (BO WP) holders.
We trust this information is helpful to you.
Regards,
