threads.answer:
Sent: ### #
Hello,
Question 1: With respect to non LMIA based work permits, is the employer obligated to file a new offer of employment when an employee receives a salary increase where there is no change in duties?
Answer
Providing a salary that is higher salary to the foreign worker than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC after the work permit was issued would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker – i.e. employer, occupation or location. [Note: that may be the reason for the cancelled application]
However, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the IRPR on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must:
be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made;
comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works;
provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer;
make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
The employer cannot amend benefit information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work
permit has been issued to the foreign worker.
Proactive notification to IRCC of inconsistencies surrounding working conditions, including salary and benefits, are not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions orprovide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC.
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker).
mmigration, Refugees
Typically, any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified asper subsection 203(1.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). An compliance inspection officer may find that a change in an employee contract that increases the salary is justified under R203(1.1) in that it is similar to a change in the provisions of a collective agreement, for example. Alternatively, an increase in wages may result in a finding that the employer did not provide “substantially the same" wages if the increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the LMIA-exemption that the work permit was issued, even resulting in the need for a Labour Market Impact Assessment. Additionally, wages paid that are higher than those in the offer of employment, it may indicate a change in duties that would mean a different occupation than offered.
In cases where the employer has promoted and, in effect, changed the foreign worker's duties from what was submitted in the Offer of Employment, the foreign worker must receive a new work permit prior to beginning the new duties – in this scenario, a new Offer of Employment would be required to be submitted along with the compliance fee. If a new work permit for the promotion or change in occupation has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non- compliance by the employer.
Question 2: What exactly does “Substantially the same, but not less favourable, wages" mean? If there is a salary increase does this mean that if the increase is substantially the same as the employee's old salary that the employer does not need to file anew offer of employment. If so what does IRCC consider to be substantially the same? 2%, 3% etc.
Answer
Per sections 209.2 and 209.3 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (Annex 1), International Mobility Program and Temporary Foreign Worker Program employers are subject to conditions over the period of employment for which the work permit was issued. The employer must provide the substantially the same, but not less favourable wages and working conditions, and the same occupation as set out in the offer of employment.
In addition, inspection Program Delivery Instructions ([http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/permit/compliance.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/permit/compliance.asp)) state the following with respect to changes in wage:
“Substantially the same – but not less favourable – wages” means that:
- Wages paid cannot be less than those outlined in the Offer of Employment provided as per R209.11
- Any unusual deductions (such as recovery of employer compliance fee, transportation costs, etc) should be stated in the Offer of Employment
Therefore, wages paid cannot be less than those outlined in the LMIA letter and annexes, nor can they be substantially higher, as the employer may have been able to hire a Canadian or permanent resident if higher wages had been advertised
in the first place.
For the Temporary Foreign Worker Program, “substantially higher” generally means higher than the rate of inflation or 2% per year, whichever is higher.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
FW: biometric for PR application-REP-2018-1397 -
Individuals applying for permanent residence will be required to provide biometrics and pay the corresponding fee each time they apply, even if they previously provided biometrics to support a temporary residence application or a different permanent residence application.
Permanent resident status in Canada provides many benefits and privileges, such as health care coverage; ability to live, work, or study anywhere in Canada; eligibility to apply for Canadian citizenship; and protection under Canadian laws, including the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. As such, we need to ensure that the person's identity, eligibility and admissibility have been assessed and verified before granting permanent resident status and the best time to do this is at the application stage.
Collecting biometrics again at the application stage is a means of identity verification. Fingerprint verification only occurs at the port of entry and permanent residence applications are often made outside Canada. If a person provided their biometrics in the past, we can compare the newly submitted biometrics with the previous ones to ensure that they are the same person.
If an individual has previously applied for permanent residence and the application was refused, abandoned or withdrawn, any biometrics provided to support this application will immediately cease to be valid.

threads.subject: Self-Employed Person-REP-2018-1367
threads.question:
Dear Madam/Sir:
For the self-employed person, would the applicant require a job offer? If not, they can apply directly for permanent residence with their family?
Also, in regards to the definition of athletics, can an applicant who is a trainer of a national team, be qualified? Is there also a financial amount, the applicant has to declare?
Thank you.
-- Best,
threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
For the self-employed person, would the applicant require a job offer? If not, they can apply directly for permanent residence with their family?
There is no requirement to produce a job offer for an applicant in the self-employed stream. However, a self-employed applicant must demonstrate the intention and the ability to create his/her own employment in Canada through cultural activities or athletics. The applicant will have the opportunity to describe the occupation in which he/she intends to be self-employed in Question 10 of Schedule 6A which can be found in the Instruction Guide on our public website. The intent of the Self-Employed Persons Class is to bestow permanent residence to applicants who will enrich Canadian culture and athletics.
All accompanying and non-accompanying family members must be included in the permanent residence application. Failure to do so may cause delays and /or have other negative consequences on the processing of your application. Also, the applicant will not be able to sponsor his family members in the future if they are not added to the application.
Question:
Also, in regards to the definition of athletics, can an applicant who is a trainer of a national team, be qualified? Is there
also a financial amount, the applicant has to declare?
A trainer can be qualified to apply under the self-employed stream as long as they meet the requirements of R88(1) of IRPR. It is the discretion of the officer to determine if the declared experience falls under self-employment in athletics or participation at a world class level in athletics.
The decision is left to the discretion of the officer who must consider an applicant's experience, intent and ability to create their own employment in Canada. This also includes a person's financial assets, as a measure of intent and ability to establish economically in Canada, as there is no minimum investment for a self-employed person. The capital required depends on the nature of the work. Applicants must have sufficient funds to create an employment for themselves, to support themselves and their family members. They must show that they have been able to support themselves and their family through their talents, and that they would likely continue to be able to do so for at least one year after they arrive in Canada.
In addition, all applicants must declare any amount above 10,000$ CAD being brought into Canada in the form of cash, documents that indicate property or capital payable to the applicant, or documents that guarantee payment of a set
amount to the applicant. Please refer to Instruction Guide.

threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
I had a client issued an ITA today. He had indicated in his EE profile that his started with his current employer in October 2017. His actual start date was October 1, 2017, and as such, he will have a year of Canadian work experience on September 30th. He also indicated several years of foreign work experience in his profile. His welcome letter to EE indicated he qualified for the FSWP, and not CEC.
His ITA indicates that he was selected under CEC. He was also given 35 points for having Canadian work experience. His points are 500.
I am a loss as to how to proceed. He will have the year of required work experience by the time we submit the e-APR, as it is not due until November 5, 2018. He has enough points even without the 35 points for the year of Canadian work experience. He meets the requirements of the Federal Skilled Worker Program (we can submit proof of settlement funds).
Is it necessary for this client to decline this ITA, and also the one he will receive in two weeks, and wait for an ITA to be issued after September 30th? Or can he submit his application after September 30th once he has the 1 year of work experience.
Basically, my question is whether the applicant must have the work experience at the time of the issuance of the ITA, or, at the time the e-APR is submitted.
Answer:
Section A11.2 stipulates that an applicant must meet the minimum requirements of the program for which they were invited at the time of ITA and at the time of submission of their application (e-APR). The officer processing the application will also verify that this is the case.
The Express Entry (EE) system does not take into account specific days but only calculates on the basis of declared year and month. Therefore, if the applicant indicates that they worked from OCT2017 to SEP2018, then the EE system will attribute CRS points for and recognize a year's worth of work experience. In addition, an officer must be satisfied on balance that the applicant did meet the minimum requirements of CEC at ITA and e-APR by cross analyzing the applicant's declarations and the evidence provided in the application. The onus is on the applicant to demonstrate that the minimum requirements are met at ITA and e-APR.
In a case such as your client's, at time of assessment, the IRCC reviewing officer will use their discretion when evaluating
nmigration, Refugees
Lon information and supporting documents in the application. If your client meets all other minimum requirements and the applicant indicated that the job was ongoing and that they now meet the requirements, the officer may consider that this meets the work experience requirement. However, if your client prefers to be sure of the outcome s/he may decline this round of invitation and wait for future rounds once the work experience meets CEC requirement.
References:
A11.2 of IRPA:
Visa or other document not to be issued
11.2 (1) An officer may not issue a visa or other document in respect of an application for permanent residence to a foreign national who was issued an invitation under Division 0.1 to make that application if— at the time the invitation was issued or at the time the officer received their application — the foreign national did not meet the criteria set out in an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(e) or did not have the qualifications on the basis of which they were ranked under an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(h) and were issued the invitation. Question:

Please note, that the candidate will still be employed by the same employer and will have at least 12 months of Canadian work experience at the time that their application is submitted 60 days after they obtained an ITA.

Answer:
Section A11.2 stipulates that an applicant must meet the minimum requirements of the program and the qualifications for which they were invited at the time of ITA and at the time of submission of their application (e-APR). The officer processing the application will also verify that this is the case.
The Express Entry (EE) system does not take into account specific days but only calculates on the basis of declared year and month. Therefore, if the applicant indicates that they started work on 01NOV2017 and they are invited on 01 OCT2018, then the EE system will attribute CRS points for and recognize a year's worth of work experience even though it is not day for day one year of work. threads.subject: Urgent Question-Do TRP holders require an eTA-REP-2018-1406-
threads.question:
Good Afternoon,
We would like some clarification as to who is exempt from the eTA requirement. The IRCC website indicates that individuals who hold a valid Canadian TRP do not require an eTA per /RPR subsection R7.1(2) and (3): Who does not need an eTA Subsections R7_1(2) and (3) describe individuals who are exempt from the eTA requirement They include the following
- individuals who hold a valid Canadian TRV or temporary resident permit (TRP)
However, IRPR subsection R7.1(2) and (3) does not list a TRP holder as exempt from having an eTA. Could you please advise which is correct?
Additionally, if a TRP holder requires an eTA, how do they go about getting one? Our experience is that the eTA applications are usually refused outright due to inadmissibility and a request for further evidence (such as a copy of the TRP) is not requested.
Your assistance is greatly appreciated.
Best regards.
threads.answer:
Good day,
Visa-exempt foreign nationals who have been issued a temporary resident permit (TRP) are not authorized to hold an eTA, as they have been found to be inadmissible to enter Canada. A11(1.01) states that an eTA can only be issued if the foreign national is 'not inadmissible and meets the requirements of the Act', so a TRP holder cannot be issued an eTA. Clients can receive an eTA in the future when they overcome their inadmissibility concerns.
Visa-exempt foreign nationals who have been issued a TRP by an overseas office to permit travel to Canada will be able to board a plane to Canada, so long as their TRP document remains valid and they have the appropriate travel document (e.g. a passport) in their possession. As per R7.1(1), foreign nationals referred to in R7(2)(a) are required to obtain an eTA when seeking to enter and remain in Canada, and as TRP holders are referred to in R7(2)(b), the eTA requirement does not apply to them.
A traveller issued a TRP at a port of entry does not require an eTA to enter Canada. An individual in possession of a TRP and who is in Canada can remain in Canada under the condition described in the TRP.
Sincere regards, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: prise de données biométriques
threads.question:
From # Bonjour,
Nous vous écrivons relativement à l’application de la nouvelle exigence concernant la prise de données biométriques. Nous avons examiné tous les sites internet à ce sujet autant de IRCC que de l’ASFC et avons appelé la frontière à plusieurs reprises sans ne recevoir de réponse à notre question.
Voici notre question :
Est-ce que dans la prise des données biométriques peut se faire à l’entrée au Canada à l’aéroport P-E Trudeau lorsque le candidat soumet sa demande de permis de travail en personne sur place (pour un pays dispensé de visa d’entrée)? Par exemple, est-ce qu’un français ayant reçu une préautorisation de l’Unité pour la Mobilité Internationale des Travailleurs (UMIT) de sa demande de permis de travail avec dispense d’EIMT peut soumettre sa lettre de préautorisation avec tout son dossier à son entrée à l’aéroport et procéder sur-le-champ à la prise des données biométriques?
Je comprends que si le candidat a en main la lettre lui demandant de procéder à la prise des données biométriques (avec le code-barres), il peut procéder à la prise de ses données à l’aéroport, mais qu’arrive-t-il s’il n’a pas sa lettre puisque sa demande est soumise au point d’entrée?
Dans le cadre de notre mandat à Montréal International, nous donnons des formations à un grand nombre d’entreprises de Montréal et nous voulons être certains de diffuser l’information exacte pour éviter un encombrement inutile de vos services.
Merci de votre aide.
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Ceux qui sont admissibles à présenter une demande de permis étudiant à un point d'entrée (PDE) peuvent soumettre leurs données biométriques au même moment. Si le demandeur est admissible à prés enter une demande à un PDE et doit donner ses données biométriques, il doit se présenter à un point d’entrée qui a l’équipement nécessaire pour faire la collecte de données biométriques. La biométrie sera prise au même moment. Cet outil peut être utilisé comme guide pour déterminer si la biométrie sera requise.
Donc, en ce qui concerne votre exemple, le demandeur que vous décrivez semble être éligible pour prés enter une demande à un PDE. Si ce dernier a l’intention de prés enter sa demande à un PDE et doit soumettre sa biométrie, il devra s’assurer de prés enter sa demande à un point d’entrée ayant l’équipement nécessaire pour la collecte, et ses données biométriques seront prises au même moment.
Nous tenons à clarifier que ceux qui ont en main la lettreleur demandant de procéder à la prise de données biométriques ne devraient pas se présenter à un PDE pour procéder à la prise de données biométriques. L’agence des services frontaliers a parfois fait des exceptions à cet égard, mais se réservele droit de refuser ce service aux clients d’IRCC, voir même de leur refuser l’entrée au Canada. Les demandeurs qui ont la lettre d’instructions pour la collecte de données biométriques devraient se prés enter à un CRDV, à un ASC ou à un bureau temporaire en Europe.
Cordialement, La boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration

Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
As per the operational instructions and guidelines regarding licensing and certification for the FSW program: The majority of licensing and certification requirements for certain occupations in Canada cannot be satisfied from outside of Canada. As such, visa officers should not penalize applicants for not meeting Canadian licensing or certification requirements. However, officers must be satisfied that the applicant is likely to accept and capable of performing the employment being offered to them, and can with reasonable probability be expected to qualify for licensing/certification once in Canada. In making this determination, visa officers may take into account the applicant's education and training, background, and prior work experience. If officers should have any concerns with respect to the applicant's ability to perform or likelihood to accept and carry out the employment being offered to them, the officer should communicate these concerns to the applicant and provide them with an opportunity to respond.
Please refer to the complete operational instructions and guidelines for the FSW program, found here: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/permanent-residence/economic-classes/federal-skilled-workers/post.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/permanent-residence/economic-classes/federal-skilled-workers/post.html).
During the period of employment used by the candidate as their skilled work experience, they must have: •performed the actions described in the lead statement for the occupation as set out in the occupational description of the
NOC [R75(2)(b)]; and
•performed a substantial number of the main duties, including all of the essential duties, of the occupation as set out in the occupational description of the NOC [R75(2)(c)].
Note: The applicant does not need to demonstrate that they meet the “employment requirements" listed in the NOC
occupational description.
Please refer to the Minimum Entry Criteria (MEC) for the FSW program to ensure your client meets all of the requirements before application submission: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/permanent-residence/economic-classes/federal-skilled-workers/assessing-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/permanent-residence/economic-classes/federal-skilled-workers/assessing-) applications-against-minimum-requirements.html.

Question:
If an applicant is currently living in Canada:

threads.answer:
Application-REP-2018-1358
Hellc
We are aware that we already sent you two responses but wanted to provide you with further clarification.
If completion of the "Supplementary Information-Your Travels (IMM 5562)" form is a requirement, an applicant should be listing any period they have left their country of origin which is usually also their country of residence.
A country of residence is the country in which an applicant habitually lives with the intent to make it a fixed or permanent home. Typically the applicant would be established and have recognized status in that country as a citizen, permanent resident or temporary resident (study/work). However, in the case of an applicant who has changed countries of residence in the last 10 years or since their 18th birthday, there should be an entry indicating the change in residence, and moving forward the client would have to list any trips outside of that new country including trips back to their country of origin or past residence.

threads.subject: Language test results-Express Entry/FSW -- REP-2018-1784
threads.question:
Dear Sir or Madam,
My understanding is that a valid test result from an approved language test will be considered for Federal Skilled Worker/Express Entry calculations. However, I would like to confirm if an applicant writes multiple exams, he or she is able to submit the best results and there are no restrictions to this approach. The alternatives, which I have not come across, would be:
1) The most recent results
2) The average of test results
omationddminc
I would like to know the official guidance for multiple language test results. I appreciate your time and attention to this question.
Kind regards,
Lnmanon
threads.answer:
Dear Ms.
Federal Skilled Worker applicants must demonstrate that they meet the required level of language proficiency in all four language skill areas by submitting the results of an English or French language test from a designated testing organization with their application.
In the case of applications received after January 1, 2015 (i.e., through Express Entry), language test results must be less than two years old when a candidate submits their Express Entry profile, and when their application for permanent residence is received.
Pursuant to paragraph R75(2)(d), the applicant must demonstrate that they meet or exceed the threshold set by the Minister for proficiency in either English or French for each of the four language skill areas: reading, writing, speaking and listening. The applicant must identify in their application for permanent residence which language—English or French—is to be considered their first official language in Canada. In order to claim points for proficiency in their second official language, the applicant must submit original language test results from a designated testing agency of their proficiency in that language with their application [R79(2)]. This requirement is made clear in the application guide; applicants will not be afforded an opportunity to provide official language test results at a later stage in the process.
If an applicant has multiple test results, they may submit only one set (reading, writing, speaking and listening) of test results as long as the tests meet the language testing requirements for Federal Skilled Workers.
Additional information about language-testing requirements is available on the immigration tab of the Canada.ca website.
Thank you for your interest in Express Entry. I hope that this information is helpful.
Regards, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Caregiver Pathway-Vacation Clarification -- REP-2018-1757
threads.question:
To Whom It May Concern:
I would like to get clarification on the allowable vacation to be counted for the Caring for Children/High Medical Needs Class.
Scenario: A caregiver's contract entitles her to 10 days of paid vacation in a year (52 week period), to comply with the
conditions of the provincial labour code and the LMIA.
If the caregiver decides to take her vacation at the end of her contract, can she submit her application for PR earlier? Specifically, someone who started working full-time as a child caregiver from April 15, 2017 would accumulate 24 months of full-time work by April 14, 2019, including her vacation days.
If she decides to bank all her vacation days and take it on March 17, 2019 to April 14, 2019, she would have completed her work requirements by March 17, 2019, since the last 4 weeks of her 24 month contract is taken as vacation.
The caregiver above would have worked full-time from April 15, 2017 to March 17, 2019 without any vacation taken (24 months less 20 days or 4 weeks of vacation). As ofMarch 17, 2019, she would have accumulated 100 weeks of consecutive full-time work.
In comparison, a caregiver who took her vacation in 2018 and 2019 would work the same number of weeks (100 weeks) albeit accumulating this only on April 14, 2019, a full 24 months from her job start date.
Questions:
- Will working 100 consecutive weeks (compared to 104 weeks) without taking any vacation be considered as equivalent to 24 months of full-time work since a caregiver is allowed to count a "reasonable period of vacation time" as per the Program Delivery Instructions?
- Will this caregiver be able to submit her application on March 17, 2019 and be considered as having met the 24 months qualifying work experience?
- Or will her work experience be considered as insufficient on March 17, 2019 (even if she will not be working from that day to April 14, 2019 - her 24 month mark), since it will be received by the processing office earlier than 24 months from her job start date?
Thank you in advance and I look forward to your response.
Sincerely,
threads.answer:
immigrauon Kepresentauves / Keprésentants immigration (IRCC)
Dear
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representative Mailbox.
In order to meet the requirements for the Caring for Children Class or the Caring for People with High Medical Needs classes, an applicant must demonstrate they have acquired 24 months of full-time work experience in Canada in one of the following NOCs: 4411, 3012, 3233, 3413, 4412.
An applicant would not satisfy the work experience requirement after completing 100 consecutive weeks of full-time work because while they may have completed the correct quantity of work (i.e. the number of weeks worked), they would have failed to meet the requirements for work duration (i.e. the number of months employed full-time in the eligible position). Both aspects are important in meeting the work experience requirement.
We do note that “a reasonable period of vacation time will be counted towards meeting the work experience requirement"’ and the applicant may take these two periods of two weeks paid vacation at any point during their two years of employment. However, in order for the vacation period to "count towards" meeting the work experience requirement, the period of vacation leave must have already taken place at the time of application for permanent residence. Therefore, in the scenario you described, the applicant may work 100 consecutive weeks (compared to 104) and chose to take their vacation during the final weeks of their employment, however, they will not be able to apply for permanent residence prior to completing the vacation as their work experience duration would be deemed insufficient.
We trust this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox.

threads.subject: Clarification on Persons Who May Apply at a Port of Entry --REP-2018-1935
threads.question:
Hello.
I am an RCIC ( and am writing for clarification relative to Persons who may apply for Work Permit at a port of entry.
The policy confirms that workers under R198 and R200 may apply for a Work Permit at the time of entry.
R198 stipulates that an FN may make application for a WP at the time of entry if they are visa exempt (they are not required to obtain a TRV prior to entry) and they are either LMIA exempt, hold an approved LMIA, are a green card holder or PR of Greenland or St. Pierre & Miquelon or applying as a Live-In Caregiver or under the SAWP.
R200 stipulates similar requirements as above however, the FN must first make application for a Work Permit before entering Canada. These are considered visa required applicants.
The IRCC operational bulletins to CBSA states the following:
However, if a person seeking entry into Canada meets the requirements of section R198 and section R200, their work permit application will be processed at the POE.
In the case where an FN holds a valid TRV with the notation "W-1" (worker) which was issued with “Employer A," I have the following questions:
1. Can that FN be processed for a new Work Permit with "Employer B” at the time of entry if the TRV remains valid?
2. If yes, must the new Work Permit be issued ONLY at a land border or can it also be issued at an international airport?
Your clarification would be greatly appreciated. Thank you!
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Hello,
If a client meets the requirements of R198 they can apply for a WP at the port of entry (POE).
R198(1) allows a person who is exempt from the requirement to obtain a temporary resident visa (TRV) to apply for a work permit at the POE. Taken together R190(3) and R198(1) allow for a foreign national (FN) to apply for the first or subsequent work permit at a POE as long as the FN has been initially authorized to enter Canada as a temporary resident and returns to Canada from the U.S. or St. Pierre and Miquelon by the end of the period initially authorized for their stay and any extension to it.
Note that the period of authorized stay is not the same as the validity of a FN's TRV. Being in possession of a valid TRV on its own would not enable the FN to benefit from this exemption if the period initially authorized for their stay, or any extension to it, has lapsed.
Finally, new work permits can be issued at all ports of entry including international airports.

threads.question:

My question is related to the meeting the financial minimum for the Parent Grandparent Program. Here is the scenario: The applicant currently has a family size of three (2017), last year (2016) he also had a family size of three but the year before that,
his family size was only two (2015). He meets the minimum financial requirement for a family size of three for the years 2017 and 2016 but did not meet it in 2015. Lnformon
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your inquiry.
In response to your question about how to calculate the family size when it has changed in the past few years.
The family size is calculated on the day on which the application is filed and the sponsor must advise IRCC (via the webform) of any change in the family composition. The size of the family determines the amount of income required to meet the sponsorship eligibility requirements.
The regulations require that the sponsor provides proof of income from the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) for the 3 consecutive taxation years immediately preceding the date of the sponsorship application to prove Minimum Necessary Income (MNI) can be met.
If the family size changes during the processing of the sponsorship application, the income requirements for each applicable year will also change.
fthe sponsor has received the Notice of Assessment (NOA) for 2018, the sponsor must provide NOA's from 2018, 2017 and 2016, and the income requirements would need to be met for a family size of three.
f the sponsor has not received the tax Notice of Assessment (NOA) for 2018, the sponsor must provide NOA's from 2017, 2016 and 2015. In 2017 and 2016, income requirements would need to be met for a family size of three and in 2015, income requirements would need to be met for a family size of two.

threads.question:
Thank you-that's very helpful!
Can you confirm if there are any parameters (in terms of length) around the break that is allowed between two programs of study? That is, we know that generally a study permit expires 90 days after program completion:
- If you finish your studies early, your permit will stop being valid 90 days after you complete your studies (no matter what day is printed on the study permit). ([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit.html)).
However, we also know that if a student has completed one program and been accepted into another one, they are allowed to work full-time for 150 days while they wait for the new program to start (insinuating that the study permit will remain valid past the 90 days of initial program completion):
You can work full time if you
- were eligible to work off campus during your previous program of study
- have a valid study permit, or you applied for a study permit extension before your study permit expired
- received a written confirmation from your current institution that you completed your program
- were issued a letter of acceptance to a new program of full-time study at a DLl and •will be starting your new program within150 calendar days of receiving confirmation that you completedyour previous program
([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/work-off-campus.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/work-off-campus.html)).
I'm wondering if there are any parameters about how long the break between two programs can be before it might impact the student's ability to combine them for a PGWP.
Thank you!
threads.answer:
## Good day,
There is no limit to length of a break, but the second program must be completed within two years of the first to be combined when determining PGWP validity duration.
While there is no limit to the length of the break, the second program must be completed within two years of the first to be combined when determining PGWP validity period. Since the second program must also be at least 8 months in duration to be PGWP-eligible, students should ensure they will complete the second program within two years if they are planning to take a break from studies.

Answer:
The requirement to obtain an educational credential prior to accumulating work experience depends on the NOC identified by the applicant. The job requirements for certain occupations require applicants to have their educational credentials before they practice in the occupation. If the applicant declares working in an occupation which requires an educational credential without first obtaining that credential, then the officer may not be satisfied on balance that the applicant meets the duties or lead statement of the identified NOC. The onus is always on the applicant to demonstrate that they meet the job requirements for the NOC identified in their application.

threads.subject: In Canada-Common-Law-Spousal --REP-2018-1993
threads.question:
Hello, The CIC checklist for common-law states “If you are applying under the Family Class, you need to show that you
previously cohabited in a common-law relationship for a minimum of 12 months"
Scenario: Couple lived together for 1 year, had a break of a couple months because the sponsor had to finish studies and are now residing together again in Canada.
Question: What is the amount of time that there can be a break in residing together for the In Canada – Spousal Common-Law Category?
Thank you
1*1 mation disclosed under the Access to Information Act
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your enquiry.
Common-law partners who submit an application under the Spouse or Common-Law Partner in Canada class must be able to establish that they have been living with their partner for at least 12 consecutive months in a marriage-like relationship. Periods away from each other of short and limited duration such as vacations or business trips are generally not viewed as a period living apart. With longer breaks in cohabitation, applicants must be able to satisfy an officer that there was a continuous common-law relationship. The circumstances of each application is assessed on its own merits, so applicants should ensure that thorough proof of their relationship is included with their application.
Please keep in mind that for common-law relationships, the longer the period of separation without any cohabitation, the more difficult it is to establish that the common-law relationship existed.
Trusting your concerns have been addressed,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
Hello,
I am hoping to clarify information regarding the language requirement for citizenship.
As you indicated below, completion of a course in Canada which is taught in either French or English may satisfy the language requirement. Does a person have to complete an educational program within any length of time, before the Citizenship application is submitted? For example, does completion of a program 6 years ago, acceptable to satisfy the language requirement? The website does not provide guidance on this question.
Thank you,
Hello,
We apologize for the delay in responding to your enquiry.
Your client can submit other forms of language evidence other than what is shown on our website, here: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-0002-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/application/application-forms-guides/guide-0002-) application-canadian-citizenship-under-subsection-5-1-adults-18-years-older.html#language and it will be considered.
Before taking an alternate course, it is recommended that your client verify with the instructor whether the results of the language training would give them the required language level to apply for citizenship. IRCC will try to verify the language proof that is sent to us. The application will not be processed and will be returned if the proof is:
not included with the application; in a language other than English or French; cannot be read; or cannot be verified
Once the applicant's file is referred to a local office, they will be scheduled for an interview where a citizenship official will assess how well they can speak English or French using the Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB). A citizenship officer will make the final decision on whether the applicant has adequate knowledge of English or French, despite the language evidence submitted upfront with the application.
Please see additional responses to your questions shown below in red.
Thank you kindly
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
threads.answer:
Hello,
There is no specified length of time for taking or completing a course in English or French prior to the submission of an application as having the ability to meet the required language level to apply for citizenship will vary for each applicant depending on their capabilities. If the applicant is confident that they have maintained the required language level or improved since taking a course six years ago then they should submit their language evidence.
